stem: A 72-year-old woman tripped at home and landed on her outstretched left arm. An X-ray in the emergency department shows a fracture through the surgical neck of the humerus. Pinprick sensation is reduced over a small patch on the outer aspect of the upper arm just below the point of the shoulder. Sensation in the forearm and hand is normal, and she can extend her wrist and fingers. Which nerve has most likely been injured?
why_correct: The axillary nerve winds around the surgical neck of the humerus, so it is vulnerable in fractures here and in anterior shoulder dislocation. It supplies deltoid and teres minor and gives sensation to the regimental badge area over the lateral upper arm. Reduced sensation in exactly this patch after a surgical neck fracture points to axillary nerve injury.
why_wrong: A. Radial nerve injury follows mid-shaft fractures and causes wrist drop, but her wrist extension is intact. B. The suprascapular nerve supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus and has no cutaneous area on the lateral arm. C. Long thoracic nerve injury causes winging of the scapula without arm numbness. D. Musculocutaneous nerve injury weakens elbow flexion and numbs the lateral forearm, not the shoulder.
pearl: Always test and document regimental badge sensation in surgical neck fractures and shoulder dislocations, both before and after any manipulation.
thinking: Fall onto outstretched arm ↓ Fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus ↓ Nerve that wraps around the surgical neck ↓ Numb patch over lateral upper arm: regimental badge area ↓ Axillary nerve
exam_trap: A, radial nerve — the best-known nerve injury with humeral fractures, but it follows mid-shaft fractures and causes wrist drop; her wrist extension is normal.
takeaway: Surgical neck fracture with a numb regimental badge area: axillary nerve injury.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 9 Oct 2026 (held pack H01). Do not return to the live bank.

presentation: Rheumatoid arthritis — escalation to biological therapy
stem: A 49-year-old man with seropositive rheumatoid arthritis attends the rheumatology clinic. Despite 6 months of combination treatment with methotrexate, sulfasalazine and hydroxychloroquine at optimal doses, he has multiple swollen, tender joints, persistently raised inflammatory markers and new erosions on hand X-rays. His disease activity score remains in the severe range. Tuberculosis screening is negative and he has no history of cancer or heart failure. What is the most appropriate next step?
correct_answer: D. A TNF inhibitor with methotrexate
why_correct: Severe active rheumatoid arthritis that has not responded to intensive combination conventional DMARDs is an indication for advanced therapy under NICE technology appraisal guidance. In a patient who has not previously had a biological drug, a TNF inhibitor such as adalimumab or etanercept, given with methotrexate, is the usual first choice. Screening for tuberculosis and other infections is completed beforehand, as here.
why_wrong: A. Rituximab is generally used after an inadequate response to, or intolerance of, a TNF inhibitor, or when TNF inhibitors cannot be used. B. Long-term steroids cause significant harm and do not adequately control erosive disease. C. Swapping one conventional DMARD for another is unlikely to help once combination therapy has failed. E. Joint injections relieve individual joints but do not control systemic erosive disease.
pearl: RA ladder: conventional DMARD (usually methotrexate) started early, short-term steroid bridging, then combination therapy, then a biological or targeted synthetic DMARD if disease stays active. Screen for TB and hepatitis before biologics.
thinking: Seropositive erosive rheumatoid arthritis ↓ Failed intensive combination conventional DMARDs ↓ Disease remains severely active ↓ Eligible for advanced therapy, TB screen negative ↓ TNF inhibitor with methotrexate
exam_trap: A, rituximab — it is a licensed biological drug for rheumatoid arthritis, so it tempts, but it is usually reserved for after a TNF inhibitor has failed or cannot be used.
takeaway: RA still severe after combination DMARDs: add a TNF inhibitor to methotrexate.

stem: A 29-year-old woman with antiphospholipid syndrome, diagnosed after two late miscarriages, stopped her warfarin a month ago. Over three days she develops abdominal pain, falling urine output with a rapidly rising creatinine, mottled skin over her legs, painful dusky fingertips and new weakness of her right arm. Imaging shows renal infarcts and a small cerebral infarct. Her platelet count is mildly low, her clotting screen and fibrinogen are normal, and the blood film shows no significant red-cell fragmentation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Thrombosis developing in three or more organs over a few days, in a patient with known antiphospholipid syndrome (here after stopping anticoagulation), is catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome. It is a rare but frequently fatal emergency caused by widespread small-vessel occlusion. Management is in critical care with anticoagulation, high-dose corticosteroids and often plasma exchange or intravenous immunoglobulin.
why_wrong: A. TTP causes a microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia with many red-cell fragments on the film, which are absent. B. DIC prolongs clotting times and consumes fibrinogen, but these are normal. C. HUS is usually diarrhoea-associated and features fragmentation haemolysis with renal failure. E. Vasculitis inflames rather than thromboses vessels and does not fit known antiphospholipid syndrome with multiple infarcts.
pearl: Antiphospholipid syndrome plus multi-organ thrombosis evolving over days = catastrophic APS. Treat aggressively in critical care: anticoagulation, steroids, and plasma exchange or IVIG.
thinking: Known antiphospholipid syndrome, anticoagulation stopped ↓ Rapid thrombosis in kidney, brain, skin and digits ↓ Normal clotting and no film fragments ↓ Not DIC or TTP ↓ Catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome
exam_trap: A, Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura — low platelets, renal impairment and neurological signs fit, but TTP requires a haemolytic anaemia with red-cell fragments, which this film lacks.
takeaway: Multi-organ thrombosis over days in antiphospholipid syndrome is catastrophic APS, a medical emergency.

stem: A 22-year-old woman in her first pregnancy attends the maternity day assessment unit at 37 weeks with a severe frontal headache and pain under the ribs. Her blood pressure is in the severe range on repeated readings, urine dipstick shows heavy proteinuria, and she has three beats of ankle clonus. The CTG is reassuring. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Oral nifedipine and home blood pressure monitoring with review in two days
options.B: Labetalol to control blood pressure and intravenous magnesium sulfate, then plan birth once stable
options.C: Enalapril to control blood pressure and diazepam for seizure prevention
options.D: Oral methyldopa and admission for bed rest with weekly review
options.E: Immediate category 1 caesarean section before treating the blood pressure

correct_answer: B. Labetalol to control blood pressure and intravenous magnesium sulfate, then plan birth once stable
why_correct: Severe hypertension with proteinuria, headache, epigastric or right upper quadrant pain and clonus is severe pre-eclampsia. Management is admission, blood pressure control (labetalol is first-line), intravenous magnesium sulfate to prevent eclamptic seizures, and planned birth, which is the definitive treatment, once the mother is stabilised. At term, birth should not be delayed.
why_wrong: A. Severe features need admission and seizure prophylaxis, not outpatient monitoring. C. ACE inhibitors are contraindicated in pregnancy, and magnesium sulfate, not diazepam, prevents eclampsia. D. Methyldopa is slow-acting, and expectant management is wrong with severe features at term. E. The mother must be stabilised before birth, as operating with uncontrolled blood pressure risks stroke.
pearl: Severe pre-eclampsia: control blood pressure first (labetalol, or nifedipine or hydralazine), give magnesium sulfate to prevent fits, then plan birth. Stabilise the mother before delivering the baby.
thinking: Pregnant with severe hypertension and proteinuria ↓ Headache, epigastric pain, clonus: severe features ↓ Risks are stroke and eclampsia ↓ Antihypertensive plus magnesium sulfate, then birth ↓ Labetalol and magnesium sulfate
exam_trap: E, Immediate category 1 caesarean section before treating the blood pressure — birth is the cure, so rushing to theatre feels decisive. But the fetus is not compromised, and operating before blood pressure is controlled and seizures are prevented puts the mother at risk.
takeaway: Severe pre-eclampsia: labetalol plus magnesium sulfate, stabilise the mother, then plan birth.

stem: A 66-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer is reviewed at home by the community palliative care nurse. His bone pain is controlled on modified-release oral morphine 45 mg twice daily, but he has occasional episodes of pain when he moves. He has no immediate-release morphine prescribed. What is the most appropriate as-required dose of immediate-release oral morphine?
why_correct: His regular dose totals 90 mg of oral morphine in 24 hours. The breakthrough dose of immediate-release oral morphine is usually one-tenth to one-sixth of the total daily dose, so 10–15 mg, rounded to a practical dose, is appropriate as required, with frequent use prompting review of the background dose.
why_wrong: A. 5 mg is below one-tenth of his daily dose and is unlikely to control breakthrough pain. B. 45 mg is a full twelve-hour dose and risks opioid toxicity. C. 30 mg is a third of the daily dose, well above the recommended range. E. 90 mg is his entire daily dose and would be dangerous as a single extra dose.
pearl: If more than two or three breakthrough doses are needed each day, review and increase the regular background opioid rather than relying on repeated rescue doses.
thinking: Modified-release morphine 45 mg twice daily ↓ Total daily dose 90 mg ↓ Breakthrough dose is one-tenth to one-sixth of the daily total ↓ Range roughly 9–15 mg ↓ 10–15 mg immediate-release morphine as required
exam_trap: B, 45 mg — it matches the dose on his prescription. But that is a twelve-hour dose; breakthrough doses are a fraction of the 24-hour total.
takeaway: Breakthrough opioid dose: one-tenth to one-sixth of the total 24-hour dose.

stem: A 72-year-old woman with advanced pancreatic cancer under the community palliative care team has worsening nausea. She feels full after a few mouthfuls, is bloated, and some time after meals vomits large volumes of undigested food, which briefly relieves the nausea. She is passing wind and opening her bowels, and has no colicky abdominal pain. Her calcium and renal function are normal. Which antiemetic is the most appropriate?
why_correct: Early satiety, bloating and large-volume vomiting that relieves nausea suggest gastric stasis (delayed gastric emptying), which is common with pancreatic cancer. Antiemetic choice in palliative care should match the likely mechanism, and a prokinetic such as metoclopramide is first-line for gastric stasis, provided there is no complete bowel obstruction or colic.
why_wrong: A. Cyclizine suits raised intracranial pressure, vestibular causes or bowel obstruction, and its anticholinergic effect can slow gastric emptying. B. Haloperidol is best for chemical or metabolic causes such as opioids, hypercalcaemia or renal failure. C. Ondansetron is mainly used for chemotherapy- or radiotherapy-related nausea and can slow gut transit. D. Lorazepam is for anticipatory or anxiety-related nausea, not gastric stasis.
pearl: Avoid giving metoclopramide and cyclizine together, as cyclizine's anticholinergic action opposes the prokinetic effect of metoclopramide.
thinking: Advanced pancreatic cancer ↓ Early satiety, bloating, large undigested vomits that relieve nausea ↓ Bowels working, no colic, normal biochemistry ↓ Gastric stasis ↓ Prokinetic: metoclopramide
exam_trap: A, cyclizine — it is a widely used first-choice antiemetic in palliative care. But its anticholinergic effect slows gastric emptying and worsens stasis; this cause calls for a prokinetic.
takeaway: Palliative nausea: match the antiemetic to the cause; gastric stasis needs metoclopramide.

stem: A 63-year-old man asks his GP whether a new tablet is worth taking. In the trial he has read about, 8% of people on placebo had a stroke over 5 years, compared with 4% of those taking the tablet. How many people need to take the tablet for 5 years to prevent one stroke?
why_correct: The absolute risk reduction is the difference in event rates: 8% minus 4% = 4%, or 0.04. The number needed to treat is the reciprocal of the absolute risk reduction: 1 divided by 0.04 = 25. So 25 people must take the tablet for 5 years to prevent one stroke.
why_wrong: A. This is the absolute risk reduction as a percentage, not the NNT. B. This would follow from an absolute reduction of 2%. C. This comes from wrongly using the 50% relative risk reduction instead of the absolute reduction. E. This would follow from an absolute reduction of 1%.
pearl: NNT = 1 divided by the absolute risk reduction (as a decimal). Always state the time period, because NNT applies over the trial duration.
thinking: Control risk 8%, treated risk 4% ↓ Absolute risk reduction = 4% = 0.04 ↓ NNT = 1/0.04 ↓ Answer: 25
exam_trap: C, 2 — the risk halves, so dividing by the relative reduction is tempting. But NNT uses the absolute difference, not the relative one.
takeaway: NNT is the reciprocal of the absolute risk reduction, over a stated time period.

stem: Researchers compare mothers of babies born with congenital heart disease with mothers of healthy babies. All mothers complete the same structured questionnaire, given by interviewers who do not know which group each mother belongs to, about medicines taken in early pregnancy. Mothers of affected babies report over-the-counter medicine use much more often, partly because they have spent months searching for a reason. What type of error is most likely?
why_correct: Recall bias occurs when cases and controls remember or report past exposures differently. Mothers of affected babies have searched their memories more thoroughly, so they report exposures more completely than controls. This systematic error is a typical problem of retrospective case-control studies and can create a false association.
why_wrong: A. Confounding needs a third factor linked to both exposure and outcome, which is not described. B. The problem is in how exposure is reported, not how participants were chosen. C. Interviewers were unaware of group status and used a structured questionnaire. D. Lead-time bias relates to screening and apparent survival, not exposure recall.
pearl: Recall bias is a case-control hazard: people with a disease, or their parents, search their memory harder for possible causes than controls do.
thinking: Case-control design asking about past exposure ↓ Cases report exposure more thoroughly ↓ Difference arises from memory and motivation, not true exposure ↓ Answer: recall bias
exam_trap: C, interviewer bias — questionnaires given by interviewers make this tempting. But the interviewers were blinded and used a fixed script; the difference comes from the mothers' recall.
takeaway: Cases remembering exposures differently from controls is recall bias — a case-control weakness.

stem: A cross-sectional survey of adults attending a health check finds that people with grey hair have a much higher rate of previous myocardial infarction than people without grey hair. A local newspaper reports that grey hair may damage the heart. Which concept best explains this association?
why_correct: A confounder is associated with both the exposure and the outcome and is not on the causal pathway. Age is linked to grey hair and independently to myocardial infarction, producing a spurious association between the two. Confounding can be handled by design (randomisation, matching, restriction) or analysis (stratification, adjustment).
why_wrong: A. A heart attack does not cause grey hair, so reverse causation does not explain this. B. Hair colour is observed, not recalled, so recall bias is unlikely. D. Nothing suggests the sample was unrepresentative in a way that creates the link. E. Effect modification describes an effect that differs between subgroups, not a spurious association.
pearl: A confounder links to both exposure and outcome and is not on the causal pathway. Age, sex and smoking are the classic culprits.
thinking: Grey hair associated with heart attacks ↓ No biological reason for grey hair to cause MI ↓ Age is linked to both grey hair and MI ↓ Answer: confounding by age
exam_trap: A, reverse causation — when an association looks implausible, reversing the direction is a tempting explanation. But a heart attack does not cause grey hair; a third factor, age, drives both.
takeaway: A third factor linked to both exposure and outcome that distorts the association is a confounder.

stem: A GP practice with 10,000 registered patients reviews its records for the year 2025. The practice manager counts the number of patients who were given a first-ever diagnosis of type 2 diabetes during that year. Which measure is being calculated?
why_correct: Incidence is the number of new cases arising in a defined population over a specified time period. Counting first-ever diagnoses over 1 year among registered patients measures incidence. Prevalence, in contrast, counts all existing cases, old and new.
why_wrong: B. Point prevalence counts all existing cases at a single moment, not new ones over time. C. Period prevalence counts all cases present at any time in the period, including long-standing ones. D. Attributable risk compares risk between exposed and unexposed groups. E. The standardised mortality ratio compares observed with expected deaths.
pearl: Incidence counts new cases over a period; prevalence counts everyone who has the condition. Prevalence roughly equals incidence multiplied by duration.
thinking: Defined population: registered patients ↓ Only first-ever diagnoses counted ↓ Over a set period of 1 year ↓ Answer: incidence
exam_trap: C, period prevalence — the measure covers a year, so 'period' sounds right. But period prevalence includes existing cases; only new cases define incidence.
takeaway: New cases in a population over a set time is incidence; all existing cases is prevalence.

stem: A 68-year-old woman tells her GP she has read that a new tablet 'cuts the risk of hip fracture by a third'. In the trial, 3% of women on placebo and 2% of women on the tablet had a hip fracture over 3 years. Which explanation of the benefit is most useful for her?

options.A: One in three women who take the tablet will avoid a hip fracture
options.B: About 3 women need to take it for 3 years to prevent one fracture
options.C: Her risk of hip fracture falls by 33 percentage points
options.D: Her risk falls by about 1 percentage point, so about 100 women need treating for 3 years
options.E: The one-third relative reduction is the best guide to her personal benefit

correct_answer: D. Her risk falls by about 1 percentage point, so about 100 women need treating for 3 years
why_correct: The relative risk reduction is one-third, but the absolute risk reduction is only 3% minus 2% = 1%. The number needed to treat is 1 divided by 0.01 = 100 over 3 years. Absolute figures convey the real benefit for an individual and support shared decision-making.
why_wrong: A. This misreads a relative reduction as the proportion of women who benefit. B. This uses the relative reduction to calculate NNT, which is incorrect. C. The fall is 1 percentage point, not 33. E. Relative figures exaggerate benefit when the baseline risk is low.
pearl: Relative risk reductions sound impressive when baseline risk is low. Convert to absolute risk reduction and NNT before advising a patient.
thinking: Risk 3% falls to 2% ↓ Relative reduction one-third, absolute reduction 1% ↓ NNT = 1/0.01 = 100 over 3 years ↓ Answer: absolute fall of about 1 point, NNT about 100
exam_trap: E, the relative reduction — it is the headline figure and is technically correct. But it overstates individual benefit when the starting risk is small.
takeaway: Explain benefit to patients in absolute terms and NNT, not relative risk reduction.

stem: At a journal club, an FY2 doctor presents a trial of a new anticoagulant. For major bleeding, the hazard ratio compared with warfarin is 1.12, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.94 to 1.33. How should this result be interpreted?

options.A: There is significantly more bleeding, because the hazard ratio is above 1
options.B: The result is significant, because the interval does not include 0
options.C: There is significantly more bleeding, because most of the interval lies above 1
options.D: The trial proves the two drugs have identical bleeding risk
options.E: The result is not statistically significant, because the interval includes 1

correct_answer: E. The result is not statistically significant, because the interval includes 1
why_correct: For ratio measures such as hazard ratio, relative risk or odds ratio, the value of no effect is 1. A 95% confidence interval that includes 1 means the result is not statistically significant at the 5% level. The width of the interval reflects the precision of the estimate.
why_wrong: A. A point estimate above 1 is not significant if the interval crosses 1. B. Zero is the line of no effect for differences, not ratios. C. Where most of the interval lies does not make it significant. D. A non-significant result does not prove equivalence; the trial cannot exclude a real difference.
pearl: Line of no effect: 1 for ratios (RR, OR, HR), 0 for differences. An interval crossing that line means not significant at the chosen level.
thinking: Ratio measure: hazard ratio ↓ Value of no effect is 1 ↓ Interval 0.94 to 1.33 includes 1 ↓ Answer: not statistically significant
exam_trap: D, identical bleeding risk — a non-significant result tempts candidates to conclude no difference exists. But absence of evidence is not evidence of absence; the interval still allows a real increase.
takeaway: For ratio measures, a 95% CI including 1 means not significant — not proof of no effect.

stem: A hospital guideline group is deciding whether to recommend a new antiemetic for preventing post-operative nausea and vomiting. Several types of evidence are available. Which should carry the most weight in judging whether the drug works?

options.A: A single large, well-conducted randomised controlled trial
options.B: A systematic review and meta-analysis of high-quality randomised controlled trials
options.C: A large prospective cohort study from several hospitals
options.D: A consensus statement from senior consultant anaesthetists
options.E: A detailed case series from a specialist centre

correct_answer: B. A systematic review and meta-analysis of high-quality randomised controlled trials
why_correct: For questions about treatment effectiveness, a systematic review and meta-analysis of well-conducted randomised controlled trials is the highest level of evidence. It pools data from several trials, increasing precision and reducing the influence of any single study. Individual trials come next, followed by observational studies, case series and expert opinion.
why_wrong: A. A single RCT is strong but ranks below a systematic review of several good RCTs. C. Cohort studies are observational and prone to confounding. D. Expert opinion is the lowest level of evidence. E. Case series have no control group and cannot establish effectiveness.
pearl: For treatment questions: systematic review of RCTs, then RCT, then cohort, then case-control, then case series, then expert opinion.
thinking: Question about whether a treatment works ↓ Randomised evidence minimises confounding ↓ Pooling several good RCTs adds precision ↓ Answer: systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs
exam_trap: A, a single large RCT — the RCT is the gold-standard design, so it feels like the top answer. But a systematic review of several good RCTs sits above any single trial.
takeaway: Systematic reviews of good-quality RCTs give the strongest evidence of treatment effect.

stem: A randomised trial compares a structured physiotherapy programme with usual care for chronic low back pain. A fifth of the physiotherapy group attended no sessions, and several people in the usual-care group paid privately for similar physiotherapy. The investigators want an analysis that keeps the benefit of randomisation. Which approach should they use?

options.A: Analyse everyone in the group to which they were randomised
options.B: Analyse only those who completed their allocated treatment
options.C: Analyse participants by the treatment they actually received
options.D: Exclude participants who crossed over and analyse the rest
options.E: Analyse only participants with complete outcome data

correct_answer: A. Analyse everyone in the group to which they were randomised
why_correct: Intention-to-treat analysis keeps participants in their originally allocated groups regardless of adherence or crossover. This preserves the balance of known and unknown confounders achieved by randomisation. It gives a realistic, usually conservative estimate of effect in real-world use.
why_wrong: B. Per-protocol analysis loses the balance created by randomisation and can overestimate benefit. C. As-treated analysis reorganises groups by choice, reintroducing confounding. D. Excluding crossovers removes non-random subgroups and biases the result. E. Complete-case analysis can introduce attrition bias.
pearl: Intention-to-treat: once randomised, always analysed in that group. It protects randomisation and reflects real-world effectiveness.
thinking: RCT with non-adherence and crossover ↓ Reorganising groups breaks randomisation ↓ Keep everyone in their allocated group ↓ Answer: intention-to-treat analysis
exam_trap: B, per-protocol analysis — analysing those who actually had the treatment sounds like a purer test of the drug. But it undermines randomisation and tends to overstate benefit.
takeaway: Intention-to-treat analysis preserves randomisation by analysing people as allocated.

stem: A trial comparing two antihypertensive drugs reports that one lowers systolic blood pressure more than the other, with p = 0.03. A colleague asks what the p-value means. What is the correct interpretation?

options.A: There is a 97% probability that the first drug is truly better
options.B: If there were no true difference, a result at least this extreme would occur about 3% of the time
options.C: There is a 3% probability that the null hypothesis is true
options.D: The difference is large enough to be clinically important
options.E: There is a 3% chance that the trial results are wrong

correct_answer: B. If there were no true difference, a result at least this extreme would occur about 3% of the time
why_correct: A p-value is the probability of obtaining the observed result, or one more extreme, if the null hypothesis were true. A value below 0.05 is conventionally called statistically significant. It does not tell you the size or clinical importance of the effect, nor the probability that any hypothesis is true.
why_wrong: A. The p-value is not the probability that the alternative hypothesis is true. C. The p-value assumes the null is true; it cannot give the probability that it is true. D. Statistical significance says nothing about clinical importance. E. The p-value does not measure the chance that results are wrong overall.
pearl: The p-value assumes the null hypothesis is true and asks how surprising the data are. It does not measure effect size or clinical importance.
thinking: p = 0.03 ↓ Assume no true difference between drugs ↓ Probability of a result this extreme by chance alone is 3% ↓ Answer: chance of such a result if the null were true
exam_trap: C, 3% probability the null is true — this is the most common misreading of p-values. But the p-value is calculated assuming the null is true, so it cannot give that probability.
takeaway: p-value: chance of a result this extreme if the null were true — not effect size.

stem: To estimate how much alcohol adults in a town drink, a team surveys patients on the hospital's medical wards. The results suggest much higher alcohol intake than national figures. What is the main problem with this study?
why_correct: Selection bias is a systematic error arising from how participants are chosen, making the sample unrepresentative of the target population. Hospital inpatients are more likely to have alcohol-related illness than the general adult population. The results therefore cannot be generalised to the town.
why_wrong: A. Recall bias concerns inaccurate memory of exposures, not who is sampled. B. Confounding distorts an association between an exposure and an outcome; this is an estimate of frequency. C. Publication bias concerns which studies get published. E. Observer bias arises from how investigators measure or record outcomes.
pearl: Selection bias is about who gets into the study. Hospital samples over-represent illness and its causes, so they rarely reflect the general population.
thinking: Aim: estimate alcohol intake in a whole town ↓ Sample drawn only from hospital inpatients ↓ Inpatients differ systematically from the general population ↓ Answer: selection bias
exam_trap: A, recall bias — self-reported drinking is notoriously inaccurate, so recall seems likely. But that would usually underestimate intake; the main problem is that the sample is unrepresentative.
takeaway: An unrepresentative sample caused by how participants are chosen is selection bias.

stem: Researchers identify 200 people with a rare cancer of the bladder and 400 people without it, matched for age and sex, and ask about previous occupational exposure to industrial dyes. Which measure of association should be reported?

options.A: The relative risk, calculated directly from the exposure groups
options.B: The incidence of bladder cancer among exposed workers
options.C: The hazard ratio from time-to-event analysis
options.E: The odds ratio, which approximates relative risk because the cancer is rare

correct_answer: E. The odds ratio, which approximates relative risk because the cancer is rare
why_correct: In a case-control study participants are selected by outcome, so the true population at risk and incidence cannot be measured. The odds ratio of exposure is therefore reported. When the outcome is rare, the odds ratio is a good approximation of the relative risk; when it is common, the odds ratio overstates it.
why_wrong: A. Relative risk needs incidence in exposed and unexposed groups, which a case-control design cannot provide. B. Incidence cannot be calculated because the number of cases was fixed by the researchers. C. Hazard ratios come from cohort or trial data with follow-up over time. D. The number needed to harm requires absolute risks, which are not available.
pearl: Case-control studies give odds ratios, because the researcher chooses how many cases to include. With a rare outcome, the OR approximates the RR.
thinking: Participants chosen by disease status ↓ Design is case-control ↓ Incidence and RR cannot be measured ↓ Answer: odds ratio, approximating RR for a rare disease
exam_trap: A, relative risk — it is the most intuitive measure of association. But it needs incidence data that a case-control study cannot supply.
takeaway: Case-control studies report odds ratios; these approximate relative risk only for rare outcomes.

stem: A cross-sectional survey of 5,000 adults shows that people with depression are much more likely to be physically inactive. A health campaign claims that inactivity causes depression. Which is the most important consideration before accepting this claim?

options.A: Whether the p-value is below 0.05, which would confirm a causal link
options.B: Whether the association is strong, which would prove causation
options.C: Excluding chance, bias and confounding, and showing inactivity came before the depression
options.D: Whether the sample size is large enough to remove confounding
options.E: Whether a biological mechanism exists, which alone would establish cause

correct_answer: C. Excluding chance, bias and confounding, and showing inactivity came before the depression
why_correct: An association does not establish causation. Chance, bias and confounding must first be excluded, and criteria such as temporality, dose-response, consistency and plausibility considered (the Bradford Hill considerations). A cross-sectional design cannot show which came first, and depression could itself cause inactivity.
why_wrong: A. Statistical significance only addresses chance, not bias, confounding or direction. B. Strength supports causation but cannot prove it alone. D. Large samples reduce random error but do not remove confounding or bias. E. Plausibility is supportive but not sufficient on its own.
pearl: Temporality is the one essential Bradford Hill criterion: the cause must come before the effect. Cross-sectional data cannot show which came first.
thinking: Association found in a cross-sectional survey ↓ Exposure and outcome measured at the same time ↓ Reverse causation, bias and confounding all possible ↓ Answer: exclude chance, bias, confounding and establish temporality
exam_trap: B, a strong association — strength is a genuine Bradford Hill consideration, so it feels convincing. But a strong association can still be caused by confounding or reverse causation.
takeaway: Before inferring cause, exclude chance, bias and confounding and confirm the exposure came first.

stem: A team carries out a meta-analysis of a new antidepressant using published trials and finds a large benefit. A regulator later reveals several registered trials that were completed but never published; most showed no benefit. What is this problem, and how is it usually looked for in a meta-analysis?

options.A: Selection bias, looked for by comparing baseline characteristics
options.B: Confounding, looked for by stratified analysis
options.C: Recall bias, looked for using validated questionnaires
options.D: Publication bias, looked for using a funnel plot
options.E: Attrition bias, looked for by intention-to-treat analysis

correct_answer: D. Publication bias, looked for using a funnel plot
why_correct: Publication bias occurs when studies with positive or significant results are more likely to be published than those with negative results. Meta-analyses based only on published studies then overstate the effect. Asymmetry on a funnel plot suggests it, and trial registration helps prevent it.
why_wrong: A. Selection bias concerns how participants enter a study, not which studies are published. B. Confounding distorts an association within a study. C. Recall bias affects how participants remember exposures. E. Attrition bias arises from losses to follow-up within a trial.
pearl: Negative trials that stay unpublished make treatments look better than they are. Funnel plot asymmetry suggests the problem; trial registration helps prevent it.
thinking: Meta-analysis shows large benefit ↓ Unpublished trials were mostly negative ↓ Positive results were preferentially published ↓ Answer: publication bias, detected with a funnel plot
exam_trap: A, selection bias — the meta-analysis did 'select' only published trials, so the term seems to fit. But the specific term for preferential publication of positive studies is publication bias.
takeaway: Preferential publication of positive trials is publication bias; look for funnel plot asymmetry.

stem: In the emergency department, a 29-year-old woman with pleuritic chest pain is judged to have a low clinical probability of pulmonary embolism. A blood test known to have very high sensitivity but low specificity for venous thromboembolism comes back negative. Why is this result useful?

options.A: Most people without the disease test negative, so a positive result confirms it
options.B: A positive result would make the disease very likely
options.C: Most people with the disease test positive, so a negative result makes it unlikely
options.D: The test gives few false positives, so it is good for confirming disease
options.E: High sensitivity guarantees a high positive predictive value

correct_answer: C. Most people with the disease test positive, so a negative result makes it unlikely
why_correct: Sensitivity is the proportion of people with the disease who test positive. A highly sensitive test has few false negatives, so a negative result helps rule the disease out (SnNout), especially when pre-test probability is low. Specificity is the proportion without the disease who test negative; highly specific tests help rule disease in (SpPin).
why_wrong: A. This describes specificity, not sensitivity. B. With low specificity, a positive result is often a false positive. D. Few false positives describes high specificity. E. Positive predictive value depends on specificity and prevalence, not sensitivity alone.
pearl: SnNout: a highly Sensitive test, when Negative, rules disease out. SpPin: a highly Specific test, when Positive, rules disease in.
thinking: Low pre-test probability ↓ Highly sensitive test is negative ↓ Few false negatives mean disease is unlikely ↓ Answer: negative result helps rule it out
exam_trap: B, a positive result makes the disease very likely — a 'good' test seems to work both ways. But with low specificity, many positives are false, so a positive result rules nothing in.
takeaway: High sensitivity means few false negatives: a negative result helps rule disease out.

stem: A 27-year-old woman at 37 weeks in her first pregnancy, being monitored for pre-eclampsia, suddenly develops severe continuous abdominal pain on the antenatal ward. There is only a small amount of dark vaginal bleeding. She is pale and sweaty, with a pulse of 118 beats per minute and a blood pressure of 92/58 mmHg, much lower than her usual readings. Her uterus is rigid and very tender. The fetal heart rate is persistently around 80 beats per minute. Her cervix is closed. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Resuscitate and proceed to category 1 caesarean section
options.B: Give nifedipine to relax the uterus
options.C: Arrange an ultrasound to locate the placenta before deciding
options.D: Give corticosteroids and continue fetal monitoring

correct_answer: A. Resuscitate and proceed to category 1 caesarean section
why_correct: Sudden severe pain, a rigid tender uterus and shock out of proportion to visible bleeding indicate a concealed placental abruption. With maternal compromise and fetal bradycardia in a term pregnancy, the mother is resuscitated and the baby delivered immediately by category 1 caesarean section. Major haemorrhage protocols should be activated as abruption can cause coagulopathy.
why_wrong: B. Tocolysis is contraindicated in abruption with fetal compromise. C. Ultrasound is unreliable for abruption and delays delivery. D. Steroids are not indicated at term and monitoring wastes time with fetal bradycardia. E. Induction is far too slow with a closed cervix and an acutely compromised fetus.
pearl: Concealed abruption: maternal shock can exceed the visible blood loss. A woody uterus with fetal distress means resuscitate and deliver.
thinking: Pre-eclampsia, sudden constant pain, woody tender uterus ↓ Shock out of proportion to visible bleeding: concealed abruption ↓ Fetal bradycardia, term, closed cervix ↓ Answer: resuscitate and category 1 caesarean section
exam_trap: C, ultrasound first — imaging feels like a sensible confirmation step. But ultrasound often misses abruption and delaying delivery risks fetal death.
takeaway: Abruption with maternal shock and fetal distress: resuscitate and deliver by category 1 caesarean.

stem: A 33-year-old woman has a vaginal delivery of twins. She had an oxytocic drug at delivery and the placenta is complete. An hour later she has a sudden heavy loss of blood. Her uterus is soft and well above the umbilicus, and becomes firmer briefly with fundal massage before relaxing again. Her bladder has been emptied and there is no tear. Her pulse is 124 beats per minute and her blood pressure is 90/52 mmHg. Help has been called and resuscitation started. She does not have asthma or hypertension. Which treatment best addresses the cause of the bleeding at this stage?

options.D: A further uterotonic such as oxytocin, ergometrine or carboprost

correct_answer: D. A further uterotonic such as oxytocin, ergometrine or carboprost
why_correct: A soft, high uterus that relaxes after massage indicates uterine atony, the commonest cause of postpartum haemorrhage, and twin pregnancy is a risk factor. The cause is treated with further uterotonics: oxytocin, ergometrine (avoided in hypertension), carboprost (avoided in asthma) and misoprostol. Resuscitation and tranexamic acid continue alongside, and surgical measures follow if drugs fail.
why_wrong: A. Tranexamic acid reduces bleeding but does not make the atonic uterus contract. B. Fluids support circulation but do not treat the cause. C. Balloon tamponade is a mechanical step used if uterotonics fail. E. Vitamin K does not treat uterine atony.
pearl: Four Ts of PPH: tone, trauma, tissue, thrombin. Atony (tone) is the commonest; treat with massage and uterotonics while resuscitating.
thinking: Heavy bleeding after twin delivery ↓ Soft, high uterus that relaxes after massage, no tear, placenta complete ↓ Cause is uterine atony ↓ Answer: further uterotonic drug
exam_trap: A, tranexamic acid — it is part of PPH management and reduces bleeding. But it does not correct uterine atony, which is the cause here.
takeaway: PPH from atony: further uterotonics treat the cause, alongside resuscitation.

stem: A 30-year-old woman at 33 weeks' gestation is on the antenatal ward with severe pre-eclampsia. Her blood tests show haemolysis, markedly raised transaminases and a low platelet count. She suddenly complains of severe epigastric and right upper quadrant pain spreading to her right shoulder, then collapses. Her pulse is 136 beats per minute and her blood pressure 78/42 mmHg. Her abdomen is distending, but the uterus is soft and not tender. She has never had uterine surgery. What is the most likely diagnosis and the most appropriate management?

options.B: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy — supportive care and planned delivery
options.C: Rupture of a subcapsular liver haematoma — resuscitation, delivery and laparotomy

correct_answer: C. Rupture of a subcapsular liver haematoma — resuscitation, delivery and laparotomy
why_correct: Haemolysis, raised liver enzymes and low platelets in pre-eclampsia indicate HELLP syndrome. Sudden severe right upper quadrant pain radiating to the shoulder, collapse and abdominal distension suggest a ruptured subcapsular liver haematoma. Management is resuscitation with activation of the major haemorrhage protocol, urgent delivery and laparotomy with liver packing or embolisation, involving hepatobiliary surgeons.
why_wrong: A. A soft, non-tender uterus makes abruption unlikely. B. Acute fatty liver of pregnancy causes liver failure but not sudden collapse with haemoperitoneum. D. Pulmonary embolism does not cause right upper quadrant pain with abdominal distension in this setting. E. Uterine rupture is very unlikely in an unscarred uterus that is not in labour.
pearl: HELLP with sudden RUQ pain, shoulder-tip pain and shock: think ruptured liver haematoma, a catastrophic haemorrhage needing surgery.
thinking: Pre-eclampsia with haemolysis, raised liver enzymes, low platelets: HELLP ↓ Sudden RUQ and shoulder-tip pain with shock ↓ Soft uterus argues against abruption ↓ Answer: ruptured liver haematoma — resuscitate, deliver, laparotomy
exam_trap: A, placental abruption — it is the classic cause of pain and shock in pre-eclampsia. But the uterus is soft and non-tender, and the pain is in the liver area.
takeaway: HELLP plus sudden RUQ pain and shock: suspect liver capsule rupture; resuscitate, deliver, operate.

stem: A 34-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his flatmate, who found several empty blister packs in his room. He says that at about 10 pm last night he swallowed around forty 500 mg paracetamol tablets in one go and took nothing else. It is now 10 am. He feels a little queasy but otherwise says he is fine. His observations are normal and his abdomen is soft. Blood samples, including a paracetamol level and liver function tests, have just been sent to the laboratory. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Wait for the paracetamol level and plot it on the treatment graph before deciding on treatment
options.B: Give activated charcoal and repeat the paracetamol level in 4 hours
options.C: Discharge with community mental health follow-up, as he is clinically well
options.D: Start intravenous acetylcysteine now, before the blood results are available
options.E: Give oral methionine and repeat liver function tests the next morning

correct_answer: D. Start intravenous acetylcysteine now, before the blood results are available
why_correct: He has taken a large, potentially hepatotoxic single overdose and is presenting around 12 hours later. When a patient with a potentially toxic ingestion presents more than 8 hours after the overdose, intravenous acetylcysteine is started immediately rather than waiting for the paracetamol level, because its protective effect falls the longer treatment is delayed. The level, liver function, INR and renal function are still measured and used to decide whether treatment should continue. Feeling well does not exclude liver injury, which usually becomes apparent later.
why_wrong: A. Waiting for the level delays treatment in a late presentation after a potentially toxic dose. B. Activated charcoal is only useful within about an hour of ingestion and has no role 12 hours later. C. Medical fitness cannot be judged before toxicity is excluded, and early symptoms of hepatotoxicity are often mild. E. Methionine is not used in UK practice and delaying effective treatment risks liver failure.
pearl: In paracetamol overdose, time since ingestion drives the plan: beyond 8 hours after a potentially toxic dose, start acetylcysteine first and let the bloods decide whether to stop.
thinking: Large single paracetamol overdose ↓ Presenting about 12 hours after ingestion ↓ Acetylcysteine efficacy falls with delay beyond 8 hours ↓ Do not wait for the level in late presenters ↓ Start IV acetylcysteine now
exam_trap: A, Wait for the paracetamol level — the treatment graph is familiar and feels like the evidence-based step, but in a late presentation after a potentially toxic dose waiting for the result wastes protective time; the level is used to decide whether to continue, not whether to start.
takeaway: Late presentation after a potentially toxic paracetamol overdose: start IV acetylcysteine without waiting for bloods.

stem: A 79-year-old man with heart failure takes lisinopril and furosemide. He attended an out-of-hours walk-in centre with acute gout in his right big toe and was prescribed naproxen. Ten days later his routine blood tests show that his creatinine has doubled from baseline and his potassium is mildly raised. What is the most likely cause of this change?

options.B: Naproxen added to his ACE inhibitor and diuretic
options.D: Urate nephropathy from the gout flare

correct_answer: B. Naproxen added to his ACE inhibitor and diuretic
why_correct: The new event is the NSAID. An ACE inhibitor, a diuretic and an NSAID together form the triple whammy: the NSAID constricts the afferent arteriole by blocking prostaglandins, the ACE inhibitor removes efferent constriction, and the diuretic reduces circulating volume, so glomerular filtration falls. Naproxen should be stopped, the other drugs reviewed during the AKI, and an alternative gout treatment chosen.
why_wrong: A. Lisinopril is long-standing; the new NSAID completed the triple whammy. C. He has been on furosemide long term and the timing points to the new drug. D. A single gout flare does not cause acute urate nephropathy. E. Age-related decline is gradual and would not double creatinine in ten days.
pearl: Before prescribing an NSAID, check for an ACE inhibitor or ARB plus a diuretic; the combination is a common cause of community-acquired AKI in older people.
thinking: AKI 10 days after a new prescription ↓ Already on ACE inhibitor and loop diuretic ↓ NSAID added for gout ↓ Triple whammy reduces glomerular perfusion ↓ Naproxen with ACE inhibitor and diuretic
exam_trap: A, Lisinopril — ACE inhibitors are well known to raise creatinine, but he has taken it for a long time; the trigger is the newly added NSAID completing the triple whammy.
takeaway: ACE inhibitor plus diuretic plus NSAID is the triple whammy: a common, avoidable cause of AKI.

stem: A 22-year-old woman had an uncomplicated vaginal delivery of her first baby three days ago and is still on the postnatal ward. She complains of a pounding headache and flashing lights. Her blood pressure is 166/110 mmHg and urinalysis shows proteinuria. While being assessed she has a generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting about a minute. Her airway is maintained and she is given oxygen. What is the most appropriate drug treatment?
why_correct: A seizure with hypertension, headache, visual symptoms and proteinuria after delivery is eclampsia, which can occur postpartum. Intravenous magnesium sulfate is the treatment of choice to control and prevent further eclamptic seizures, with a loading dose followed by an infusion and monitoring of reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output. Severe hypertension is treated in parallel, and senior obstetric and anaesthetic help is called.
why_wrong: B. Benzodiazepines are less effective than magnesium sulfate for eclamptic seizures. C. Levetiracetam is an epilepsy treatment and is less effective than magnesium for eclampsia. D. Blood pressure control is essential but does not treat or prevent the seizures. E. Phenytoin is inferior to magnesium sulfate in eclampsia.
pearl: Eclampsia can occur in the days after delivery; new headache, visual disturbance and raised blood pressure postpartum need urgent review.
thinking: Recently delivered woman ↓ Severe hypertension, headache, visual symptoms, proteinuria ↓ Generalised seizure ↓ Postpartum eclampsia ↓ IV magnesium sulfate
exam_trap: B, Intravenous lorazepam — benzodiazepines are first-line for most seizures, but in eclampsia magnesium sulfate is the specific and more effective treatment.
takeaway: Eclampsia, before or after delivery, is treated with IV magnesium sulfate plus BP control.

stem: A 33-year-old woman attends the early pregnancy assessment unit with two days of brown vaginal spotting and cramping pain in her right lower abdomen. Her last period was 7 weeks ago and a home pregnancy test was positive. She was treated for chlamydia some years ago. Her pulse is 78 beats per minute and blood pressure 122/76 mmHg. There is mild tenderness in the right iliac fossa without guarding. What is the most appropriate initial investigation?

options.C: CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis

why_correct: In a haemodynamically stable woman with a positive pregnancy test and pain or bleeding, transvaginal ultrasound is the first-line investigation to locate the pregnancy and look for an adnexal mass or free fluid suggesting ectopic pregnancy. Serum hCG levels complement the scan, particularly when the pregnancy location is unknown.
why_wrong: A. Serial hCG supports the scan but does not replace it as the first-line test. B. A plain X-ray has no role in diagnosing ectopic pregnancy and involves radiation. C. CT exposes a possible pregnancy to radiation and is not the test of choice. E. Laparoscopy is for unstable patients or where the diagnosis remains uncertain after imaging.
pearl: Any woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain or bleeding needs a pregnancy test; if it is positive, consider ectopic pregnancy until the pregnancy is located.
thinking: Positive pregnancy test ↓ Lower abdominal pain and spotting ↓ Previous pelvic infection raises ectopic risk ↓ Haemodynamically stable ↓ Transvaginal ultrasound first
exam_trap: A, Serial serum hCG — hCG trends are useful, but only as an adjunct; the scan is the first-line test to locate the pregnancy.
takeaway: Stable woman with suspected ectopic: transvaginal ultrasound first, hCG as an adjunct.

presentation: Suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage with normal CT
stem: A 38-year-old man was lifting weights at the gym when he felt a sudden, severe pain at the back of his head, reaching its worst within a few seconds. He vomited and went home to rest, coming to the emergency department the following morning. A non-contrast CT head performed 14 hours after the onset of the headache is normal. Neurological examination is normal. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Discharge with analgesia and GP follow-up
options.C: Lumbar puncture to look for xanthochromia
options.E: Start IV antibiotics for possible meningitis

correct_answer: C. Lumbar puncture to look for xanthochromia
why_correct: A thunderclap headache reaching maximum intensity within seconds must be investigated for subarachnoid haemorrhage. CT is less sensitive when it is performed more than 6 hours after onset, so a normal scan does not exclude bleeding. NICE advises considering lumbar puncture at least 12 hours after onset to look for xanthochromia, so it can be done now.
why_wrong: A. Discharge before subarachnoid haemorrhage has been excluded is unsafe. B. MRI is not the standard next test for suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage after a normal CT. D. Repeating the CT does not improve sensitivity as blood is cleared and becomes harder to see. E. There is no fever or other feature to suggest meningitis.
pearl: Xanthochromia takes about 12 hours to develop, so lumbar puncture is timed for at least 12 hours after headache onset; earlier samples can be falsely reassuring.
thinking: Sudden severe headache peaking in seconds ↓ Suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage ↓ CT done late is normal ↓ Late CT can miss blood ↓ Lumbar puncture for xanthochromia
exam_trap: A, discharge — a normal CT and normal examination feel reassuring, but a late CT can miss subarachnoid haemorrhage and a missed bleed can be fatal.
takeaway: Thunderclap headache with a normal late CT: lumbar puncture for xanthochromia.
review_note: answer hinges on movable time thresholds; needs reframing or confirmation against NICE NG228 (dropped from pack 09, 17 Oct 2026)

stem: A 31-year-old woman attends the early pregnancy unit with seven weeks of amenorrhoea and a day of light brown vaginal bleeding. She has only a mild right-sided pelvic ache that needs no analgesia. Her pulse and blood pressure are normal. Transvaginal ultrasound shows no intrauterine pregnancy and a small right adnexal mass separate from the ovary, with no fetal heartbeat and no free fluid. Serum hCG is 2400 IU/L. She lives nearby and can return for follow-up. What is the most appropriate management?

options.B: Discharge with a repeat urine pregnancy test in 3 weeks
options.C: Offer a choice of methotrexate or laparoscopic surgery

correct_answer: C. Offer a choice of methotrexate or laparoscopic surgery
why_correct: An empty uterus with an adnexal mass separate from the ovary indicates a tubal ectopic pregnancy. She is stable, has minimal pain, a small mass with no heartbeat, a moderate hCG and can attend follow-up, so NICE guidance supports offering a choice between systemic methotrexate and laparoscopic surgery after discussing the benefits and risks of each.
why_wrong: A. Laparotomy is for a haemodynamically unstable woman with rupture. B. A tubal ectopic can rupture, so she needs active management and hCG follow-up, not discharge. D. Misoprostol is used to manage miscarriage, not ectopic pregnancy. E. This is not pelvic infection, and antibiotics do not treat an ectopic pregnancy.
pearl: Methotrexate needs reliable follow-up with serial hCG levels until negative, and women should avoid pregnancy for at least 3 months afterwards. Surgery is preferred with significant pain, a large mass, a heartbeat or a high hCG.
thinking: Positive pregnancy with bleeding and pelvic ache ↓ Empty uterus and adnexal mass on ultrasound ↓ Tubal ectopic, unruptured and stable ↓ Small mass, no heartbeat, moderate hCG, can attend follow-up ↓ Offer methotrexate or laparoscopic surgery
exam_trap: D, Misoprostol — tempting because it manages early pregnancy loss, but it treats miscarriage, not an ectopic pregnancy in the tube.
takeaway: Stable unruptured ectopic with moderate hCG and small mass: choice of methotrexate or surgery.

stem: A 26-year-old woman sees her GP with painful periods that have worsened over three years, pain deep inside during intercourse, and pain on opening her bowels during menstruation. Paracetamol and an NSAID help only partly. She does not wish to become pregnant at present. On examination there is tenderness in the posterior fornix. A pelvic ultrasound is normal. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy
options.B: Reassure her that a normal ultrasound excludes endometriosis
options.D: Hormonal treatment with the combined pill or a progestogen

correct_answer: D. Hormonal treatment with the combined pill or a progestogen
why_correct: Worsening dysmenorrhoea, deep dyspareunia and cyclical painful defecation suggest endometriosis. NICE advises that suspected endometriosis can be treated with hormonal therapy (the combined pill or a progestogen) alongside analgesia without first confirming the diagnosis, as long as she is not trying to conceive. Referral is needed if symptoms persist despite treatment or there are features of deep disease.
why_wrong: A. Radical surgery is a last resort and inappropriate for a young woman at this stage. B. A normal ultrasound does not exclude endometriosis, especially superficial disease. C. GnRH agonists are second-line, specialist treatments. E. Laparoscopy may be needed if first-line treatment fails, but hormonal treatment can be started first in primary care.
pearl: The classic endometriosis pattern is cyclical pain, deep dyspareunia and painful defecation during periods. A normal scan does not rule it out.
thinking: Young woman with progressive cyclical pelvic pain ↓ Deep dyspareunia and painful defecation ↓ Suspected endometriosis ↓ Not trying to conceive, analgesia insufficient ↓ Hormonal treatment
exam_trap: E, Diagnostic laparoscopy — tempting because it confirms the diagnosis, but first-line hormonal treatment can be tried before surgery when fertility is not the current aim.
takeaway: Suspected endometriosis not wanting pregnancy: start hormonal treatment before laparoscopy.

stem: A 66-year-old woman tells her GP she has felt bloated nearly every day for three months, fills up quickly at meals and has lost some weight. Her CA125 is raised and pelvic ultrasound shows a solid and cystic left adnexal mass with ascites. She is referred urgently to gynaecology. What is the most appropriate next investigation to assess the extent of disease?

options.A: CT of the abdomen and pelvis, with chest imaging
options.D: PET-CT as the first staging test

correct_answer: A. CT of the abdomen and pelvis, with chest imaging
why_correct: Persistent bloating, early satiety and weight loss with a raised CA125 and a complex adnexal mass with ascites strongly suggest ovarian cancer. NICE recommends CT of the abdomen and pelvis (with chest imaging where indicated) to establish the extent of disease and plan surgery or other treatment through the gynaecological oncology team.
why_wrong: B. NICE advises against routine MRI for the initial assessment of suspected ovarian cancer. C. Repeating the scan delays diagnosis of a likely malignancy. D. PET-CT is not a routine first staging test. E. Laparoscopy is not the first step; cross-sectional imaging comes first, with tissue diagnosis planned after.
pearl: Persistent bloating in a woman over 50 should prompt a CA125 test. The Risk of Malignancy Index combines ultrasound findings, menopausal status and CA125 to guide referral.
thinking: Postmenopausal woman with persistent bloating and early satiety ↓ Raised CA125 and complex mass with ascites ↓ Likely ovarian cancer ↓ Need to know extent before treatment ↓ CT abdomen and pelvis
exam_trap: B, MRI pelvis — tempting because MRI gives detailed pelvic images, but it does not stage the abdomen and is not recommended routinely.
takeaway: Suspected ovarian cancer: CT abdomen and pelvis to assess the extent of disease.

stem: A 50-year-old teacher has had no periods for a year. Hot flushes wake her several times a night, she feels irritable and intercourse has become uncomfortable because of dryness. She has her uterus and has no personal or family history of breast cancer, venous thromboembolism or liver disease. Her blood pressure is normal. She wants the most effective treatment for her symptoms. What should be offered?

options.E: HRT containing oestrogen with a progestogen

correct_answer: E. HRT containing oestrogen with a progestogen
why_correct: She has typical menopausal vasomotor, mood and genitourinary symptoms and no contraindications, so NICE recommends HRT as the most effective treatment. Because she has a uterus, she needs a progestogen with the oestrogen to protect the endometrium from hyperplasia and cancer; no blood test is needed to diagnose menopause at her age.
why_wrong: A. Unopposed oestrogen in a woman with a uterus raises the risk of endometrial cancer. B. SSRIs are less effective and are not first line when HRT is suitable. C. A moisturiser only helps dryness and does nothing for flushes or mood. D. Clonidine is a less effective option for women who cannot take HRT.
pearl: Women over 45 with typical symptoms do not need FSH testing to diagnose menopause. Oestrogen-only HRT is only for women without a uterus.
thinking: Woman over 45 with no periods for a year ↓ Flushes, mood change and vaginal dryness ↓ Menopause, clinical diagnosis ↓ No contraindications, uterus present ↓ Combined HRT
exam_trap: A, Oestrogen-only HRT — tempting because oestrogen relieves symptoms, but with an intact uterus a progestogen is essential to prevent endometrial cancer.
takeaway: Menopausal woman with a uterus: HRT must include a progestogen with the oestrogen.

stem: A 29-year-old woman in her second pregnancy, who had a caesarean section previously, is 30 weeks pregnant. She attends the maternity assessment unit after waking to find the bed soaked with fresh red blood. She has no abdominal pain and no contractions. Her pulse and blood pressure are normal, the uterus is soft and non-tender, and the CTG is reassuring. Her anomaly scan reported a placenta covering the internal cervical os. What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.A: Digital vaginal examination to assess cervical dilatation
options.C: Admit, gain IV access, group and crossmatch, and give antenatal corticosteroids
options.E: Discharge with review at the next antenatal clinic

correct_answer: C. Admit, gain IV access, group and crossmatch, and give antenatal corticosteroids
why_correct: Painless, bright red bleeding with a soft, non-tender uterus and a known placenta over the os is antepartum haemorrhage from placenta praevia. With mother and fetus currently stable, she needs admission, large-bore IV access, crossmatched blood and monitoring, plus antenatal corticosteroids because preterm delivery may become necessary. Anti-D is given if she is rhesus negative.
why_wrong: A. Digital examination is contraindicated in placenta praevia as it can provoke catastrophic haemorrhage. B. Immediate delivery is for maternal instability or fetal compromise, which are not present. D. Vaginal delivery is contraindicated when the placenta covers the os. E. Discharge after a significant antepartum haemorrhage with a placenta praevia is unsafe.
pearl: Painless bleeding plus a soft uterus means praevia until proven otherwise: no digital examination. A previous caesarean also raises the risk of placenta accreta.
thinking: Painless bright red bleeding in the third trimester ↓ Soft, non-tender uterus, reassuring CTG ↓ Known placenta over the os ↓ Stable mother and fetus, preterm delivery possible ↓ Admit, resuscitation preparation and corticosteroids
exam_trap: A, digital examination — assessing the cervix is routine with bleeding in later pregnancy, but with a placenta praevia it can trigger torrential haemorrhage and is contraindicated.
takeaway: Bleeding from placenta praevia: admit, prepare blood, give steroids if preterm, and never examine digitally.

stem: A 19-year-old woman sees her GP because her periods come only every two to three months and she is embarrassed by coarse dark hairs on her chin and persistent spots along her jawline. Her BMI is in the normal range. Blood tests show a mildly raised testosterone with normal prolactin and thyroid function, and an ultrasound reports multifollicular ovaries. She is in a relationship and does not want to become pregnant for several years. What is the most appropriate first-line management?

options.A: Clomifene citrate from day 2 of the cycle

why_correct: Irregular cycles with clinical and biochemical hyperandrogenism and multifollicular ovaries fit PMOS (formerly PCOS). In a woman who does not want to conceive, the combined oral contraceptive pill is first line: it regulates bleeding, protects the endometrium, reduces ovarian androgen production and increases sex hormone binding globulin, improving hirsutism and acne. It also provides the contraception she needs.
why_wrong: A. Clomifene induces ovulation and is used only when pregnancy is wanted. B. Metformin can help metabolic features but is not first line for cycle control, hirsutism or acne. C. Spironolactone is an add-on antiandrogen that needs reliable contraception because it can harm a male fetus. D. A progestogen-only implant gives contraception but does not treat hirsutism and may worsen acne.
pearl: In PMOS, match treatment to the goal: COC for cycles, skin and contraception; ovulation induction only for fertility. Screen for metabolic risk whatever the BMI.
thinking: Oligomenorrhoea with hirsutism and acne ↓ Raised testosterone, other causes excluded, multifollicular ovaries ↓ PMOS ↓ No wish to conceive, wants cycle and skin control ↓ Combined oral contraceptive pill
exam_trap: B, metformin — it is closely associated with PMOS and insulin resistance, but it does little for hirsutism or acne and is not first line for menstrual control when pregnancy is not wanted.
takeaway: PMOS without a fertility wish: the combined pill treats cycles, hirsutism and acne together.

stem: A 36-year-old woman attends her GP surgery in December with headaches, nausea and tiredness for two weeks. The headaches are worse in the mornings and ease when she spends the day at work. Her two children have also been complaining of headaches and feeling sick, and she mentions that the family's elderly gas boiler has been making a strange noise. She has no fever, the neurological examination is normal, and her oxygen saturation is 98% on air. What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
why_correct: Several members of the same household with headache, nausea and fatigue that improve away from home, in winter, with a faulty gas appliance, strongly suggests chronic carbon monoxide exposure. Pulse oximetry is unreliable because it cannot distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin, so a normal reading is expected. She needs urgent assessment with a carboxyhaemoglobin level on co-oximetry, high-flow oxygen started as soon as poisoning is suspected, and the household must not return until the appliance is made safe.
why_wrong: A. Influenza causes fever and myalgia and would not improve each day she leaves the house. B. Tension-type headache would not explain nausea in several family members linked to the home. D. Medication-overuse headache needs regular analgesic use and does not affect the whole household. E. Gastroenteritis causes vomiting and diarrhoea over days, not morning headaches that resolve away from home.
pearl: Think carbon monoxide when several people or pets in one home have headaches that improve away from it. Normal saturations do not exclude it; ask for co-oximetry.
thinking: Headache, nausea and fatigue ↓ Several household members affected ↓ Symptoms ease away from home, faulty gas boiler in winter ↓ Normal oximetry does not reassure ↓ Carbon monoxide poisoning
exam_trap: A, influenza — a winter illness affecting a whole family sounds infectious, but there is no fever and symptoms ease whenever she leaves the house, which points to an environmental exposure.
takeaway: Household clusters of headache that improve away from home suggest carbon monoxide; oximetry reads falsely normal.

stem: A 52-year-old farm labourer is brought to the emergency department after spending the morning spraying crops in hot weather without a mask. He is drooling, has a wheeze with copious bronchial secretions, and has had diarrhoea and urinary incontinence. His pupils are very small, his pulse is 46/min, and fine twitching is visible in the muscles of his arms and chest. What is the most likely cause?
why_correct: Organophosphate pesticides inhibit acetylcholinesterase, so acetylcholine accumulates. Muscarinic effects cause salivation, bronchorrhoea, bronchospasm, diarrhoea, urinary incontinence, miosis and bradycardia, and nicotinic effects cause fasciculations and later weakness. Treatment includes decontamination with protective equipment, airway support and atropine titrated to dry the chest secretions.
why_wrong: A. Opioids cause small pupils and respiratory depression but a dry chest without secretions or fasciculations. C. Anticholinergic toxicity causes the opposite picture: dry skin, dilated pupils, tachycardia and urinary retention. D. Serotonin syndrome causes hyperthermia, clonus, tachycardia and dilated pupils. E. Beta-blocker overdose causes bradycardia and hypotension but not secretions, diarrhoea or fasciculations.
pearl: Cholinergic toxicity drowns the patient in secretions: the killer is the wet chest. Atropine is titrated until secretions dry, not to the pupil size.
thinking: Agricultural pesticide exposure ↓ Drooling, bronchorrhoea, diarrhoea and incontinence ↓ Miosis and bradycardia ↓ Fasciculations from nicotinic excess ↓ Organophosphate poisoning
exam_trap: A, opioid toxicity — pinpoint pupils strongly suggest opioids, but opioids do not cause profuse secretions, diarrhoea and fasciculations, which define a cholinergic toxidrome.
takeaway: Pinpoint pupils with secretions, bradycardia and fasciculations after pesticide exposure suggest organophosphate poisoning.

stem: A 23-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after her flatmate found her beside several empty boxes of amitriptyline. She is drowsy and agitated, with dry flushed skin and dilated pupils. Her pulse is 128/min and her blood pressure is low. Her ECG shows a sinus tachycardia with a broad QRS complex, and shortly after arrival she has a brief generalised seizure. Her airway is being managed. What is the most appropriate specific treatment?
why_correct: Tricyclic antidepressants block cardiac sodium channels, widening the QRS and causing arrhythmias, hypotension and seizures, alongside anticholinergic features. Intravenous sodium bicarbonate provides a sodium load and alkalinises the blood, which reduces drug binding to sodium channels, narrows the QRS and improves blood pressure. It is indicated when there is QRS widening, arrhythmia, hypotension or acidosis.
why_wrong: B. Flumazenil can precipitate seizures, particularly when a tricyclic has been taken, and is contraindicated. C. Amiodarone can worsen conduction problems and is not used for tricyclic cardiotoxicity. D. Calcium is used for calcium channel blocker toxicity and hyperkalaemia, not tricyclic sodium channel blockade. E. Naloxone reverses opioids and does not affect tricyclic toxicity.
pearl: Tricyclic overdose: anticholinergic signs plus a broad QRS, hypotension and seizures. Sodium bicarbonate is the antidote of choice for the cardiac effects.
thinking: Tricyclic overdose ↓ Anticholinergic features: dry skin, dilated pupils, tachycardia ↓ Broad QRS, hypotension and seizure ↓ Sodium channel blockade ↓ Intravenous sodium bicarbonate
exam_trap: C, amiodarone — a broad-complex ECG suggests an antiarrhythmic, but the QRS widening is due to sodium channel blockade, which amiodarone can worsen; sodium bicarbonate treats the cause.
takeaway: Tricyclic overdose with a broad QRS or hypotension is treated with intravenous sodium bicarbonate.

stem: A 63-year-old right-handed man is brought to the emergency department by his wife, who noticed at breakfast that the right side of his face had dropped. He understands what is said to him but his speech is halting and effortful, and he cannot find the words he wants. His right arm is markedly weak, while his right leg is only mildly affected. He has no double vision, vertigo or difficulty swallowing. Which arterial territory is most likely to be involved?
why_correct: Right-sided face and arm weakness greater than leg weakness, with expressive aphasia in a right-handed man, localises to the dominant left hemisphere in the middle cerebral artery territory. The middle cerebral artery supplies the lateral motor cortex representing the face and arm, and the frontal language area. He needs urgent brain imaging to guide reperfusion therapy.
why_wrong: B. Anterior cerebral artery strokes affect the leg more than the arm and face. C. A right middle cerebral artery stroke would cause left-sided weakness and typically neglect rather than aphasia. D. Posterior cerebral artery strokes cause a contralateral homonymous hemianopia rather than marked motor and language deficits. E. Vertebrobasilar strokes cause brainstem or cerebellar signs such as diplopia, vertigo and dysphagia.
pearl: Face and arm worse than leg means middle cerebral artery; leg worse than arm means anterior cerebral artery. Aphasia localises to the dominant hemisphere.
thinking: Sudden right face and arm weakness ↓ Leg relatively spared ↓ Expressive aphasia in a right-handed man ↓ Lateral cortex of the dominant hemisphere ↓ Left middle cerebral artery
exam_trap: B, left anterior cerebral artery — it is also a left-sided anterior circulation territory, but it mainly affects the leg; marked face and arm weakness with aphasia points to the middle cerebral artery.
takeaway: Contralateral face and arm weakness with aphasia localises to the dominant middle cerebral artery territory.

presentation: Lithium toxicity risk during intercurrent illness
stem: A 47-year-old man with bipolar disorder, stable for years on lithium, telephones the GP practice. For the past two days he has had diarrhoea and vomiting after a family meal, and he is struggling to keep fluids down. He feels weak and a little shaky. He asks whether he should carry on with his tablets as usual. What is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: Arrange same-day medical review with an urgent lithium level and kidney function
options.B: Continue lithium as normal and take loperamide
options.C: Take ibuprofen regularly for the abdominal cramps
options.D: Take an extra dose of lithium to replace tablets lost through vomiting
options.E: Reduce fluid intake until the vomiting settles

correct_answer: A. Arrange same-day medical review with an urgent lithium level and kidney function
why_correct: Vomiting and diarrhoea cause dehydration and sodium loss, which reduce renal lithium clearance, so the lithium level can climb into the toxic range quickly. Shakiness and weakness may be early signs of toxicity. He needs same-day assessment with a lithium level, renal function and electrolytes, and advice on whether to withhold lithium while he is unable to keep fluids down.
why_wrong: B. Carrying on unchanged ignores the risk of a rapidly rising lithium level during fluid loss. C. NSAIDs reduce renal lithium clearance and can themselves precipitate toxicity. D. Extra doses risk serious toxicity, as lithium has a narrow therapeutic range. E. Reducing fluids worsens dehydration and lithium accumulation.
pearl: Dehydration, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and diuretics all raise lithium levels. Coarse tremor, vomiting, diarrhoea, ataxia and confusion suggest toxicity.
thinking: Patient on lithium ↓ Vomiting and diarrhoea causing fluid and sodium loss ↓ Reduced renal lithium clearance ↓ Shakiness may signal early toxicity ↓ Same-day review with lithium level and renal function
exam_trap: B, continue as normal with loperamide — it seems sensible for simple gastroenteritis, but it ignores the danger that fluid loss poses to lithium clearance and the hint of early toxicity.
takeaway: Vomiting or diarrhoea on lithium needs urgent review with a lithium level, as toxicity can develop quickly.

stem: A 64-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and persistent albumin in her urine started ramipril three months ago. Since then she has had an irritating, tickly dry cough that disturbs her sleep. She has no breathlessness, fever or sputum, her chest is clear and a chest radiograph is normal. Her blood pressure is now at target. She asks whether her medication could be changed. What is the most appropriate option?

options.D: Switch to an angiotensin receptor blocker such as losartan

correct_answer: D. Switch to an angiotensin receptor blocker such as losartan
why_correct: A persistent dry cough beginning after starting an ACE inhibitor, with a clear chest and normal radiograph, is most likely due to accumulation of bradykinin. An angiotensin receptor blocker blocks the same pathway without affecting bradykinin, so it rarely causes cough. It also preserves the renal protection she needs for diabetic kidney disease with albuminuria.
why_wrong: A. Another ACE inhibitor will cause the same class-effect cough. B. Suppressing the cough with codeine leaves the cause in place and adds side effects. C. Amlodipine controls blood pressure but loses the protection against progression of albuminuric kidney disease. E. An inhaled corticosteroid treats airway inflammation, which is not the cause here.
pearl: ACE inhibitor cough is a class effect and can start weeks or months after starting. An ARB is the natural substitute when renin-angiotensin blockade is needed.
thinking: New dry cough after starting ramipril ↓ Clear chest and normal radiograph ↓ Bradykinin-mediated class effect ↓ Diabetes with albuminuria needs renin-angiotensin blockade ↓ Switch to an ARB
exam_trap: C, amlodipine — it is a reasonable antihypertensive and would stop the cough, but with diabetic albuminuria she needs the kidney protection that renin-angiotensin blockade provides.
takeaway: ACE inhibitor cough: switch to an angiotensin receptor blocker, especially when renal protection is needed.

stem: A 55-year-old man who takes bendroflumethiazide for hypertension wakes at 3 am with excruciating pain at the base of his right big toe. By morning the joint is swollen and the overlying skin is red and shiny, and he cannot bear even the bedsheet touching it. A year ago he had a similar episode in the same toe that settled by itself within a week. His temperature is 37.4 degrees C and he otherwise feels well. What is the most likely diagnosis?
