why_correct: A sudden, intensely painful, red, swollen first metatarsophalangeal joint, peaking within hours, in a man taking a thiazide diuretic, with a previous self-limiting attack in the same joint, is acute gout. Thiazides reduce urate excretion. Treatment of the flare is with an NSAID, colchicine or a short course of steroid, and urate-lowering therapy is discussed once he has had recurrent attacks.
why_wrong: A. Septic arthritis must always be considered in a hot joint, but recurrent self-limiting attacks in the big toe without systemic illness favour gout. B. Pseudogout mainly affects the knees and wrists of older people. C. Cellulitis affects skin and soft tissue rather than producing exquisite joint tenderness with recurrent episodes. D. Reactive arthritis follows infection and usually affects large lower-limb joints with eye or urinary features.
pearl: Podagra plus a thiazide or loop diuretic is a classic gout combination. If there is doubt about infection, aspirate the joint before treating.
thinking: Sudden severe pain at the base of the big toe ↓ Red, shiny, exquisitely tender joint ↓ Previous self-limiting attack in the same joint ↓ Thiazide diuretic reducing urate excretion ↓ Acute gout
exam_trap: A, septic arthritis — any hot swollen joint must raise this, but he is systemically well and has had a previous attack that resolved by itself, which favours gout.
takeaway: Recurrent acute attacks at the first MTP joint, especially on a thiazide, suggest gout.

stem: A 19-year-old university student attends her GP with three months of a dry cough that wakes her most nights. She becomes wheezy and tight-chested when cycling in cold air, and the symptoms ease completely over a few days at a time. She had eczema as a child. Examination today is normal and she has never smoked. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Variable wheeze, chest tightness and nocturnal cough triggered by exercise and cold air, with symptom-free spells and a personal history of atopy, is the typical pattern of asthma. A normal examination between episodes does not exclude it. The diagnosis should then be supported with objective testing before starting treatment, in line with current UK guidance.
why_wrong: A. Reflux can cause nocturnal cough but does not cause exercise-induced wheeze and chest tightness. B. Bronchiectasis produces a chronic productive cough with daily sputum, not intermittent dry symptoms. D. Postnasal drip causes cough and throat clearing but not wheeze or chest tightness. E. COPD is a disease of older smokers with persistent, progressive symptoms rather than variable ones.
pearl: Variability is the signature of asthma: symptoms that come and go, worsen at night or with exercise and cold air, and settle completely in between, often with atopy in the background.
thinking: Young non-smoker with nocturnal cough ↓ wheeze and chest tightness with exercise and cold air ↓ symptom-free between episodes and childhood eczema ↓ variable airflow obstruction with atopy ↓ Asthma
exam_trap: A, Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease — night-time cough tempts towards reflux, but reflux does not explain wheeze and chest tightness brought on by exercise and cold air.
takeaway: Episodic wheeze, night cough and exercise triggers with normal periods between suggest asthma.

stem: A 55-year-old man with three previous attacks of gout started allopurinol two weeks ago. He now telephones his GP because his left first metatarsophalangeal joint has again become red, hot and very painful over 24 hours. He is afebrile, otherwise well and can bear weight. He asks whether the new tablet has caused this. What is the best explanation?

options.A: Allopurinol has failed and should be stopped
options.B: Starting urate-lowering therapy can trigger a flare as crystal deposits are mobilised
options.C: This is an allopurinol hypersensitivity reaction
options.D: Allopurinol raises serum urate during the first weeks of treatment
options.E: The new pain indicates septic arthritis caused by allopurinol

correct_answer: B. Starting urate-lowering therapy can trigger a flare as crystal deposits are mobilised
why_correct: When urate-lowering therapy is started, falling serum urate destabilises existing crystal deposits in the joints, which can provoke acute flares in the early months. Patients should be warned about this in advance, and allopurinol should be continued during a flare while the flare itself is treated. Prophylaxis, such as low-dose colchicine, is usually offered while urate-lowering therapy is being started and titrated.
why_wrong: A. A flare soon after starting does not mean treatment failure, and stopping allopurinol is the wrong response. C. Allopurinol hypersensitivity presents with a rash, fever and possible organ involvement, not a single inflamed joint. D. Allopurinol lowers serum urate; it is the fall in urate that mobilises crystals. E. Allopurinol does not cause septic arthritis, and he is afebrile and well.
pearl: Warn every patient starting allopurinol or febuxostat that early flares can happen, keep the urate-lowering drug going through a flare, and consider colchicine cover during titration.
thinking: Recurrent gout, allopurinol started two weeks ago ↓ new typical flare in the big toe, systemically well ↓ falling urate destabilises existing crystal deposits ↓ continue allopurinol and treat the flare ↓ Starting urate-lowering therapy can trigger a flare as crystal deposits are mobilised
exam_trap: A, Allopurinol has failed and should be stopped — the timing tempts patients and doctors to blame and stop the drug, but early flares are expected and stopping it undermines long-term urate control.
takeaway: Early gout flares after starting allopurinol are expected: warn, give cover, and do not stop it.

stem: A 41-year-old man attends his GP with three months of pain in both hands and wrists. Each morning his hands are so stiff that he cannot do up his shirt buttons for about two hours, and they loosen with use. Several knuckles and middle finger joints on both hands are swollen and boggy, and squeezing across the knuckles is painful. He has no rash, nail changes, back pain or recent infection. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Symmetrical, persistent synovitis of the small joints of the hands and wrists, with prolonged early-morning stiffness that eases with activity and a positive metacarpophalangeal squeeze test, is the pattern of rheumatoid arthritis. Persistent synovitis warrants urgent referral to rheumatology, even if blood tests such as rheumatoid factor are normal.
why_wrong: B. Psoriatic arthritis is usually asymmetrical, often affects distal joints and is associated with skin or nail changes. C. Osteoarthritis causes brief morning stiffness and bony swelling of the distal joints and thumb base. D. Gout typically affects one joint acutely with severe pain and redness. E. Reactive arthritis follows an infection and usually affects large joints of the legs asymmetrically.
pearl: Symmetrical small-joint swelling with long morning stiffness and a positive squeeze test should prompt urgent rheumatology referral; do not wait for a positive rheumatoid factor.
thinking: Bilateral hand and wrist pain for three months ↓ prolonged morning stiffness easing with use ↓ boggy swelling of MCP and PIP joints, positive squeeze test ↓ symmetrical inflammatory polyarthritis without skin or infective features ↓ Rheumatoid arthritis
exam_trap: B, Psoriatic arthritis — an inflammatory hand arthritis in a man may tempt towards psoriatic arthritis, but the symmetrical MCP and PIP pattern without skin, nail or distal joint involvement fits rheumatoid arthritis.
takeaway: Symmetrical small-joint synovitis with long morning stiffness: suspect RA and refer urgently.

stem: A 69-year-old woman tells her GP that for the past six weeks she has struggled to lift her arms to brush her hair and finds it hard to get up from a low chair. Her shoulders, neck and hips ache and are very stiff for about two hours each morning. On examination, power in her arms and legs is normal once she gets going. She has no headache, scalp tenderness, visual symptoms or jaw pain. Her ESR and CRP are raised and her creatine kinase is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Bilateral shoulder and hip girdle pain and prolonged morning stiffness in an older adult, with normal muscle strength, raised inflammatory markers and a normal creatine kinase, is characteristic of polymyalgia rheumatica. It typically responds rapidly to low-dose oral prednisolone. Giant cell arteritis symptoms should be asked about at every review.
why_wrong: A. Polymyositis causes genuine proximal weakness with a raised creatine kinase. B. Fibromyalgia causes widespread pain with normal inflammatory markers. D. Frozen shoulder restricts movement at the shoulder and does not explain hip girdle stiffness or raised inflammatory markers. E. Hypothyroid myopathy can cause proximal aching but typically with raised creatine kinase and no rise in ESR or CRP.
pearl: PMR is pain and stiffness, not weakness: patients struggle because it hurts, but power is normal on testing. Always ask about headache, jaw claudication and visual symptoms.
thinking: Older woman with shoulder and hip girdle symptoms ↓ prolonged morning stiffness with normal power ↓ raised ESR and CRP but normal creatine kinase ↓ inflammatory girdle syndrome, not a myopathy ↓ Polymyalgia rheumatica
exam_trap: A, Polymyositis — difficulty lifting the arms and rising from a chair sounds like proximal weakness, but power is normal on testing and the creatine kinase is normal, which rules out an inflammatory myopathy.
takeaway: Girdle pain and morning stiffness with normal strength and raised ESR in an older adult is PMR.

stem: A 34-year-old woman attends the emergency department after noticing in the mirror that the left side of her mouth droops and she dribbles when drinking. The day before she had an ache behind her left ear. Food tastes odd. On examination she cannot wrinkle the left side of her forehead or fully close her left eye. There are no vesicles in or around the ear, and limb power, sensation and speech are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Acute unilateral facial weakness involving the forehead indicates a lower motor neurone facial nerve lesion. With preceding ear pain and altered taste, and no vesicles, limb signs or parotid mass, this is Bell palsy. Oral prednisolone should be started within 72 hours of onset, together with eye protection using lubricants and taping the eye at night.
why_wrong: A. Ramsay Hunt syndrome causes a similar palsy but with a painful vesicular rash in the ear or palate, which is absent. C. A stroke causes an upper motor neurone pattern that spares the forehead, often with limb or speech involvement. D. Myasthenia gravis causes fatigable, often bilateral weakness with ptosis and diplopia. E. A parotid tumour causes a gradually progressive palsy, usually with a palpable mass.
pearl: Forehead involved means lower motor neurone. Look in the ear for vesicles, check for a parotid mass, then start prednisolone within 72 hours and protect the eye.
thinking: Sudden one-sided facial droop ↓ forehead involved and eye cannot close = lower motor neurone lesion ↓ ear ache and altered taste, no vesicles, no mass, no limb signs ↓ idiopathic facial nerve palsy ↓ Bell palsy
exam_trap: C, Middle cerebral artery stroke — sudden facial droop prompts stroke thinking, but a stroke spares the forehead because of bilateral cortical innervation, while here the whole half of the face is weak.
takeaway: Sudden facial weakness including the forehead, with no other signs, is Bell palsy: steroids and eye care.

stem: A 22-year-old woman attends a sexual health clinic with a week of bilateral lower abdominal pain, pain deep inside during intercourse and bleeding after sex. She has a new sexual partner and they do not use condoms. Her temperature is 37.9°C. On bimanual examination there is tenderness in both adnexa and pain on moving the cervix. A pregnancy test is negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Bilateral lower abdominal pain, deep dyspareunia, postcoital bleeding and low-grade fever in a young woman with a new partner, with adnexal and cervical motion tenderness, indicate ascending genital tract infection. Because the diagnosis is clinical, antibiotics should be started promptly after testing for chlamydia and gonorrhoea, with partner notification.
why_wrong: A. A negative pregnancy test makes ectopic pregnancy very unlikely. B. Endometriosis causes cyclical pain over months, not an acute febrile illness with a new partner. D. Appendicitis causes right-sided pain without postcoital bleeding or cervical motion tenderness. E. Ovarian torsion causes sudden severe unilateral pain, often with vomiting.
pearl: PID is a clinical diagnosis. A low threshold for treatment matters because delay increases the risk of infertility, ectopic pregnancy and chronic pelvic pain.
thinking: Young woman with a new partner ↓ bilateral lower abdominal pain, deep dyspareunia, postcoital bleeding, low-grade fever ↓ adnexal and cervical motion tenderness, pregnancy test negative ↓ ascending genital tract infection ↓ Pelvic inflammatory disease
exam_trap: A, Ectopic pregnancy — lower abdominal pain and bleeding in a young woman rightly raise ectopic pregnancy, but the negative pregnancy test excludes it and the infective picture fits PID.
takeaway: Pelvic pain with cervical motion tenderness and a negative pregnancy test: treat as PID promptly.

stem: A 39-year-old woman tells her GP that over the past year her periods have become much heavier, with large clots and flooding through her clothes. Her abdomen feels bloated and she needs to pass urine more often. Periods are not especially painful. A pregnancy test is negative. Abdominal examination reveals a firm, non-tender, knobbly mass rising out of the pelvis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Increasingly heavy menstrual bleeding with pressure symptoms and a firm, irregular, non-tender pelvic mass arising from the uterus is typical of fibroids (leiomyomas). Assessment is with a full blood count and pelvic ultrasound. Treatment depends on symptoms, fibroid size and fertility wishes.
why_wrong: A. Adenomyosis causes a uniformly bulky, tender uterus with painful periods, not an irregular knobbly mass. C. Endometrial cancer more often presents with postmenopausal or intermenstrual bleeding and does not typically cause an irregular uterine mass. D. An ovarian cyst causes an adnexal mass, without heavy menstrual bleeding. E. Endometriosis causes cyclical pain and dyspareunia rather than a palpable irregular uterus.
pearl: Heavy periods plus pressure symptoms plus an irregular, non-tender uterus mean fibroids. A smooth, tender, bulky uterus with painful periods suggests adenomyosis instead.
thinking: Progressively heavy periods with clots ↓ bloating and urinary frequency = pressure effects ↓ firm, irregular, non-tender pelvic mass, pregnancy excluded ↓ benign smooth-muscle tumours distorting the uterus ↓ Uterine fibroids
exam_trap: A, Adenomyosis — it also causes heavy bleeding and an enlarged uterus, but it gives a smooth, tender, globular uterus with painful periods, not a knobbly non-tender mass.
takeaway: Heavy periods with pressure symptoms and an irregular enlarged uterus suggest fibroids.

stem: A 63-year-old woman whose periods stopped ten years ago tells her GP that she has twice noticed fresh blood spotting on her underwear in the past month. She has never used hormone replacement therapy. She has type 2 diabetes and a raised BMI. Abdominal examination is normal. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Prescribe vaginal oestrogen and review in three months
options.B: Arrange a cervical screening test only
options.C: Suspected cancer pathway referral for assessment of the endometrium
options.D: Reassure her that occasional spotting is normal after the menopause
options.E: Start continuous combined hormone replacement therapy

correct_answer: C. Suspected cancer pathway referral for assessment of the endometrium
why_correct: Any vaginal bleeding after the menopause is abnormal and must be investigated to exclude endometrial cancer. Obesity and diabetes increase her risk further. She should be referred on the suspected cancer pathway, where assessment usually starts with transvaginal ultrasound and proceeds to endometrial sampling or hysteroscopy if needed.
why_wrong: A. Vaginal atrophy is common, but treating it before excluding cancer may delay a malignant diagnosis. B. A cervical screening test does not assess the endometrium and is not a diagnostic test for bleeding. D. Postmenopausal bleeding is never normal. E. Starting HRT would cause further bleeding and confuse the picture.
pearl: Postmenopausal bleeding means endometrial cancer until proven otherwise. Obesity, diabetes and unopposed oestrogen are classic risk factors.
thinking: Bleeding a decade after the menopause ↓ not on HRT ↓ obesity and diabetes increase endometrial cancer risk ↓ endometrial assessment needed urgently ↓ Suspected cancer pathway referral for assessment of the endometrium
exam_trap: A, Prescribe vaginal oestrogen and review in three months — atrophic vaginitis is the commonest cause of postmenopausal bleeding and tempts as a treatable diagnosis, but cancer must be excluded first.
takeaway: Any postmenopausal bleeding needs suspected cancer referral to assess the endometrium.

stem: A 28-year-old woman who is 30 weeks pregnant mentions at her antenatal appointment that she has had intense vulval itching and soreness for five days. She recently finished a course of antibiotics for a chest infection. There is a thick, white, curd-like discharge with no unpleasant smell. The vulva is red with small superficial fissures. She has no new sexual partner. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Itching and soreness with a thick, white, odourless curd-like discharge and vulval erythema is classic vulvovaginal candidiasis. Pregnancy and recent antibiotic use are both predisposing factors. In pregnancy, a topical imidazole such as a clotrimazole pessary is used, and oral fluconazole should be avoided.
why_wrong: A. Bacterial vaginosis causes a thin, grey, fishy-smelling discharge with little itching. B. Trichomoniasis causes a frothy, yellow-green, offensive discharge. D. Herpes causes painful ulcers or blisters rather than discharge. E. Chlamydia is often asymptomatic or causes intermenstrual bleeding or cervicitis, not intense vulval itching.
pearl: Thick white itchy discharge without odour is thrush. Pregnancy, antibiotics, diabetes and immunosuppression predispose to it. In pregnancy use topical treatment, not oral fluconazole.
thinking: Pregnant woman after antibiotics ↓ intense vulval itching and soreness ↓ thick white curd-like odourless discharge, red fissured vulva ↓ fungal overgrowth favoured by pregnancy and antibiotics ↓ Vulvovaginal candidiasis
exam_trap: A, Bacterial vaginosis — it is the commonest cause of abnormal discharge and is also linked to antibiotics, but it causes a thin fishy-smelling discharge without marked itching.
takeaway: Itchy thick white odourless discharge is thrush; in pregnancy treat topically, not with fluconazole.

stem: A 31-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after collapsing at home. She has sudden severe left-sided lower abdominal pain and pain at the tip of her left shoulder. Her last period was six weeks ago and she has had some brown vaginal spotting. She has a copper intrauterine device. She is pale and clammy, with a pulse of 128/min and low blood pressure. The abdomen is tender with guarding. A urine pregnancy test is positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A positive pregnancy test with sudden unilateral pelvic pain, collapse, shoulder-tip pain from blood irritating the diaphragm and signs of shock indicates intraperitoneal haemorrhage from a ruptured ectopic pregnancy. An intrauterine device does not exclude it, and when pregnancy does occur with a device in place it is more likely to be ectopic. She needs immediate resuscitation and urgent gynaecology review for surgery.
why_wrong: B. Ovarian torsion causes sudden severe pain with vomiting but does not explain a positive pregnancy test with shoulder-tip pain and shock. C. An incomplete miscarriage causes cramping with heavy visible bleeding through an open cervix, and her scanty spotting does not explain her shock. D. A ruptured cyst can cause pain and some haemoperitoneum but is less likely given a positive test and six weeks of amenorrhoea. E. Appendicitis causes gradually worsening right-sided pain with fever.
pearl: In any woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain, check a pregnancy test. Shoulder-tip pain and shock with a positive test mean ruptured ectopic pregnancy: resuscitate and call gynaecology.
thinking: Six weeks of amenorrhoea with a positive pregnancy test ↓ sudden unilateral pelvic pain and spotting ↓ shoulder-tip pain, guarding, tachycardia and hypotension = haemoperitoneum ↓ intrauterine device increases the chance any pregnancy is ectopic ↓ Ruptured ectopic pregnancy
exam_trap: C, Incomplete miscarriage — bleeding and pain in early pregnancy tempt towards miscarriage, but the scanty spotting does not explain the shock, which comes from concealed intra-abdominal bleeding.
takeaway: Positive pregnancy test with pain, shoulder-tip pain and shock means ruptured ectopic pregnancy.

stem: A 42-year-old woman sees her GP because for six months her periods have been so heavy that she changes pads every hour on the first two days and has had to leave work. She becomes breathless climbing stairs and looks pale. Her cycle is regular and she has no other symptoms. A pregnancy test is negative. Which blood test should be done for every woman presenting like this?
why_correct: NICE guidance on heavy menstrual bleeding recommends a full blood count for all women with heavy menstrual bleeding, to detect anaemia that needs treatment. Her breathlessness and pallor make this especially relevant. Other blood tests are requested only when the history or examination suggests a specific cause.
why_wrong: B. Thyroid tests are only indicated when there are features of thyroid disease. C. Serum ferritin is not recommended as a routine test in heavy menstrual bleeding. D. A coagulation screen is reserved for heavy bleeding since menarche or a personal or family history suggesting a bleeding disorder. E. Female hormone testing does not help in managing heavy menstrual bleeding.
pearl: Heavy periods: full blood count for everyone; thyroid tests, coagulation screen and other tests only when the history points to them.
thinking: Heavy menstrual bleeding affecting daily life ↓ breathless and pale = possible anaemia ↓ regular cycle, no features of thyroid or bleeding disorder ↓ routine test recommended for all ↓ Full blood count
exam_trap: C, Serum ferritin — iron deficiency is the main concern so ferritin seems logical, but it is not a routine test here; a full blood count is what identifies anaemia that needs treatment.
takeaway: Every woman with heavy menstrual bleeding should have a full blood count.

stem: An 84-year-old man with heart failure has had his furosemide dose doubled two weeks ago because of ankle swelling. He now has painful leg cramps, constipation and episodes of palpitations. His ankle swelling has improved. The ECG shows flattened T waves and prominent U waves. Which electrolyte disturbance is most likely?
why_correct: Loop diuretics increase delivery of sodium to the distal nephron, which increases potassium loss in the urine. Muscle cramps, constipation, palpitations and ECG changes of flattened T waves and U waves after a dose increase are typical of hypokalaemia. Potassium should be checked and replaced, and magnesium should also be checked as it is often low too.
why_wrong: A. Hyperkalaemia causes tall tented T waves, not U waves, and is more typical of potassium-sparing diuretics. C. Loop diuretics increase calcium excretion, so hypercalcaemia is not expected. D. Hyponatraemia can occur with diuretics but causes confusion and does not produce U waves. E. Loop diuretics cause magnesium loss, not excess.
pearl: Loop and thiazide diuretics lose potassium; spironolactone, amiloride and ACE inhibitors retain it. U waves and flat T waves point to low potassium.
thinking: Furosemide dose increased ↓ cramps, constipation, palpitations ↓ flattened T waves and U waves on ECG ↓ renal potassium loss from a loop diuretic ↓ Hypokalaemia
exam_trap: D, Hyponatraemia — diuretics commonly lower sodium and this tempts, but the U waves and flattened T waves are specific to low potassium.
takeaway: Cramps and U waves after a furosemide increase suggest hypokalaemia.

stem: A 72-year-old woman with heart failure and chronic kidney disease takes ramipril. Three weeks ago spironolactone was added to her treatment. She now feels generally weak and has had episodes of palpitations. Her ECG shows tall, peaked T waves and a slightly widened QRS complex. Which adverse effect is most likely responsible?
why_correct: Spironolactone is an aldosterone antagonist that reduces potassium excretion, and combining it with an ACE inhibitor in a patient with chronic kidney disease significantly raises the risk of hyperkalaemia. Weakness, palpitations, peaked T waves and QRS widening indicate significant hyperkalaemia needing urgent treatment, including cardiac protection with intravenous calcium.
why_wrong: B. Hypokalaemia causes flattened T waves and U waves and is associated with loop or thiazide diuretics. C. Hypocalcaemia prolongs the QT interval and causes tetany and perioral tingling. D. Hypernatraemia causes thirst and confusion, not peaked T waves. E. Hypomagnesaemia is associated with arrhythmias and loop diuretics rather than spironolactone.
pearl: Spironolactone plus an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker plus reduced kidney function is a high-risk combination for hyperkalaemia; check potassium soon after starting and regularly afterwards.
thinking: Spironolactone added to ramipril in chronic kidney disease ↓ weakness and palpitations ↓ peaked T waves and widened QRS ↓ reduced renal potassium excretion ↓ Hyperkalaemia
exam_trap: B, Hypokalaemia — patients with heart failure on diuretics often have low potassium, which tempts, but spironolactone is potassium-sparing and peaked T waves indicate a high potassium.
takeaway: Spironolactone with an ACE inhibitor in kidney disease causes hyperkalaemia: check potassium.

stem: A 52-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and protein in her urine was started on lisinopril two months ago. She returns to her GP with a persistent tickly, non-productive cough that keeps her awake. She has no fever, breathlessness or wheeze, she does not smoke, her chest is clear and a chest X-ray is normal. She asks why her new tablet could cause a cough. Which mechanism best explains this?

options.C: Blockade of beta-2 receptors in the airways
options.D: Direct histamine release from mast cells

why_correct: Angiotensin-converting enzyme also breaks down bradykinin, so ACE inhibitors cause bradykinin to accumulate in the airways, which sensitises the cough reflex and causes a dry, persistent cough. If the cough is troublesome, switching to an angiotensin receptor blocker is appropriate, because it does not affect bradykinin and preserves the kidney benefit.
why_wrong: B. ACE inhibitors lower angiotensin II levels rather than increasing them. C. Beta-2 blockade is a mechanism of bronchospasm with non-selective beta blockers, not ACE inhibitors. D. Direct mast cell histamine release is not the mechanism of ACE inhibitor cough. E. Reduced aldosterone explains the potassium rise with ACE inhibitors, not cough.
pearl: ACE inhibitor cough and angioedema both come from bradykinin build-up. Switching to an angiotensin receptor blocker usually solves the cough because these drugs do not block bradykinin breakdown.
thinking: Recently started on an ACE inhibitor ↓ dry, persistent cough with a clear chest and normal X-ray ↓ ACE normally degrades bradykinin ↓ accumulating bradykinin sensitises the cough reflex ↓ Reduced breakdown of bradykinin
exam_trap: E, Reduced aldosterone secretion — it is a real effect of ACE inhibitors and tempts on that basis, but it explains hyperkalaemia, not the cough.
takeaway: ACE inhibitor cough is caused by bradykinin build-up; switch to an angiotensin receptor blocker.

stem: A 28-year-old man was started on carbamazepine for epilepsy three weeks ago. He attends his GP with two days of fever and aching, followed by a painful red rash on his face and trunk with dusky patches, some of which are blistering. His lips are crusted and bleeding, it hurts to swallow and his eyes are red and sore. What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Stop carbamazepine immediately and arrange emergency hospital admission
options.B: Reduce the carbamazepine dose and review in one week
options.C: Switch to oxcarbazepine and review in one week
options.D: Continue carbamazepine and start oral prednisolone
options.E: Continue carbamazepine and prescribe an oral antihistamine

correct_answer: A. Stop carbamazepine immediately and arrange emergency hospital admission
why_correct: A febrile prodrome followed by a painful, dusky, blistering rash with mucosal involvement of the mouth and eyes, weeks after starting carbamazepine, is Stevens–Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis. This is a medical emergency. The drug must be stopped immediately and the patient admitted for specialist care, often in a burns or intensive care setting, with ophthalmology input.
why_wrong: B. Any continuation of the causative drug worsens the reaction and outcome. C. Oxcarbazepine is structurally related and can cross-react, and outpatient review is unsafe. D. Continuing the drug is dangerous, and steroids in primary care are not the appropriate management. E. An antihistamine does not treat a severe cutaneous adverse reaction.
pearl: Skin pain, blistering and mucosal involvement after a new drug signal SJS/TEN. Aromatic anticonvulsants such as carbamazepine are classic culprits, typically within the first two months.
thinking: Carbamazepine started three weeks ago ↓ febrile prodrome then painful dusky blistering rash ↓ oral, lip and eye involvement ↓ severe cutaneous adverse drug reaction ↓ Stop carbamazepine immediately and arrange emergency hospital admission
exam_trap: C, Switch to oxcarbazepine and review in one week — switching anticonvulsants seems sensible for seizure control, but oxcarbazepine can cross-react, and this emergency needs admission, not outpatient review.
takeaway: Painful blistering rash with mucosal involvement after carbamazepine: stop it and admit urgently.

stem: A 71-year-old woman is having a colonoscopy under intravenous midazolam. Partway through the procedure she stops responding to voice and her oxygen saturation keeps falling despite supplemental oxygen and a jaw thrust. She has been given no opioid, takes no regular sedatives and has no history of epilepsy. Which drug should be given to reverse her sedation?
why_correct: Midazolam is a benzodiazepine, and flumazenil is a competitive antagonist at the benzodiazepine binding site of the GABA-A receptor. Reversal of over-sedation during a procedure in a patient who is not benzodiazepine-dependent and has no seizure history is one of the safest settings in which to use it. Airway support continues alongside, and she needs monitoring afterwards because flumazenil is shorter acting than midazolam.
why_wrong: A. Naloxone reverses opioids, and she has received none. C. Atropine treats bradycardia and does not reverse sedation. D. Sugammadex reverses the neuromuscular blockers rocuronium and vecuronium, which are not used for endoscopic sedation. E. Protamine sulfate reverses heparin and has no effect on sedatives.
pearl: Flumazenil wears off sooner than most benzodiazepines, so re-sedation can occur; keep the patient monitored after reversal rather than returning them straight to an unobserved area.
thinking: Sedation with midazolam during endoscopy ↓ unresponsive with falling saturations, no opioid given ↓ benzodiazepine effect needs reversing, low seizure risk ↓ Flumazenil
exam_trap: A, naloxone — it is the reflex reversal agent in a sedated, hypoxic patient, but no opioid was given and naloxone does nothing at the benzodiazepine receptor.
takeaway: Midazolam over-sedation during a procedure is reversed with flumazenil, with monitoring for re-sedation.

stem: A 19-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by paramedics after her flatmate found her beside an empty bottle of her mother's temazepam. She opens her eyes only to pain and her breathing is slow and shallow. Intravenous naloxone given en route produced no change. She does not take any regular medicines, there is no evidence of other substances, and her ECG shows normal QRS and QT intervals. Which drug specifically reverses the agent she has taken?
why_correct: Temazepam is a benzodiazepine, and flumazenil competitively blocks the benzodiazepine site on the GABA-A receptor, reversing sedation and respiratory depression. Airway support comes first, and flumazenil is considered only when the risk of seizures is low. Here she is not a regular user and the ECG gives no suggestion of a pro-convulsant co-ingestant such as a tricyclic.
why_wrong: A. Phytomenadione (vitamin K) reverses warfarin and has no sedative-reversing action. B. Naloxone has already failed, and more of it will not reverse a benzodiazepine. C. Activated charcoal does not reverse established sedation and is hazardous when the airway is not protected. D. Physostigmine reverses anticholinergic toxicity, not benzodiazepine effects.
pearl: Before giving flumazenil, ask whether the patient is benzodiazepine-dependent or has taken a pro-convulsant such as a tricyclic; if either is likely, supportive care is safer.
thinking: Reduced consciousness and hypoventilation after temazepam ↓ no response to naloxone ↓ not a regular user, ECG gives no sign of a tricyclic ↓ benzodiazepine receptor antagonist ↓ Flumazenil
exam_trap: B, more naloxone — escalating the familiar antidote is tempting, but naloxone acts only at opioid receptors and has already failed.
takeaway: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, but only after checking for dependence and pro-convulsant co-ingestion.

stem: A 64-year-old woman who takes bendroflumethiazide for hypertension describes a year of separate attacks in which first her right ankle and later her left knee became hot, swollen and very painful, each settling completely within about ten days. Between attacks she is well. On examination there are several small, firm, chalky-white nodules on the rim of her right ear. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Recurrent, self-limiting attacks of acute monoarthritis with full recovery between episodes suggest a crystal arthropathy. A thiazide diuretic, which reduces renal urate excretion, and tophi on the ear point specifically to urate deposition. Joint aspiration showing needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals would confirm gout.
why_wrong: A. Calcium pyrophosphate disease also causes recurrent attacks, often in the knee of an older person, but it does not produce ear tophi and is not linked to thiazides. B. Rheumatoid arthritis is a persistent, symmetrical small-joint polyarthritis, not separate attacks that resolve fully. C. Septic arthritis does not keep recurring and resolving on its own in different joints over a year. E. Reactive arthritis follows a gut or genital infection and usually affects several lower-limb joints at once.
pearl: Thiazide and loop diuretics raise serum urate and are common precipitants of gout in older women; review the drug chart before starting long-term urate-lowering therapy.
thinking: Recurrent self-limiting acute monoarthritis ↓ well and fully recovered between attacks ↓ thiazide use + chalky ear nodules (tophi) ↓ urate crystal deposition ↓ Gout
exam_trap: A, calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease — a recurrent hot knee in an older woman suggests it, but tophi and a thiazide point to urate.
takeaway: Recurrent self-limiting monoarthritis with tophi in a patient on a thiazide is gout.

stem: A 49-year-old man comes to the emergency department on crutches the morning after a wedding reception. Overnight the joint at the base of his left great toe became so tender that he could not bear to pull a sock over it. The joint is swollen, and the skin over it is shiny and dusky red. He is afebrile and otherwise well, with no history of injury. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Sudden overnight onset of severe pain, swelling and shiny red skin over the first metatarsophalangeal joint, after an evening of likely heavy eating and drinking, is the classic picture of acute gout. The first MTP joint is the commonest site of a first attack. Joint aspiration for crystals confirms it, but the clinical picture here is typical.
why_wrong: B. Septic arthritis must be considered in any hot joint, but it usually affects a systemically unwell patient and the first MTP joint is an uncommon site. C. Cellulitis causes spreading redness of the skin and soft tissue rather than pain centred on the joint itself. D. Hallux valgus causes chronic deformity and pressure pain, not an acute inflammatory attack overnight. E. Calcium pyrophosphate disease mainly affects the knee and wrist of older adults.
pearl: Alcohol, particularly beer, and purine-rich meals can trigger acute gout; colchicine or an NSAID started early shortens the attack.
thinking: Sudden overnight acute monoarthritis ↓ first MTP joint, exquisite tenderness, shiny red skin ↓ heavy food and alcohol intake, afebrile and well ↓ Gout
exam_trap: B, septic arthritis — the joint is hot and exquisitely tender, but he is afebrile and well and the site is classic for gout; aspirate if any doubt remains.
takeaway: Sudden, exquisitely painful swelling of the big toe joint in a well man is acute gout until shown otherwise.

stem: A 58-year-old woman who has type 2 diabetes telephones her GP practice. She caught a stomach bug from her grandchildren and has been vomiting and passing watery stools for 24 hours. She cannot keep fluids down, feels dizzy and has passed very little urine today. She takes metformin twice daily and asks what to do about her tablets. What is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: Withhold metformin until she is eating and drinking normally, and arrange same-day assessment
options.B: Continue metformin at the usual dose with small sips of water
options.C: Halve the metformin dose until the vomiting stops
options.D: Take an extra dose of metformin to compensate for the illness
options.E: Stop metformin permanently and start gliclazide

correct_answer: A. Withhold metformin until she is eating and drinking normally, and arrange same-day assessment
why_correct: Dehydrating illness can cause acute kidney injury, and metformin then accumulates and increases the risk of lactic acidosis. Standard sick day guidance is to pause metformin temporarily and restart once eating and drinking normally. Her reduced urine output and inability to keep fluids down mean she also needs prompt clinical assessment.
why_wrong: B. Continuing the full dose despite significant dehydration risks AKI-related harm. C. A reduced dose still carries the same risk while the kidneys are under threat. D. Extra doses are unsafe and do not treat the illness. E. A permanent switch is unnecessary because metformin is only paused during the illness.
pearl: Sick day guidance pauses metformin (along with drugs such as ACE inhibitors, diuretics and SGLT2 inhibitors) during dehydrating illness, restarting once eating and drinking normally.
thinking: Type 2 diabetes on metformin ↓ vomiting and diarrhoea with poor intake and reduced urine output ↓ risk of AKI and metformin accumulation ↓ temporarily withhold and assess ↓ Withhold metformin and arrange same-day assessment
exam_trap: C, Halve the metformin dose — a reduced dose sounds like a cautious compromise, but the danger comes from impaired renal clearance, so the drug should be paused entirely.
takeaway: Dehydrating illness on metformin: pause the drug, restart once eating and drinking normally, and assess.

presentation: Warfarin — Raised INR After New Drug
stem: A 74-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation has had stable INR results on the same warfarin dose for over a year. Eight days ago she was prescribed clarithromycin for a chest infection. At the anticoagulation clinic today her INR is well above her target range. She has no bleeding and says she has not changed her diet or missed any tablets. What is the most likely explanation?

options.B: A recent increase in green leafy vegetables in her diet
options.D: An interaction with the recently prescribed antibiotic
options.E: Laboratory error, as the INR cannot change this quickly

correct_answer: D. An interaction with the recently prescribed antibiotic
why_correct: Clarithromycin inhibits the hepatic enzymes that metabolise warfarin, increasing its anticoagulant effect and raising the INR. A previously stable INR that rises shortly after a new drug is started should always prompt consideration of an interaction. Many antibiotics, antifungals and other drugs interact with warfarin, so INR checks are advised when they are started.
why_wrong: A. Missing doses lowers the INR rather than raising it. B. Vitamin K-rich foods reduce warfarin effect and lower the INR. C. Resistance would lower, not raise, the INR. E. The INR can change within days after a new interacting drug, so this result is plausible.
pearl: Macrolides, fluconazole, metronidazole and several other drugs potentiate warfarin. Check the INR within a few days of starting any interacting drug.
thinking: Long-standing stable INR ↓ new drug started a week earlier ↓ INR now raised with no other change ↓ enzyme inhibition increases warfarin effect ↓ Interaction with the antibiotic
exam_trap: B, Increase in green leafy vegetables — dietary change is a well-known cause of INR instability, but vitamin K lowers the INR, the opposite of what is seen here.
takeaway: A rising INR after a new prescription on warfarin should prompt a check for a drug interaction.

stem: A 67-year-old man has been on the surgical ward for six days receiving intravenous gentamicin for an intra-abdominal infection. He now reports a constant ringing in his ears and feels unsteady when walking. His creatinine has risen each day for the past three days. Which pair of adverse effects is he showing?
why_correct: Aminoglycosides such as gentamicin damage both the inner ear, causing tinnitus, hearing loss and vestibular unsteadiness, and the renal tubules. Toxicity is more likely with prolonged courses and accumulation, which is why levels and renal function are monitored. A rising creatinine and new ear symptoms should prompt review of the drug and its levels.
why_wrong: A. Neuropathy and optic neuritis are linked with antituberculous drugs such as isoniazid and ethambutol. B. Tendon damage and QT prolongation are associated with fluoroquinolones. C. Cholestatic jaundice is a recognised effect of co-amoxiclav and flucloxacillin. E. Red man syndrome is associated with rapid vancomycin infusion.
pearl: Gentamicin toxicity affects the ear and kidney. Vestibular damage may show as unsteadiness rather than deafness, and can be permanent.
thinking: Several days of IV gentamicin ↓ tinnitus and unsteadiness ↓ rising creatinine ↓ aminoglycoside damage to inner ear and kidney ↓ Ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity
exam_trap: E, Red man syndrome and thrombocytopenia — vancomycin is also a monitored, potentially nephrotoxic antibiotic, so it tempts, but this patient is on gentamicin and the ear symptoms are the key.
takeaway: Gentamicin can damage the ear and kidney: monitor levels and renal function, and act on new ear symptoms.

stem: A 63-year-old man with psoriatic arthritis takes weekly methotrexate. Five days ago an out-of-hours doctor prescribed trimethoprim for a urinary infection. He now attends the GP surgery with a painful sore mouth, a temperature and small purple spots on his shins. He has no cough or breathlessness. Which complication of his treatment is most likely?
why_correct: Mouth ulceration, fever and petechiae in a patient on methotrexate suggest pancytopenia from bone marrow suppression. Trimethoprim is also a folate antagonist and markedly increases this risk when combined with methotrexate. He needs an urgent full blood count, methotrexate withheld and assessment for neutropenic sepsis.
why_wrong: A. Pneumonitis presents with cough and breathlessness, which he does not have. B. Hepatotoxicity causes deranged liver tests rather than ulcers and petechiae. D. Stevens-Johnson syndrome causes widespread mucocutaneous blistering and skin detachment, not isolated petechiae. E. Trimethoprim can raise potassium but this does not explain fever, ulcers or bruising.
pearl: Methotrexate plus trimethoprim or co-trimoxazole is a dangerous combination for marrow suppression. Sore throat, ulcers, fever or bruising on methotrexate needs an urgent FBC.
thinking: Weekly methotrexate ↓ recent trimethoprim, another folate antagonist ↓ mouth ulcers, fever and petechiae ↓ suggests falling white cells and platelets ↓ Bone marrow suppression
exam_trap: A, Methotrexate pneumonitis — fever on methotrexate brings pneumonitis to mind, but there are no respiratory symptoms, whereas ulcers and petechiae point to the marrow.
takeaway: Ulcers, fever or bruising on methotrexate suggest marrow suppression, especially after trimethoprim.

stem: A 58-year-old man is on the surgical ward the day after a laparotomy, using a morphine patient-controlled analgesia pump. A nurse calls you because he is difficult to rouse, his pupils are pinpoint and his breathing is slow and shallow. His oxygen saturations keep dropping despite supplemental oxygen and airway support. Which drug should be given?
why_correct: Reduced consciousness, pinpoint pupils and respiratory depression in a patient receiving morphine indicate opioid toxicity. Naloxone is a competitive opioid antagonist that reverses this, given in titrated doses alongside airway support. Its effect can wear off before that of the opioid, so further doses or an infusion and close monitoring may be needed.
why_wrong: A. Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, not opioids. B. Doxapram is a respiratory stimulant and is not the specific treatment for opioid toxicity. C. Glucagon is used for beta-blocker toxicity or hypoglycaemia. E. Sugammadex reverses certain neuromuscular blocking drugs and would not explain pinpoint pupils a day after surgery.
pearl: Naloxone has a shorter duration of action than many opioids, so patients can re-sedate. Stop the PCA, titrate naloxone and keep monitoring.
thinking: Post-operative morphine PCA ↓ drowsy with pinpoint pupils ↓ slow shallow breathing and falling saturations ↓ opioid toxicity needs specific reversal ↓ Naloxone
exam_trap: A, Flumazenil — it is the other well-known reversal agent for sedation, but it acts only on benzodiazepines and has no effect on morphine.
takeaway: Pinpoint pupils with respiratory depression on opioids: support the airway and give titrated naloxone.

stem: A 19-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by a friend after taking a whole packet of paracetamol following an argument. She took all the tablets at once, four and a half hours ago. She now feels completely well, has no abdominal pain, and her observations are normal. Which is the best next step?

options.A: Start acetylcysteine immediately without measuring a level
options.B: Give activated charcoal and discharge with GP follow-up
options.C: Measure a plasma paracetamol concentration now and base treatment on the result
options.D: Discharge home as she is well, with mental health follow-up
options.E: Repeat liver function tests in 24 hours before deciding on treatment

correct_answer: C. Measure a plasma paracetamol concentration now and base treatment on the result
why_correct: Paracetamol overdose is often asymptomatic early, even when serious liver injury is developing. For a single ingestion at a known time, a paracetamol level taken at least four hours after ingestion is plotted against the treatment line to decide whether acetylcysteine is needed. Baseline liver function, renal function and INR are taken at the same time, and she will need a psychosocial assessment.
why_wrong: A. Immediate acetylcysteine without a level is for staggered or uncertain-time ingestions or late presentations, not a single dose with a timed level available. B. Charcoal is only useful within about an hour of ingestion, and discharge would miss treatable toxicity. D. Feeling well does not exclude a dangerous overdose. E. Waiting for liver tests to become abnormal loses the window in which acetylcysteine works best.
pearl: Liver tests may stay normal for many hours after a toxic paracetamol dose. For a single timed ingestion, the timed level decides treatment, not symptoms.
thinking: Single paracetamol overdose at a known time ↓ more than four hours ago ↓ asymptomatic does not mean safe ↓ timed level guides acetylcysteine ↓ Measure the paracetamol concentration now
exam_trap: A, Start acetylcysteine immediately — treating first sounds safe, but with a single, timed ingestion beyond four hours the level is available now and decides whether treatment is needed.
takeaway: Single timed paracetamol overdose: take a level from four hours and treat according to the nomogram.

stem: An ambulance crew brings a 46-year-old man to the emergency department after he swallowed an unknown number of over-the-counter tablets. He is restless and sweaty, complains of a high-pitched buzzing in both ears, and is breathing deeply and rapidly. An arterial blood gas shows a low carbon dioxide level together with a reduced bicarbonate. Which type of poisoning is most likely?
why_correct: Tinnitus, sweating and hyperventilation after an overdose are characteristic of salicylate poisoning. Salicylates stimulate the respiratory centre, causing respiratory alkalosis, and also uncouple oxidative phosphorylation, producing a metabolic acidosis, giving the mixed picture on the gas. Management includes a salicylate level, correcting fluid and electrolyte losses, and urinary alkalinisation or haemodialysis in severe cases.
why_wrong: A. Tricyclic poisoning causes anticholinergic features, seizures and broad QRS complexes rather than tinnitus. B. Opioids depress breathing rather than stimulating it. D. Paracetamol poisoning is usually asymptomatic early and does not cause tinnitus. E. Ethylene glycol causes metabolic acidosis with deep breathing but not tinnitus, and is not taken as tablets.
pearl: Salicylate poisoning classically gives a mixed respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis. Tinnitus is a key bedside clue.
thinking: Overdose of over-the-counter tablets ↓ tinnitus and sweating ↓ deep rapid breathing ↓ gas shows low CO2 and low bicarbonate, a mixed picture ↓ Salicylate poisoning
exam_trap: E, Ethylene glycol poisoning — it also causes a metabolic acidosis with deep, rapid breathing, but it does not cause tinnitus and is not an over-the-counter tablet overdose.
takeaway: Overdose with tinnitus, sweating and hyperventilation suggests salicylate poisoning.

stem: A 23-year-old woman is admitted to the acute medical unit having taken an overdose the previous evening. She has vomited repeatedly, is sweaty, and describes a constant buzzing in her ears with muffled hearing. A venous blood gas shows a metabolic acidosis with a raised anion gap. Which drug did she most likely take?
why_correct: Vomiting, sweating, tinnitus with reduced hearing and a raised anion gap metabolic acidosis after an overdose point to aspirin. Salicylates disrupt cellular metabolism, producing acid, and directly affect the inner ear. A salicylate level guides treatment such as urinary alkalinisation or haemodialysis in severe cases.
why_wrong: A. Amitriptyline causes drowsiness, anticholinergic signs, seizures and arrhythmias rather than tinnitus. B. Paracetamol causes delayed liver injury and does not cause tinnitus. C. Iron causes vomiting and acidosis but not tinnitus or hearing change. D. Lithium toxicity causes tremor, ataxia and confusion rather than tinnitus with acidosis.
pearl: Tinnitus or deafness after an overdose should prompt a salicylate level, even when the patient does not name the drug taken.
thinking: Overdose with repeated vomiting ↓ tinnitus and muffled hearing ↓ raised anion gap metabolic acidosis ↓ combination fits salicylate toxicity ↓ Aspirin
exam_trap: C, Iron sulfate — iron overdose also causes vomiting and a metabolic acidosis, but it does not affect hearing, which is the discriminating clue.
takeaway: Overdose with vomiting, acidosis and ear symptoms suggests aspirin: check a salicylate level.

stem: A 30-year-old man attends the GP surgery with three days of sore throat, runny nose and a dry cough. He is afebrile with no tonsillar exudate or enlarged neck glands. He asks for antibiotics because he is going on holiday next week. The GP explains that this is most likely viral, so antibiotics would not shorten it, advises on self-care, and explains when to seek help. No prescription is issued. Which principle is the GP demonstrating?
why_correct: Antimicrobial stewardship means using antimicrobials only when they are likely to benefit the patient, to reduce resistance and avoid unnecessary adverse effects. Explaining that a self-limiting viral illness will not respond to antibiotics, giving self-care advice and safety-netting is a core stewardship approach in primary care. NICE guidance supports a no-antibiotic or back-up strategy for most respiratory tract infections.
why_wrong: A. Delayed prescribing involves issuing a back-up prescription to use if symptoms worsen, which did not happen here. C. Therapeutic duplication is prescribing overlapping drugs. D. Defensive practice is acting mainly to protect the clinician rather than to benefit the patient. E. Polypharmacy refers to the use of multiple medicines.
pearl: Most upper respiratory tract infections are viral and self-limiting. Explaining the expected course and safety-netting is as important as the decision not to prescribe.
thinking: Viral-sounding upper respiratory illness ↓ patient requests antibiotics ↓ GP explains no benefit and offers self-care with safety-netting ↓ responsible use of antimicrobials ↓ Antimicrobial stewardship
exam_trap: A, Delayed antibiotic prescribing — it is a stewardship tool and sounds similar, but it involves issuing a back-up prescription, and none was given here.
takeaway: Withholding antibiotics for viral illness, with explanation and safety-netting, is antimicrobial stewardship.

stem: A 55-year-old taxi driver attends the GP surgery for review two weeks after a flare of gout in his right ankle, which has now settled. It is his third flare this year. He is overweight and asks what changes he can make himself to reduce further attacks. Which advice is most appropriate?

options.A: Replace water with fruit juice to stay hydrated
options.B: Reduce his alcohol intake, particularly beer
options.C: Lose weight quickly with a very low-calorie fasting diet
options.D: Increase his intake of offal and shellfish for protein
options.E: Avoid all physical activity to protect his joints

correct_answer: B. Reduce his alcohol intake, particularly beer
why_correct: Alcohol, particularly beer, raises serum urate and is a common trigger for gout flares, so reducing intake is recommended. Other helpful measures include gradual weight loss, regular exercise and staying well hydrated with water. With recurrent flares he should also be offered urate-lowering therapy.
why_wrong: A. Fructose-sweetened drinks, including some fruit juices, raise urate. C. Rapid weight loss or fasting can raise urate and provoke flares, whereas gradual loss is beneficial. D. Offal and shellfish are purine-rich and increase urate. E. Regular activity is encouraged and does not worsen gout.
pearl: Lifestyle advice in gout: limit alcohol (especially beer), avoid sugary drinks, lose weight gradually and keep active. Recurrent flares warrant urate-lowering therapy.
thinking: Recurrent gout flares ↓ asking about self-help ↓ identify factors that lower urate ↓ alcohol is a key modifiable trigger ↓ Reduce alcohol, particularly beer
exam_trap: C, Lose weight quickly with a very low-calorie fasting diet — weight loss helps gout, so it tempts, but rapid weight loss and fasting can raise urate and trigger attacks.
takeaway: Reducing alcohol, especially beer, is a key self-help measure to reduce gout flares.

stem: A 46-year-old man is seen in the rheumatology clinic with three months of painful, swollen hands. Squeezing across his knuckles is painful on both sides, and several finger joints are swollen. He feels stiff for well over an hour each morning. Hand X-rays are normal. Which antibody test is most specific for rheumatoid arthritis?
why_correct: Anti-CCP antibodies are highly specific for rheumatoid arthritis and support the diagnosis in a patient with symmetrical small-joint synovitis. A positive result also predicts a more erosive course. NICE recommends testing rheumatoid factor first in suspected rheumatoid arthritis and anti-CCP if rheumatoid factor is negative, but anti-CCP is the more specific test.
why_wrong: A. Rheumatoid factor is common in RA but is also found in other conditions and healthy older people, so it is less specific. B. ANA is sensitive for lupus but not specific for RA. D. HLA-B27 is a genetic marker associated with spondyloarthritis, not an antibody test for RA. E. Anti-dsDNA is specific for systemic lupus erythematosus.
pearl: Rheumatoid factor is more widely used but less specific; anti-CCP is highly specific and predicts erosive disease. Normal early X-rays do not exclude RA.
thinking: Symmetrical small-joint swelling ↓ prolonged morning stiffness ↓ suspected rheumatoid arthritis ↓ choose the most specific antibody ↓ Anti-CCP antibody
exam_trap: A, Rheumatoid factor — it is the best known and is tested first in practice, but it is less specific than anti-CCP.
takeaway: Anti-CCP is the most specific antibody test for rheumatoid arthritis.

stem: A 71-year-old man with long-standing seropositive rheumatoid arthritis is seen in pre-assessment before an elective hip replacement. He mentions a few months of pain at the back of his head and upper neck, tingling in both hands and increasing clumsiness with buttons. Examination shows brisk reflexes in all four limbs and upgoing plantar responses. Which complication needs to be considered?
why_correct: Long-standing rheumatoid arthritis can weaken the ligaments stabilising the atlantoaxial joint, allowing subluxation that compresses the upper cervical cord. Occipital and neck pain with upper motor neurone signs in all four limbs suggests cervical myelopathy from this cause. It needs urgent imaging and specialist review, and is particularly important before anaesthesia because neck manipulation during intubation can cause cord injury.
why_wrong: A. Nerve root compression causes lower motor neurone signs in one dermatome, not brisk reflexes in all limbs. C. Carpal tunnel syndrome causes median nerve sensory symptoms without upper motor neurone signs or neck pain. D. Mononeuritis multiplex causes patchy lower motor neurone deficits. E. Peripheral neuropathy reduces reflexes rather than making them brisk.
pearl: Neck pain with upper motor neurone signs in rheumatoid arthritis suggests atlantoaxial subluxation. Flag it before any general anaesthetic.
thinking: Long-standing rheumatoid arthritis ↓ occipital and neck pain ↓ hand clumsiness with brisk reflexes and upgoing plantars ↓ high cervical cord compression ↓ Atlantoaxial subluxation
exam_trap: C, Bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome — it is common in RA and causes tingling hands, but it cannot produce brisk reflexes or extensor plantars.
takeaway: Rheumatoid arthritis with neck pain and upper motor neurone signs suggests atlantoaxial subluxation.

stem: A 39-year-old man attends the GP surgery with two months of pain in the small joints of his hands and feet. The GP wants to judge whether this is more likely to be inflammatory or mechanical. Which additional feature of the history would most suggest an inflammatory arthritis?

options.A: Pain that is worse at the end of a working day
options.B: Stiffness on waking that lasts more than an hour and eases with activity
options.C: Brief stiffness after sitting that resolves within minutes
options.D: Pain that is relieved by resting the joints
options.E: Episodes of the joints locking or giving way

correct_answer: B. Stiffness on waking that lasts more than an hour and eases with activity
why_correct: Prolonged early morning stiffness that improves with use is a hallmark of inflammatory joint disease, reflecting synovitis that eases as the joints are moved. Along with joint swelling and symmetrical small-joint involvement, it should prompt urgent rheumatology referral. Mechanical problems tend to worsen with use and improve with rest.
why_wrong: A. Pain building up through the day with use suggests a mechanical or degenerative process. C. Short-lived stiffness after inactivity is typical of osteoarthritis. D. Inflammatory pain typically improves with movement, whereas rest relieves mechanical pain. E. Locking and giving way suggest a mechanical internal joint problem.
pearl: Inflammatory: prolonged morning stiffness, better with activity. Mechanical: brief stiffness, worse with use, better with rest.
thinking: Small-joint pain in hands and feet ↓ need to separate inflammatory from mechanical ↓ inflammatory pain eases with movement ↓ long morning stiffness is characteristic ↓ Prolonged morning stiffness easing with activity
exam_trap: D, Pain relieved by resting the joints — rest sounds like a sensible response to inflammation, but inflammatory symptoms worsen with immobility and improve with movement.
takeaway: Morning stiffness lasting over an hour and easing with activity suggests inflammatory arthritis.

stem: A 64-year-old woman attends her GP because she now has to stop for breath halfway up the hill to the shops. She has had a morning cough with small amounts of clear sputum for several winters and needed antibiotics twice last year for chest infections. She smoked 20 cigarettes a day for 40 years and stopped last year. There is no history of childhood wheeze or hay fever. Post-bronchodilator spirometry shows an obstructive pattern with only a small change after salbutamol. Which condition best accounts for her symptoms?
why_correct: Progressive exertional breathlessness and a chronic productive cough in a long-term smoker, with airflow obstruction that persists after a bronchodilator, is COPD. The minimal bronchodilator response and lack of atopic history point away from asthma. Management includes smoking cessation support, pulmonary rehabilitation where appropriate, vaccinations and inhaled therapy.
why_wrong: A. Asthma usually shows variable symptoms and marked bronchodilator reversibility, often with an atopic history. B. Bronchiectasis causes daily copious purulent sputum and is confirmed on CT, not suggested by small amounts of clear sputum. C. Heart failure causes breathlessness with orthopnoea and oedema, not fixed airflow obstruction on spirometry. E. Pulmonary fibrosis causes a restrictive pattern with fine inspiratory crackles, not obstruction.
pearl: COPD is diagnosed clinically in a person with risk factors and confirmed by post-bronchodilator spirometry showing airflow obstruction; a large bronchodilator response should make you reconsider asthma.
thinking: Long-term smoker in middle age ↓ chronic morning cough, recurrent winter infections and progressive exertional breathlessness ↓ obstructive spirometry with little bronchodilator response ↓ no atopic or childhood history ↓ COPD
exam_trap: A, Asthma — obstructive spirometry and wheezy chest infections tempt towards asthma, but the persistent obstruction after salbutamol, heavy smoking history and lack of atopy fit COPD.
takeaway: Persistent post-bronchodilator airflow obstruction in a long-term smoker with chronic cough and breathlessness is COPD.

stem: A 71-year-old woman is seen on a GP home visit. For three days she has had shivering attacks, a cough bringing up rust-coloured sputum and a sharp pain in her right side when she breathes in. Her temperature is 38.6°C and she is mildly tachypnoeic but fully oriented. There is dullness to percussion at the right base with bronchial breathing and coarse crackles over the same area. Which diagnosis best fits?
why_correct: Fever, rigors, productive cough and pleuritic pain with focal signs of consolidation (dullness, bronchial breathing and crackles over one zone) indicate community-acquired pneumonia. Rust-coloured sputum is classically associated with pneumococcal infection. Severity should then be assessed with a validated score such as CRB-65 to help decide between home and hospital management.
why_wrong: A. Pulmonary embolism can cause pleuritic pain and low-grade fever but not focal consolidation with purulent sputum. B. An effusion gives stony dullness with reduced, not bronchial, breath sounds. D. Lung cancer is a slower illness with weight loss and does not present as a three-day febrile illness. E. Acute bronchitis causes cough without focal chest signs.
pearl: Bronchial breathing over an area of dullness means consolidated lung; dullness with absent breath sounds suggests fluid instead.
thinking: Three days of fever, rigors and productive cough ↓ pleuritic right-sided pain ↓ dullness, bronchial breathing and crackles in one zone indicate consolidation ↓ acute infective picture in the community ↓ Community-acquired pneumonia
exam_trap: B, Pleural effusion — dullness at the base tempts towards fluid, but an effusion quietens breath sounds, whereas bronchial breathing over the dull area signals consolidation.
takeaway: Acute fever and productive cough with focal consolidation signs is community-acquired pneumonia.

stem: A 24-year-old woman with asthma is brought to the emergency department by her partner after two days of worsening wheeze despite frequent use of her blue inhaler. She is now drowsy and responds only to voice, her lips look blue and she is too breathless to attempt a peak flow reading. On auscultation there is very little air entry and almost no audible wheeze. How should this attack be classified?
why_correct: A silent chest, cyanosis and altered consciousness during an asthma attack are features of life-threatening asthma, indicating exhaustion and impending respiratory failure. Reduced wheeze here reflects very poor airflow, not improvement. She needs immediate senior and critical care involvement alongside oxygen, nebulised bronchodilators and systemic steroids.
why_wrong: A. Acute severe asthma describes marked distress, such as being unable to complete sentences, but without cyanosis, a silent chest or drowsiness. B. A moderate exacerbation involves worsening symptoms with no severe or life-threatening features. C. Anaphylaxis follows an allergen exposure, often with urticaria, angioedema or hypotension. E. A panic attack would not cause cyanosis, a silent chest or drowsiness.
pearl: A quiet chest in a breathless asthmatic is an alarm sign, not reassurance: falling wheeze with rising exhaustion means airflow is critically reduced.
thinking: Known asthmatic with an attack unresponsive to her reliever ↓ drowsy and cyanosed with minimal air entry ↓ silent chest and altered consciousness are life-threatening features ↓ risk of respiratory arrest, escalate immediately ↓ Life-threatening asthma
exam_trap: A, Acute severe asthma — being unable to perform a peak flow tempts towards a severe attack, but cyanosis, drowsiness and a silent chest move this into the life-threatening category.
takeaway: Silent chest, cyanosis or drowsiness in an asthma attack means life-threatening asthma; escalate at once.

stem: A 63-year-old man speaks to his GP by telephone. For a week, every time he looks up to reach a high shelf or lies back on his pillow, the room spins violently for less than a minute and then settles. Between attacks he feels completely normal. He has no hearing loss, tinnitus, headache, weakness or difficulty speaking. At a face-to-face review the following day, the Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre to the right reproduces his vertigo with a burst of torsional nystagmus after a short delay. Which condition is responsible?
why_correct: Short episodes of rotatory vertigo triggered by specific head positions, with normal hearing and a positive Dix-Hallpike test showing delayed torsional nystagmus, is benign paroxysmal positional vertigo. It is caused by displaced otoconia in a semicircular canal, most often the posterior canal. It is treated with a particle repositioning manoeuvre such as the Epley manoeuvre rather than vestibular sedatives.
why_wrong: A. Vestibular neuritis causes continuous vertigo lasting days after a viral illness, not brief positional spells. C. Ménière disease causes attacks lasting hours with fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness. D. A posterior circulation TIA is not reproducibly triggered by head position and usually has other neurological symptoms. E. Labyrinthitis causes prolonged vertigo with hearing loss.
pearl: Timing is the key to vertigo: seconds with position change suggests BPPV, hours with hearing symptoms suggests Ménière disease, and days of constant vertigo suggests vestibular neuritis.
thinking: Brief rotatory vertigo lasting under a minute ↓ triggered by looking up and lying back ↓ no hearing or neurological symptoms ↓ positive Dix-Hallpike with delayed torsional nystagmus ↓ Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
exam_trap: D, Vertebrobasilar transient ischaemic attack — vertigo on looking up tempts towards posterior circulation ischaemia in an older man, but reproducible positional triggering, a typical Dix-Hallpike response and no neurological deficit fit BPPV.
takeaway: Seconds-long vertigo on head position change with a positive Dix-Hallpike test is BPPV.

stem: A 74-year-old woman sees her GP with a two-week history of a new headache over her left temple. Her scalp feels sore when she brushes her hair, and her jaw starts to ache after a few minutes of chewing meat. She has felt stiff around her shoulders in the mornings, and yesterday the vision in her left eye went blurred for several minutes. Which diagnosis must be urgently considered?
why_correct: A new temporal headache in an older adult with scalp tenderness, jaw claudication and transient visual disturbance is giant cell arteritis until proven otherwise. With visual symptoms she needs immediate high-dose glucocorticoids and same-day specialist assessment, as delay risks permanent blindness. Inflammatory markers and temporal artery ultrasound or biopsy should not delay treatment.
why_wrong: A. Polymyalgia rheumatica explains the shoulder stiffness but not the headache, jaw claudication or visual disturbance, which indicate arteritis. C. TMJ dysfunction causes jaw pain on movement but not scalp tenderness or visual symptoms. D. Tension-type headache is a bilateral, band-like headache without jaw or visual symptoms. E. Acute angle-closure glaucoma causes a red, painful eye with haloes, not jaw claudication.
pearl: Jaw claudication is one of the most specific features of giant cell arteritis; with any visual symptoms, start steroids the same day and do not wait for test results.
thinking: Older woman with a new temporal headache ↓ scalp tenderness and jaw claudication ↓ shoulder girdle stiffness suggests associated polymyalgia ↓ transient visual blurring signals risk of permanent loss ↓ Giant cell arteritis
exam_trap: A, Polymyalgia rheumatica alone — morning shoulder stiffness tempts towards PMR, but the cranial symptoms and visual disturbance mean arteritis, which needs urgent higher-dose treatment.
takeaway: New headache with jaw claudication and visual symptoms in an older adult is giant cell arteritis; treat urgently.

stem: A 28-year-old woman at 16 weeks of pregnancy is telephoned by her midwife. The urine sample sent at her booking appointment has shown a significant pure growth of Escherichia coli, sensitive to nitrofurantoin, amoxicillin and cefalexin. She has no dysuria, frequency, loin pain or fever and feels well. How should this result be managed?

options.A: No action because she has no symptoms
options.B: Repeat the urine culture at her next routine appointment
options.C: Prescribe an antibiotic guided by the sensitivities
options.D: Arrange a renal tract ultrasound first
options.E: Advise increased fluid intake and cranberry products

correct_answer: C. Prescribe an antibiotic guided by the sensitivities
why_correct: Bacteriuria found on screening in pregnancy should be treated even without symptoms, because it increases the risk of pyelonephritis and has been linked with preterm birth. The antibiotic is chosen according to sensitivities and safety in pregnancy, and a repeat culture is sent afterwards to confirm clearance. Trimethoprim is avoided in the first trimester and nitrofurantoin at term.
why_wrong: A. Unlike in non-pregnant adults, asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy should not be left untreated. B. Waiting until the next visit leaves her at risk of pyelonephritis. D. A renal ultrasound is not needed before treating uncomplicated bacteriuria. E. Fluids and cranberry products are not a treatment for confirmed bacteriuria.
pearl: Asymptomatic bacteriuria is screened for at booking and treated in pregnancy, followed by a test-of-cure culture; outside pregnancy it is generally not treated in otherwise healthy adults.
thinking: Pregnant woman at booking ↓ significant growth of E. coli on urine culture ↓ no urinary symptoms ↓ pregnancy raises the risk of progression to pyelonephritis ↓ Prescribe an antibiotic guided by the sensitivities
exam_trap: A, No action because she has no symptoms — this is right for most non-pregnant adults and so tempts, but pregnancy is a key exception where screening-detected bacteriuria is treated.
takeaway: Treat asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy with a sensitivity-guided antibiotic and check clearance.

stem: A 31-year-old woman at 32 weeks of pregnancy rings her community midwife because she has been scratching her hands and the soles of her feet all night for a week. Apart from scratch marks, her skin looks normal and there is no rash elsewhere. She feels otherwise well, with no headache, visual disturbance or abdominal pain, and her blood pressure at a check yesterday was normal. Which test will most help confirm the likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Itching of the palms and soles, worse at night, without a rash in the third trimester suggests intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy. Raised serum bile acids confirm the diagnosis, and liver function tests are usually checked at the same time. Higher bile acid levels are linked with a greater risk of stillbirth, so results guide monitoring and timing of birth under obstetric care.
why_wrong: A. A full blood count does not diagnose cholestasis. B. Thyroid disease can cause generalised itch but does not explain the classic palmar and plantar pattern in late pregnancy. C. Iron deficiency is common in pregnancy but is not the key test for this presentation. D. A protein:creatinine ratio assesses pre-eclampsia, which presents with hypertension and proteinuria rather than isolated itch.
pearl: Itch without a rash in late pregnancy, especially of the palms and soles and worse at night, should prompt bile acid and liver function testing; the itch resolves after birth.
thinking: Third trimester ↓ intense itching of the palms and soles, worse at night ↓ no primary rash, only scratch marks ↓ suspect obstetric cholestasis ↓ Serum bile acids
exam_trap: D, Urine protein:creatinine ratio — liver involvement in late pregnancy tempts towards checking for pre-eclampsia, but her blood pressure is normal and isolated palmar and plantar itch points to cholestasis.
takeaway: Itch of the palms and soles without a rash in late pregnancy needs serum bile acids.

stem: A 33-year-old woman is in labour at term, attempting a vaginal birth after one earlier caesarean birth. Her labour has been augmented with oxytocin. She suddenly develops a constant, tearing lower abdominal pain between contractions, the contractions stop, and she becomes tachycardic. On vaginal examination the presenting part is higher than it was an hour earlier. The CTG shows a prolonged fetal bradycardia. Which complication is most likely?
why_correct: Sudden severe constant pain, loss of contractions, maternal tachycardia, recession of the presenting part and acute fetal bradycardia in a woman with a previous caesarean scar indicate uterine rupture. Oxytocin augmentation increases the risk. This is an obstetric emergency requiring immediate senior help, maternal resuscitation and a category 1 caesarean section.
why_wrong: A. Abruption causes pain and fetal distress with a tense, woody uterus, but contractions continue and the presenting part does not recede. C. Amniotic fluid embolism presents with sudden collapse, breathlessness and coagulopathy rather than localised tearing pain. D. Cord prolapse causes fetal bradycardia with cord felt or seen below the presenting part, without maternal pain. E. Hyperstimulation causes excessively frequent contractions, not cessation of contractions.
pearl: Key signs of uterine rupture are a scarred uterus, sudden pain, cessation of contractions, loss of station and an abnormal CTG; fetal heart changes are often the earliest sign.
thinking: Labour after a previous caesarean with oxytocin augmentation ↓ sudden tearing pain and contractions stopping ↓ maternal tachycardia and presenting part rising ↓ acute fetal bradycardia ↓ Uterine rupture
exam_trap: A, Placental abruption — sudden pain with fetal bradycardia tempts towards abruption, but cessation of contractions and loss of station in a scarred uterus point to rupture.
takeaway: Sudden pain, stopped contractions and loss of station with fetal bradycardia after a caesarean means uterine rupture.

stem: A 29-year-old woman who conceived by IVF is at 39 weeks on the labour ward. Her 20-week scan reported a low-lying placenta, but a later scan showed it had moved clear of the cervix. Shortly after the midwife performs an amniotomy, there is a gush of bright red blood. Within a minute the CTG shows a sudden, profound fetal bradycardia. She has no abdominal pain, her uterus is soft and she is haemodynamically stable. What is the most likely cause of the bleeding?

options.E: Cervical trauma from the amniotomy hook

why_correct: Painless bleeding at the moment of membrane rupture followed immediately by profound fetal bradycardia, with a stable mother, indicates tearing of unprotected fetal vessels running through the membranes: vasa praevia. The blood lost is fetal, so the baby can exsanguinate rapidly. A history of a low-lying placenta and IVF conception are risk factors, and an immediate category 1 caesarean with neonatal resuscitation is needed.
why_wrong: A. Abruption usually causes pain and a tender, tense uterus. B. Placenta praevia was excluded on the later scan and causes maternal bleeding without such immediate fetal compromise. C.
