Uterine rupture causes severe pain and maternal instability, usually with a uterine scar. E. Minor cervical trauma would not cause sudden profound fetal bradycardia.
pearl: In vasa praevia the bleeding is fetal, so even a small loss is catastrophic for the baby while the mother remains well; risk factors include a low-lying placenta, IVF and placental variants.
thinking: Bleeding immediately after membrane rupture ↓ sudden profound fetal bradycardia ↓ mother stable, painless, soft uterus ↓ fetal vessels torn within the membranes ↓ Vasa praevia
exam_trap: B, Placenta praevia — painless bright red bleeding with a history of a low-lying placenta tempts towards praevia, but the placenta moved clear and the bleeding coincided with membrane rupture and immediate fetal compromise.
takeaway: Painless bleeding at membrane rupture with immediate fetal bradycardia means vasa praevia.

stem: A 26-year-old woman is reviewed on the postnatal ward four days after an emergency caesarean section for a prolonged labour. She has a temperature of 38.4°C with pain low in her abdomen, and her lochia has become offensive. The uterus is bulky and tender on palpation. Her wound is clean and dry, her breasts are soft and non-tender, and her calves are normal. Which diagnosis best fits?
why_correct: Fever, lower abdominal pain, offensive lochia and a tender uterus after delivery are typical of postpartum endometritis. Caesarean section, especially after prolonged labour, is the main risk factor. She should be assessed for sepsis and started on broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics, with an ultrasound if retained products are suspected.
why_wrong: A. Mastitis causes a painful, red, firm area of breast, and her breasts are normal. B. The wound is clean and dry, so a wound infection does not explain her signs. C. Pyelonephritis causes loin pain and urinary symptoms rather than uterine tenderness and offensive lochia. D. DVT causes leg swelling and pain, and her calves are normal.
pearl: Postpartum fever has a short list of sources: uterus, wound, breasts, urinary tract, chest and legs; offensive lochia with a tender uterus localises it to the endometrium.
thinking: Postnatal fever after caesarean section ↓ lower abdominal pain with offensive lochia ↓ bulky, tender uterus ↓ wound, breasts and legs normal ↓ Endometritis
exam_trap: B, Surgical wound infection — fever after a caesarean tempts towards the wound, but it is clean and dry, while offensive lochia and uterine tenderness point to the endometrium.
takeaway: Postnatal fever with offensive lochia and a tender uterus is endometritis.

stem: An 83-year-old man is admitted from his care home to the orthopaedic ward with a fractured neck of femur. He arrives with a bag of medicine boxes, some dispensed via his GP and some via a hospital cardiology clinic. The care home's medicines chart lists a different dose of one of his heart tablets from that printed on the box. You are the foundation doctor writing his inpatient drug chart. What should you do first to reduce the risk of a medication error?

options.A: Prescribe each medicine exactly as printed on the boxes he brought
options.B: Carry out medicines reconciliation using more than one reliable source
options.C: Withhold all his regular medicines until after surgery
options.D: Copy the care home chart onto the drug chart
options.E: Ask the patient to recall each medicine and dose

correct_answer: B. Carry out medicines reconciliation using more than one reliable source
why_correct: Medicines reconciliation means compiling an accurate list of what the patient is actually taking by comparing several sources, such as the GP record, care home chart, medicine labels and specialist letters, and resolving any discrepancies. It identifies omissions, duplications and dose errors at transfer of care, when errors are most common. Pharmacy teams should be involved soon after admission.
why_wrong: A. Labels may be out of date and already conflict with another source, so they cannot be used alone. C. Stopping all medicines can cause harm, for example from omitting cardiac drugs or anticoagulants. D. The care home chart is only one source and already conflicts with another. E. Recall by a frail, injured older patient is unreliable as the only source.
pearl: Transfers of care are high-risk points for medication errors; reconcile using at least two sources and document what was checked and any changes made.
thinking: Admission from a care home after a fall ↓ medicines from several prescribers with a dose discrepancy ↓ transfer of care is a high-risk point for errors ↓ compare several reliable sources and resolve differences ↓ Carry out medicines reconciliation using more than one reliable source
exam_trap: D, Copy the care home chart onto the drug chart — the care home chart looks authoritative, but it already conflicts with the boxes, so relying on it alone could carry an error forward.
takeaway: On admission, reconcile medicines from more than one reliable source before prescribing.

stem: A 37-year-old woman was started on lamotrigine for epilepsy by her neurologist three weeks ago. She now has a widespread blistering rash with painful mouth ulcers and sore eyes, and she is admitted to hospital. Once she is receiving appropriate treatment, the ward doctor wants to report the suspected drug reaction. Which route should be used?

options.A: The local incident reporting system only
options.B: Notification to the UK Health Security Agency
options.C: A letter to the drug manufacturer only
options.D: Referral to the General Medical Council

why_correct: Suspected adverse drug reactions in the UK are reported to the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency through the Yellow Card scheme. Serious reactions, such as suspected Stevens-Johnson syndrome, should always be reported, even if causality is uncertain. Any health professional, and patients themselves, can submit a report.
why_wrong: A. Local incident systems record safety events within a trust but do not replace national adverse reaction reporting. B. UKHSA receives notifications of specified infectious diseases, not drug reactions. C. Contacting the manufacturer alone does not feed into the national monitoring system. D. The GMC regulates doctors and is not involved in reporting drug reactions.
pearl: Report any suspected serious adverse reaction to any medicine through the Yellow Card scheme, and all suspected reactions to products under additional monitoring (black triangle).
thinking: New antiepileptic started weeks ago ↓ blistering rash with mucosal involvement, a serious reaction ↓ suspected adverse drug reaction ↓ national reporting system run by the MHRA ↓ The Yellow Card scheme
exam_trap: A, The local incident reporting system only — hospital doctors are used to filing incident reports, but a suspected adverse drug reaction must be reported nationally through the Yellow Card scheme.
takeaway: Report suspected adverse drug reactions in the UK through the MHRA Yellow Card scheme.

stem: A 42-year-old woman with three children is seen in the gynaecology clinic with periods that have become progressively heavier and more painful over two years. Bimanual examination finds a symmetrically bulky, soft and tender uterus. Transvaginal ultrasound shows diffuse thickening of the myometrium with a heterogeneous texture, but no discrete masses. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Adenomyosis is the presence of endometrial tissue within the myometrium, typically in parous women in their late thirties and forties. It causes heavy, painful periods and a diffusely enlarged, boggy, tender uterus. Ultrasound shows diffuse, heterogeneous myometrial thickening rather than well-defined fibroids.
why_wrong: A. Fibroids cause an irregularly enlarged, firm uterus and appear as discrete, well-defined masses on ultrasound. B. Endometrial cancer typically presents with postmenopausal or intermenstrual bleeding, not progressive painful periods with a uniformly bulky uterus. C. Endometriosis causes cyclical pain and dyspareunia, usually with a normal-sized uterus. E. A polyp causes intermenstrual bleeding and is seen within the cavity, not as diffuse myometrial change.
pearl: Bulky, boggy, tender, symmetrically enlarged uterus in a parous woman with heavy painful periods suggests adenomyosis; discrete masses suggest fibroids.
thinking: Parous woman in her forties ↓ progressive heavy, painful periods ↓ uniformly bulky, tender uterus ↓ diffuse myometrial thickening without discrete masses ↓ Adenomyosis
exam_trap: A, Uterine fibroids — it tempts because fibroids are the commonest cause of heavy bleeding with an enlarged uterus, but they appear as discrete masses and make the uterus irregular rather than diffusely bulky and tender.
takeaway: Heavy painful periods with a diffusely bulky, tender uterus is adenomyosis.

stem: A 22-year-old woman with newly diagnosed focal epilepsy is started on carbamazepine by the neurology team. She has used the combined pill for several years and is in a stable relationship. She asks her GP whether she needs to think about anything regarding her pill. What is the key issue to discuss?

options.A: Her pill will raise carbamazepine to toxic levels
options.B: Carbamazepine will cause her periods to stop permanently
options.C: Her pill will be less effective at preventing pregnancy
options.D: Her pill will lower carbamazepine levels and worsen seizure control
options.E: There is no clinically relevant interaction

correct_answer: C. Her pill will be less effective at preventing pregnancy
why_correct: Carbamazepine induces liver enzymes, which speed up the metabolism of oestrogen and progestogen and reduce the contraceptive effectiveness of the combined pill. She should be advised to use a method unaffected by enzyme inducers, such as a copper or levonorgestrel intrauterine device or the progestogen-only injection, in line with FSRH guidance. Pre-pregnancy counselling about antiseizure medicines is also important.
why_wrong: A. The pill does not significantly increase carbamazepine levels. B. Carbamazepine does not cause permanent amenorrhoea. D. Combined pills reduce lamotrigine levels, not carbamazepine levels. E. The interaction is clinically important and can lead to unplanned pregnancy.
pearl: Enzyme-inducing antiseizure drugs reduce the effectiveness of hormonal contraception. Intrauterine methods or the progestogen-only injection remain reliable.
thinking: Combined pill user ↓ starts carbamazepine ↓ hepatic enzyme induction ↓ faster metabolism of contraceptive hormones ↓ Her pill will be less effective at preventing pregnancy
exam_trap: D, Her pill will lower carbamazepine levels and worsen seizure control — it tempts because combined pills do lower lamotrigine levels, but with carbamazepine the problem is the other way round: the antiseizure drug weakens the pill.
takeaway: Enzyme-inducing antiseizure drugs make the combined pill unreliable; switch to an unaffected method.

stem: An 18-year-old woman visits her practice nurse before moving into university halls of residence. Her records show she was absent from school on the day of the Year 9 meningococcal immunisation and has never had it since. She is otherwise fully immunised. She asks which vaccine will protect her against the meningococcal groups covered by the routine teenage programme. Which vaccine should be offered?
why_correct: The routine UK adolescent programme includes the MenACWY conjugate vaccine, which protects against meningococcal groups A, C, W and Y and reduces carriage in teenagers. Those who missed it remain eligible for a catch-up dose up to their 25th birthday, and first-time university entrants are specifically encouraged to have it. She should be offered MenACWY now.
why_wrong: A. MenB vaccine is given in the infant programme and does not protect against groups A, C, W or Y. B. Hib/MenC covers only group C, and is not the adolescent vaccine. C. HPV vaccine protects against human papillomavirus, not meningococcal disease. E. Pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine protects against pneumococcus and is used mainly for older and at-risk groups.
pearl: MenACWY is the routine teenage meningococcal vaccine, and people who missed it can catch up until their 25th birthday. Encourage it before university.
thinking: Teenager who missed the school meningococcal dose ↓ moving into shared university accommodation ↓ adolescent vaccine covers groups A, C, W and Y ↓ catch-up eligibility applies ↓ MenACWY conjugate vaccine
exam_trap: A, MenB vaccine — it tempts because group B is an important cause of meningococcal disease, but MenB is part of the infant schedule and does not cover the groups in the adolescent programme.
takeaway: Missed the teenage meningococcal dose? Offer MenACWY catch-up, especially before university.

stem: A 58-year-old man with hereditary haemochromatosis, managed with regular venesection, presents to the emergency department with a hot, swollen right knee that came on overnight. There has been no injury. He is apyrexial and otherwise well. A knee radiograph shows fine linear calcification within the joint cartilage. Which condition is most likely?
correct_answer: E. Acute calcium pyrophosphate crystal arthritis (pseudogout)
why_correct: Haemochromatosis is a recognised cause of calcium pyrophosphate deposition, and cartilage calcification (chondrocalcinosis) on the radiograph supports it. An acute hot knee in this setting is most likely pseudogout. The knee should still be aspirated to exclude infection; the fluid shows weakly positively birefringent, rhomboid crystals.
why_wrong: A. Gout more often affects the first toe joint and does not cause chondrocalcinosis. B. Septic arthritis must always be excluded by aspiration, but he is apyrexial and the radiograph and history favour crystal arthritis. C. Reactive arthritis follows a gut or genital infection, which is not described. D. Haemarthrosis is usually caused by trauma or anticoagulation, neither of which is present.
pearl: Think of metabolic causes when pseudogout presents in a younger patient: haemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism and hypomagnesaemia are the classic associations.
thinking: Acute hot, swollen knee ↓ History of haemochromatosis ↓ Chondrocalcinosis on radiograph ↓ No fever, trauma or infection history ↓ Pseudogout, still aspirate to exclude sepsis
exam_trap: A, gout — it is the commonest crystal arthritis, but haemochromatosis and cartilage calcification point specifically to calcium pyrophosphate disease.
takeaway: Haemochromatosis with an acute hot knee and chondrocalcinosis points to pseudogout; still aspirate.

stem: A 63-year-old man who has smoked about a packet a day since his teens sees the practice nurse because he gets breathless walking up hills. He has coughed up white sputum most winter mornings for several years. He never had childhood wheeze or hay fever, and his symptoms change little from day to day. Post-bronchodilator spirometry shows an obstructive pattern that does not reverse. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A long smoking history, exertional breathlessness, chronic productive cough and persistent airflow obstruction after bronchodilator are the features of COPD. The lack of atopy and of day-to-day variation makes asthma less likely. Stopping smoking is the single most effective intervention to slow disease progression.
why_wrong: A. Asthma typically starts earlier, varies over time, is linked with atopy and shows reversible obstruction. B. Bronchiectasis causes daily large volumes of purulent sputum and recurrent infections. D. Pulmonary fibrosis causes a dry cough, fine crackles and a restrictive pattern on spirometry. E. Heart failure causes orthopnoea and oedema, not chronic sputum with fixed obstruction.
pearl: Spirometry confirms COPD by showing obstruction that persists after bronchodilator; marked reversibility or variability should make you reconsider asthma.
thinking: Long-term heavy smoker ↓ Breathless on exertion, chronic morning sputum ↓ No atopy or variability ↓ Fixed obstruction after bronchodilator ↓ COPD
exam_trap: A, asthma — wheeze and breathlessness overlap, but asthma shows variability and reversibility, whereas fixed obstruction in a heavy smoker with no atopy points to COPD.
takeaway: A heavy smoker with chronic sputum, breathlessness and fixed obstruction on spirometry has COPD.

stem: A 26-year-old woman in her first pregnancy attends the antenatal clinic. Her booking blood results show she is RhD negative with no red cell antibodies detected. The midwife recommends routine antenatal anti-D immunoglobulin, and she asks what it is designed to prevent. Which condition does it aim to prevent?

options.B: Haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn
options.D: ABO incompatibility jaundice in the newborn
options.E: A transfusion reaction if she bleeds at delivery

correct_answer: B. Haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn
why_correct: If an RhD-negative woman carries an RhD-positive baby, fetal red cells crossing into her circulation can sensitise her to make anti-D antibodies. In this or a later pregnancy, these IgG antibodies cross the placenta and destroy fetal red cells, causing haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn. Anti-D immunoglobulin clears fetal cells before she becomes sensitised.
why_wrong: A. Neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia involves platelet antigens, not RhD, and is not prevented by anti-D. C. Anti-D has no effect on pre-eclampsia. D. ABO incompatibility is a separate cause of neonatal haemolysis that anti-D does not prevent. E. Transfusion reactions are prevented by cross-matching, not by anti-D prophylaxis.
pearl: Anti-D only works before sensitisation; once a woman has formed her own anti-D antibodies, prophylaxis is of no benefit and the pregnancy needs specialist monitoring.
thinking: RhD-negative mother, possible RhD-positive fetus ↓ fetomaternal haemorrhage can sensitise her ↓ maternal anti-D IgG crosses placenta ↓ fetal red cell destruction ↓ anti-D prophylaxis prevents haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn
exam_trap: D, ABO incompatibility jaundice in the newborn — it is also an antibody-mediated neonatal haemolysis, but it involves ABO antigens and is not prevented by anti-D.
takeaway: Anti-D prevents RhD sensitisation and so prevents haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn.

stem: A 74-year-old woman develops sudden severe mid-back pain while bending to lift a bag of shopping. She has had no fall or other injury. A spinal X-ray shows a wedge compression fracture of the T12 vertebra. She has no weight loss or night sweats, and her full blood count, calcium, ESR and serum protein electrophoresis are all normal. Which underlying condition is most likely?
why_correct: A vertebral compression fracture from minimal stress, such as bending or lifting, in an older woman is a fragility fracture, and osteoporosis is the most likely cause. Normal blood count, calcium, ESR and protein electrophoresis make malignancy unlikely. She should have a fracture risk assessment with DXA scanning and be considered for bone-protective treatment, calcium and vitamin D.
why_wrong: A. Myeloma can cause vertebral collapse, but normal blood count, calcium, ESR and electrophoresis make it unlikely. B. Osteomalacia causes bone pain, muscle weakness and abnormal calcium, phosphate or vitamin D. C. Metastases are unlikely with no cancer history, no systemic features and normal bloods. D. Paget disease causes bone pain and deformity with a raised alkaline phosphatase, not typical wedge fractures.
pearl: Many vertebral fragility fractures are found incidentally or dismissed as back strain; a vertebral fracture strongly predicts future hip and wrist fractures.
thinking: Older woman with minimal-trauma vertebral fracture ↓ fragility fracture ↓ normal FBC, calcium, ESR, electrophoresis ↓ malignancy unlikely ↓ osteoporosis, arrange DXA and bone protection
exam_trap: A, multiple myeloma — it is a classic cause of vertebral collapse in older people, but the normal blood count, calcium, ESR and electrophoresis argue strongly against it.
takeaway: A low-trauma fracture in an older adult is a fragility fracture; assess for osteoporosis.

stem: A 69-year-old man sees his GP because his hats have become tight and he has recently been fitted with a hearing aid. He also has an aching right shin, which looks bowed and feels warmer than the left. Blood tests show a raised alkaline phosphatase, with normal calcium, phosphate, albumin, bilirubin and transaminases. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Skull enlargement, deafness, bowing and warmth of a long bone with an isolated raised alkaline phosphatase are classic features of Paget disease of bone. Disordered, excessive bone turnover produces enlarged, weak and vascular bone. Calcium and phosphate are usually normal. Diagnosis is supported by X-ray and isotope bone scan, and bisphosphonates are used for bone pain.
why_wrong: B. Osteomalacia typically causes low calcium or phosphate, proximal muscle weakness and diffuse bone pain. C. Prostate metastases can raise alkaline phosphatase but do not cause skull enlargement, bowing and warmth of a limb. D. Primary hyperparathyroidism causes raised calcium. E. Multiple myeloma usually causes a normal alkaline phosphatase, raised calcium and anaemia.
pearl: Deafness in Paget disease comes from skull involvement compressing the auditory nerve or affecting the ossicles; increasing hat size is a classic history clue.
thinking: Older man with enlarging skull and deafness ↓ bowed, warm tibia ↓ isolated raised alkaline phosphatase ↓ normal calcium, phosphate and liver tests ↓ Paget disease of bone
exam_trap: C, bone metastases from prostate cancer — sclerotic metastases also raise alkaline phosphatase in older men, but they do not cause skull enlargement, deafness and a warm bowed tibia.
takeaway: Isolated raised ALP with bone pain, bowing or skull enlargement in an older adult suggests Paget disease.

stem: A 33-year-old woman sees her GP six weeks after giving birth. The delivery was complicated by a massive postpartum haemorrhage requiring several units of blood. Her breast milk never came in despite repeated attempts to feed. She feels exhausted, cold all the time and lightheaded when she stands up. She has not had a period since the birth. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Massive postpartum haemorrhage can cause ischaemic necrosis of the pituitary, which enlarges in pregnancy and is vulnerable to hypotension. Failure of lactation is often the first sign, from prolactin deficiency, followed by amenorrhoea, fatigue, cold intolerance and postural dizziness from deficiencies of gonadotrophins, TSH and ACTH. She needs pituitary hormone testing and, if cortisol is deficient, steroid replacement before thyroxine.
why_wrong: A. Postnatal depression causes low mood and fatigue but does not prevent lactation or cause postural hypotension. B. Postpartum thyroiditis does not explain failure of lactation and amenorrhoea. C. Asherman syndrome causes amenorrhoea from uterine scarring but no lactation failure or systemic symptoms. D. Primary adrenal failure would not explain absent lactation and cold intolerance, and is not linked to haemorrhage.
pearl: In hypopituitarism, always replace glucocorticoid before thyroxine, because starting thyroxine first can precipitate an adrenal crisis.
thinking: Massive postpartum haemorrhage ↓ pituitary infarction ↓ failure of lactation (prolactin) ↓ amenorrhoea, cold intolerance, postural dizziness (gonadotrophins, TSH, ACTH) ↓ Sheehan syndrome
exam_trap: A, postnatal depression — exhaustion after a difficult delivery fits, but it does not explain failure of lactation, cold intolerance and postural dizziness.
takeaway: Failure to lactate after major postpartum haemorrhage suggests Sheehan syndrome; test pituitary function.

presentation: Dry mouth, dry eyes and parotid swelling
stem: A 52-year-old woman tells her GP that her eyes feel gritty all the time, she needs a drink of water to swallow dry food such as crackers, and she keeps a glass by her bed at night. Over the past year she has had several bouts of tender swelling in front of both ears. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Persistent dry eyes and dry mouth with recurrent parotid swelling in a middle-aged woman are characteristic of Sjögren syndrome, an autoimmune disease of the exocrine glands. Investigations include anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies and specialist rheumatology assessment. It also carries an increased risk of lymphoma, so persistent gland enlargement needs review.
why_wrong: A. Mumps causes an acute, self-limiting parotitis with fever rather than chronic dryness and recurrent episodes. B. Systemic sclerosis mainly causes skin thickening, Raynaud phenomenon and organ fibrosis. C. A salivary stone causes unilateral swelling with meals and does not cause dry eyes. E. Rheumatoid arthritis can be associated with secondary Sjögren syndrome but would present with inflammatory joint disease.
pearl: Dry eyes plus dry mouth with parotid swelling suggests Sjögren syndrome; check anti-Ro and anti-La and remember the increased lymphoma risk.
thinking: Middle-aged woman ↓ Gritty dry eyes and dry mouth ↓ Recurrent bilateral parotid swelling ↓ Autoimmune exocrine gland disease ↓ Sjögren syndrome
exam_trap: C, salivary gland calculus — gland swelling suggests obstruction, but a stone is usually unilateral, meal-related and does not cause dry eyes.
takeaway: Chronic dry eyes and dry mouth with parotid swelling point to Sjögren syndrome.

presentation: Inflammatory back pain in a young adult
stem: A 26-year-old man attends his GP with six months of pain in his lower back and buttocks. The pain wakes him in the second half of the night, and he is stiff for a long time in the morning, easing as he walks around. Ibuprofen helps considerably, but rest makes it worse. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Chronic back pain beginning in a young adult, with night waking, prolonged morning stiffness, improvement with activity and a good response to NSAIDs, is the inflammatory pattern typical of axial spondyloarthritis. Buttock pain reflects sacroiliac joint involvement. He should be referred to rheumatology for assessment, as delays in diagnosis are common.
why_wrong: A. Mechanical back pain usually worsens with activity and improves with rest. B. Disc prolapse typically causes acute pain with radicular leg symptoms. C. Fibromyalgia causes widespread pain and fatigue rather than localised inflammatory back pain. D. Spinal stenosis affects older adults and causes leg pain on walking that eases with sitting or bending forward.
pearl: Inflammatory back pain: onset under about 40, insidious, improves with exercise, worse with rest, night pain and good NSAID response. Refer to rheumatology.
thinking: Young man with chronic back pain ↓ Night waking and prolonged morning stiffness ↓ Better with movement, worse with rest ↓ Buttock pain and NSAID response ↓ Axial spondyloarthritis
exam_trap: A, mechanical back pain — it is by far the commonest cause, but it follows the opposite pattern, worsening with activity and easing with rest.
takeaway: Back pain that improves with exercise and worsens with rest in a young adult suggests axial spondyloarthritis.

stem: A 38-year-old woman tells her GP that for the past eight months her periods have been so heavy that she floods through pads, passes clots and has to change protection overnight. Her cycle is regular, and she has no bleeding between periods or after sex. Her cervical screening is up to date and abdominal examination is normal. Which investigation should be offered to her routinely?
why_correct: NICE advises that all women presenting with heavy menstrual bleeding should have a full blood count, because chronic blood loss commonly causes iron-deficiency anaemia that may need treatment in its own right. Further tests are guided by the history and examination rather than done routinely. With a regular cycle, no intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding and a normal examination, she may be offered treatment without further investigation.
why_wrong: A. Ultrasound is reserved for women with a suspected structural cause, such as an enlarged uterus or pelvic mass on examination. C. Ferritin is not routinely needed; the full blood count is the recommended first test. D. Thyroid tests are indicated only if there are other features of thyroid disease. E. Coagulation testing is for women with features suggesting a bleeding disorder, such as heavy periods since menarche or other bleeding problems.
pearl: Heavy menstrual bleeding is defined by its impact on a woman's quality of life rather than by measured blood loss; a full blood count is the one routine test.
thinking: Heavy, regular periods with clots and flooding ↓ No intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding, normal examination ↓ Main routine concern is anaemia from blood loss ↓ Full blood count
exam_trap: C, Serum ferritin — iron deficiency is the worry, so measuring iron stores seems logical, but guidance recommends a full blood count for everyone and does not advise routine ferritin testing.
takeaway: Every woman with heavy menstrual bleeding needs a full blood count; other tests depend on the history.

stem: A 64-year-old woman is on the orthopaedic ward five days after a total knee replacement. She suddenly becomes short of breath and complains of a sharp pain in the right side of her chest that is worse when she breathes in. Her heart rate is 112 beats/min, oxygen saturation is 91% on air and her temperature is normal. Her chest is clear on auscultation, and she has no rash or confusion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Sudden pleuritic chest pain, breathlessness, tachycardia and hypoxia with a clear chest in a patient a few days after lower limb joint replacement are classic for pulmonary embolism. Major orthopaedic surgery and post-operative immobility are among the strongest risk factors for venous thromboembolism. She needs prompt risk assessment, imaging and anticoagulation unless contraindicated.
why_wrong: A. Pneumonia usually develops with fever, productive cough and focal chest signs rather than abruptly. B. Atelectasis tends to occur in the first day or two after surgery, often with low-grade fever and reduced basal air entry. C. Myocardial infarction causes central, pressing pain rather than pain worse on inspiration. D. Fat embolism usually follows long bone fractures within a few days and features confusion and a petechial rash.
pearl: Hypoxia with a clear chest on auscultation is a useful clue that the problem lies in the pulmonary circulation rather than the airways or lung tissue.
thinking: Recent major lower limb surgery ↓ Abrupt pleuritic pain and breathlessness ↓ Tachycardia and hypoxia with a clear chest ↓ Pulmonary embolism
exam_trap: D, Fat embolism syndrome — orthopaedic surgery makes it seem relevant, but it typically follows long bone fractures with confusion and petechiae, which are absent here.
takeaway: Sudden pleuritic pain and hypoxia a few days after major surgery is pulmonary embolism until proven otherwise.

stem: A 45-year-old man arrives in the emergency department two days after a long-haul flight with sudden breathlessness and a sharp left-sided chest pain on inspiration. He is tachycardic, his blood pressure is normal and his oxygen saturation is mildly reduced on air. The chest X-ray is unremarkable. His two-level Wells score indicates that pulmonary embolism is likely, and his renal function is normal. Which investigation should be arranged next?
why_correct: When the two-level Wells score indicates that pulmonary embolism is likely, NICE recommends an immediate CT pulmonary angiogram, with interim anticoagulation if there is any delay. A D-dimer is used to rule out PE only when the score indicates PE is unlikely. With normal renal function and no contrast allergy, CTPA is the imaging of choice.
why_wrong: A. A negative D-dimer cannot safely exclude PE when clinical probability is high, so it adds delay without changing management. B. Echocardiography helps assess right heart strain in unstable patients but is not the confirmatory test here. C. A V/Q scan is used when CTPA is unsuitable, such as with significant renal impairment or contrast allergy. E. Leg Doppler is used if there are symptoms of deep vein thrombosis and does not exclude PE.
pearl: Wells score decides the path: PE likely means go straight to CTPA; PE unlikely means D-dimer first, with imaging only if it is positive.
thinking: Pleuritic pain and breathlessness after prolonged travel ↓ Wells score indicates PE likely ↓ Skip D-dimer and image directly ↓ CT pulmonary angiogram
exam_trap: A, D-dimer — it is the familiar first test for suspected PE, but it is only useful to rule out PE when the probability is low; in a 'likely' Wells score it wastes time.
takeaway: PE likely on Wells score: go straight to CTPA rather than D-dimer.

stem: A 19-year-old woman collapses in a shopping centre. Her friend says she suddenly went stiff and cried out, then all four limbs jerked for about two minutes. She bit the side of her tongue and was incontinent of urine. Paramedics find her drowsy and disorientated for around twenty minutes before she gradually returns to normal. Her capillary glucose is normal. Which diagnosis best explains this event?
why_correct: A sudden tonic phase with an epileptic cry, followed by bilateral clonic jerking, lateral tongue biting, incontinence and prolonged post-ictal confusion are the classic features of a generalised tonic-clonic seizure. Prolonged confusion afterwards is the strongest discriminator from syncope. A first seizure should prompt an ECG, bloods and referral to a first seizure clinic, plus advice about driving.
why_wrong: A. Syncope may cause a few brief jerks, but recovery is rapid without prolonged confusion. C. Non-epileptic attacks often have eyes closed, asynchronous movements and lack a typical post-ictal state. D. Arrhythmic collapse is usually abrupt with quick recovery and no tonic phase. E. Hypoglycaemia is excluded by the normal capillary glucose.
pearl: Lateral tongue biting and prolonged post-ictal confusion favour epileptic seizure; brief jerks with rapid recovery favour syncope.
thinking: Sudden stiffening with a cry then four-limb jerking ↓ Lateral tongue bite and incontinence ↓ Prolonged confusion afterwards, normal glucose ↓ Generalised tonic-clonic seizure
exam_trap: A, Vasovagal syncope — convulsive syncope with a few jerks is common and often misread, but it recovers within moments and does not leave twenty minutes of disorientation.
takeaway: Prolonged post-ictal confusion distinguishes a generalised seizure from syncope.

stem: A 70-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis who takes methotrexate presents with a two-day history of a hot, swollen right knee. She has a temperature of 38.4°C and will not allow the knee to be moved, even passively. Her other joints are no worse than usual. Which investigation is most important?

options.E: Aspiration of the knee for Gram stain, microscopy and culture

correct_answer: E. Aspiration of the knee for Gram stain, microscopy and culture
why_correct: A single hot, swollen joint with fever and severe pain on any movement must be treated as septic arthritis until proven otherwise. Pre-existing joint disease and immunosuppression increase her risk. Synovial fluid aspiration for Gram stain, microscopy for crystals and culture is the key investigation and should ideally be done before antibiotics, which must not be delayed.
why_wrong: A. X-ray changes appear late and cannot diagnose or exclude infection. B. Serum urate is unreliable in an acute flare and does not exclude infection. C. CRP will be raised but cannot distinguish septic arthritis from a rheumatoid or crystal flare. D. Blood cultures should also be taken, but they are frequently negative and do not replace joint aspiration.
pearl: Rheumatoid arthritis, immunosuppression, prosthetic joints and older age all raise the risk of septic arthritis; a single joint flaring out of step with the others is a warning sign.
thinking: Single hot swollen knee with fever ↓ Refuses all movement ↓ Immunosuppressed with damaged joint = high risk ↓ Joint aspiration for Gram stain, microscopy and culture
exam_trap: D, Blood cultures — they are part of the sepsis work-up and are worth taking, but they are often negative and only synovial fluid analysis confirms the diagnosis.
takeaway: A hot swollen joint with fever needs aspiration for microscopy and culture before antibiotics where possible.

stem: A 35-year-old man falls from a ladder and sustains a displaced fracture of the middle of his right humeral shaft. In the emergency department he cannot lift his right hand or fingers up from a pronated position, and he has reduced sensation over the back of the hand between the thumb and index finger. Elbow flexion and shoulder abduction are normal. Which nerve is damaged?
why_correct: The radial nerve runs in the spiral groove of the humeral shaft and is vulnerable to mid-shaft fractures as well as prolonged compression, as in 'Saturday night palsy'. Injury causes wrist drop, from weakness of the wrist and finger extensors, with sensory loss over the dorsal first web space. Most closed injuries recover with time, but the deficit must be documented before and after any manipulation.
why_wrong: A. Ulnar nerve injury causes weakness of intrinsic hand muscles and sensory loss in the little finger. B. Median nerve injury affects thumb opposition and sensation on the palmar radial fingers. C. Axillary nerve injury follows surgical neck fractures or dislocation and weakens shoulder abduction, which is normal here. E. Musculocutaneous injury weakens elbow flexion, which is preserved.
pearl: Always document distal neurovascular status before and after reducing a humeral shaft fracture, as radial nerve injury is the commonest associated nerve lesion.
thinking: Mid-shaft humeral fracture ↓ Cannot extend wrist or fingers = wrist drop ↓ Numb dorsal first web space ↓ Radial nerve in the spiral groove
exam_trap: C, Axillary nerve — a humeral fracture brings it to mind, but it is injured with surgical neck fractures and affects shoulder abduction, not wrist extension.
takeaway: Wrist drop with a numb dorsal first web space indicates radial nerve injury.

stem: A 31-year-old woman who had a vaginal delivery with epidural analgesia four days ago phones the maternity triage line and is asked to attend. She has a frontal headache, flashing lights in her vision and pain under her right ribs. The headache is not affected by sitting up or lying down. Blood pressure reads 162/108 mmHg and urine dipstick shows 2+ protein. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Pre-eclampsia can first present or worsen after delivery, most often in the first few days. New hypertension with proteinuria, headache, visual disturbance and right upper quadrant pain are features of severe disease and carry a risk of eclampsia and HELLP syndrome. She needs urgent obstetric assessment, antihypertensive treatment and consideration of magnesium sulfate.
why_wrong: A. A post-dural puncture headache is postural, worse on sitting or standing and eased by lying down, and does not cause hypertension or proteinuria. B. Migraine does not explain significant hypertension, proteinuria and upper abdominal pain. C. Venous sinus thrombosis is a postpartum risk but does not explain proteinuria and hepatic pain. E. Tension-type headache does not cause visual disturbance or proteinuria.
pearl: Pre-eclampsia does not end with delivery; any postnatal woman with severe headache or visual symptoms needs her blood pressure and urine checked.
thinking: Recently delivered woman with headache ↓ Visual disturbance and right upper quadrant pain ↓ Severe hypertension with proteinuria, non-postural headache ↓ Postpartum pre-eclampsia
exam_trap: A, Post-dural puncture headache — a recent epidural makes it tempting, but that headache is postural and does not cause hypertension, proteinuria or visual disturbance.
takeaway: Severe postnatal headache with hypertension and proteinuria is pre-eclampsia until proven otherwise.

stem: A 68-year-old woman who has taken prednisolone for polymyalgia rheumatica for two years develops sudden mid-back pain after lifting a bag of shopping. An X-ray shows a wedge fracture of a thoracic vertebra. She has no weight loss or night pain. Full blood count, calcium, alkaline phosphatase, renal function and protein electrophoresis are normal. What is the most likely underlying condition?
why_correct: A vertebral fracture from a low-energy action such as lifting shopping is a fragility fracture, the hallmark of osteoporosis. Long-term oral glucocorticoids, postmenopausal status and older age are major risk factors. Normal blood tests make myeloma, metastases and metabolic bone diseases less likely; fracture risk assessment and bone-protective treatment are indicated.
why_wrong: A. Myeloma is an important differential, but normal blood count, calcium, renal function and protein electrophoresis make it unlikely. C. Osteomalacia causes bone pain and weakness with a raised alkaline phosphatase and often low calcium or phosphate. D. Paget's disease typically causes a markedly raised alkaline phosphatase. E. Metastases usually cause progressive, night or rest pain, often with weight loss or raised calcium.
pearl: Anyone taking long-term oral glucocorticoids should be assessed for fracture risk, and many older patients warrant bone protection from the outset.
thinking: Vertebral fracture after minimal force ↓ Long-term prednisolone in an older woman ↓ Bloods exclude myeloma and metabolic bone disease ↓ Osteoporosis
exam_trap: A, Multiple myeloma — a vertebral collapse in an older person should prompt a myeloma screen, but her bloods and protein electrophoresis are normal and steroid use explains fragility.
takeaway: A low-trauma vertebral fracture on long-term steroids indicates osteoporosis once red flags are excluded.

presentation: Adrenal insufficiency after stopping long-term steroids
stem: A 58-year-old woman with polymyalgia rheumatica has taken prednisolone for ten months. Feeling much better, she stopped her tablets suddenly last week without telling anyone. She now attends the GP with profound fatigue, nausea, loss of appetite and dizziness when she stands. She has no shoulder or hip girdle stiffness. Her blood pressure is low and falls further on standing. Which is the most likely explanation?

options.A: Adrenal insufficiency from suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis

correct_answer: A. Adrenal insufficiency from suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis
why_correct: Prolonged glucocorticoid therapy suppresses ACTH release, and the adrenal glands atrophy and cannot produce enough cortisol when the drug is stopped abruptly. The result is adrenal insufficiency, with fatigue, nausea and hypotension, which can progress to a life-threatening adrenal crisis. Steroids taken for more than a few weeks should be withdrawn gradually, and patients should carry a steroid emergency card and be warned not to stop suddenly.
why_wrong: B. A relapse of polymyalgia would cause recurrent girdle pain and stiffness, which she does not have. C. Steroid-induced hyperglycaemia occurs while taking steroids and improves after stopping them. D. Hypothyroidism develops gradually and is not caused by stopping prednisolone. E. A perforated ulcer causes sudden severe abdominal pain and peritonism.
pearl: Patients on long-term oral steroids should have sick day rules explained and carry a steroid emergency card so that emergency hydrocortisone is not delayed.
thinking: Months of prednisolone ↓ Abrupt self-discontinuation ↓ Fatigue, nausea and postural hypotension without girdle symptoms ↓ Adrenal insufficiency from HPA axis suppression
exam_trap: B, relapse of polymyalgia rheumatica — tempting because symptoms began after stopping treatment, but relapse would bring back girdle pain and stiffness, not nausea and hypotension.
takeaway: Never stop long-term steroids abruptly; HPA suppression can cause adrenal insufficiency and crisis.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAQ15361). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A 63-year-old woman attends the GP with aching fingers that are worse after gardening and housework. Her hands feel stiff for a short while each morning but loosen quickly. There are hard, knobbly swellings at the ends of several fingers and the base of her right thumb is tender and squared. Her knuckles are not swollen, her nails are normal and she has no rash. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Activity-related hand pain with brief morning stiffness, bony swellings of the distal interphalangeal joints (Heberden's nodes) and squaring of the thumb base are typical of hand osteoarthritis. NICE allows a clinical diagnosis without imaging in people over 45 with this typical history. Management centres on exercise, joint protection, weight management where relevant and topical NSAIDs.
why_wrong: A. Rheumatoid arthritis causes soft, symmetrical synovitis of the MCP and PIP joints with prolonged morning stiffness and usually spares the DIPs. C. Psoriatic arthritis can involve DIP joints but causes soft tissue swelling and dactylitis, usually with nail changes or psoriasis. D. Gout causes acute, red, very painful attacks rather than chronic bony swelling. E. Pseudogout typically causes acute attacks in large joints such as the knee or wrist.
pearl: Heberden's nodes affect the DIP joints and Bouchard's nodes the PIP joints; both are bony and hard, unlike the boggy swelling of inflammatory arthritis.
thinking: Activity-related hand pain with brief stiffness ↓ Hard bony swellings at the DIP joints ↓ Squared thumb base, MCPs spared, no psoriasis ↓ Osteoarthritis
exam_trap: C, psoriatic arthritis — tempting because it is the inflammatory arthritis that involves the DIP joints, but the swellings here are hard and bony with no nail changes, psoriasis or dactylitis.
takeaway: Hard DIP swellings with activity-related pain and brief stiffness are hand osteoarthritis.

stem: A 78-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her daughter because over several days she has become muddled, nauseated and unsteady on her feet. Indapamide was started for hypertension four weeks ago. She has no urinary symptoms and appears clinically euvolaemic. Blood tests show a markedly low sodium and a low potassium; glucose and calcium are normal. Which is the most likely cause?

options.C: Syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion from lung cancer

why_correct: Thiazide and thiazide-like diuretics such as indapamide impair the kidney's ability to dilute urine and commonly cause hyponatraemia, especially in older women and in the first weeks of treatment. Coexisting hypokalaemia supports a diuretic cause. The drug should be stopped and the sodium corrected cautiously to avoid osmotic demyelination.
why_wrong: A. Addison's disease causes hyponatraemia with hyperkalaemia and hypotension, not hypokalaemia. B. Infection can cause delirium in older people, but she has no urinary symptoms and this would not explain the electrolyte pattern. C. SIADH from cancer is possible but less likely than a recently started drug known to cause hyponatraemia. D. Hypothyroidism is an uncommon cause of hyponatraemia and would not explain hypokalaemia.
pearl: Always check sodium and potassium within a few weeks of starting a thiazide or thiazide-like diuretic in an older person.
thinking: Older woman with confusion and unsteadiness ↓ Thiazide-like diuretic started recently ↓ Low sodium with low potassium, euvolaemic ↓ Indapamide-induced hyponatraemia
exam_trap: B, urinary tract infection with delirium — tempting because infection is a common cause of confusion in older people, but there are no urinary symptoms and the electrolytes point to the new diuretic.
takeaway: New confusion soon after starting a thiazide-like diuretic: check sodium and suspect drug-induced hyponatraemia.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAQ15208). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A 59-year-old woman attends her GP for a blood pressure review. Amlodipine was started two months ago. Since then both ankles become puffy by the evening, improving overnight. She has no breathlessness on exertion or lying flat. Her jugular venous pressure is not raised, her chest is clear, her calves are soft and non-tender, and urine dipstick is negative for protein. Which is the most likely cause of her ankle swelling?
why_correct: Dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers such as amlodipine dilate precapillary arterioles, raising capillary pressure and causing dependent ankle oedema. It is common, dose-related and occurs without signs of fluid overload. Options include reducing the dose or switching or adding another antihypertensive; diuretics are generally ineffective for this type of oedema.
why_wrong: B. Heart failure would usually cause breathlessness, orthopnoea, a raised JVP or crackles. C. Bilateral DVT is uncommon and would cause calf pain and tenderness rather than symmetrical evening swelling. D. Nephrotic syndrome causes heavy proteinuria, which is absent. E. Hypothyroidism causes non-pitting swelling with other systemic features and is not linked to starting amlodipine.
pearl: Ankle oedema from amlodipine responds poorly to diuretics because it is caused by vasodilation, not fluid retention.
thinking: Bilateral ankle swelling after starting amlodipine ↓ No breathlessness, normal JVP and clear chest ↓ No proteinuria or calf tenderness ↓ Calcium-channel blocker-induced peripheral oedema
exam_trap: B, heart failure — tempting because ankle swelling is a classic sign of it, but she has no breathlessness, a normal JVP and a clear chest.
takeaway: Bilateral ankle oedema without fluid overload soon after starting amlodipine is a drug adverse effect.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAQ15209). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A 46-year-old man living in a homeless hostel sees the visiting GP. For two months he has had a productive cough, occasionally with streaks of blood, and he wakes drenched in sweat most nights. His trousers have become loose. Another resident of the hostel was recently started on a long course of treatment for a chest infection. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: A cough lasting weeks with haemoptysis, night sweats and weight loss in someone living in crowded shared accommodation, with a likely infectious contact, is the classic picture of pulmonary tuberculosis. Homelessness is a recognised UK risk group. He needs a chest X-ray and sputum samples for microscopy and culture, and active TB should be notified.
why_wrong: B. Community-acquired pneumonia is an acute illness over days, not two months of sweats and weight loss. C. Asthma causes variable wheeze and cough without haemoptysis or weight loss. D. Lung cancer is possible with haemoptysis and weight loss, but the drenching sweats and probable infectious contact make TB more likely here. E. Sarcoidosis usually causes a dry cough and is not linked to infectious contacts.
pearl: Chronic cough plus night sweats plus weight loss equals TB until proven otherwise, especially in UK risk groups such as homeless people, prisoners, recent migrants from high-incidence countries and those with a known contact.
thinking: Two-month productive cough with blood streaks ↓ Night sweats and weight loss ↓ Shared hostel and a resident on long-term treatment ↓ Pulmonary tuberculosis
exam_trap: D, Lung cancer — haemoptysis with weight loss is a cancer red flag and must not be ignored, but drenching night sweats and a probable infectious contact make TB the most likely single diagnosis.
takeaway: Weeks of cough, sweats and weight loss in a UK risk group: investigate for TB.

stem: A 55-year-old man who has never smoked has a telephone consultation with his GP. He developed a cold in the spring and has had a dry, tickly cough ever since, now four months later. He feels otherwise well, has no breathlessness and has not coughed up blood. How should his cough be classified?
why_correct: In adults, a cough that has continued for more than eight weeks is defined as chronic, so a cough lasting four months clearly meets this definition even though it began with a viral illness. Classifying it correctly matters because chronic cough warrants assessment, usually including a chest X-ray and spirometry, and consideration of common causes such as asthma, reflux and upper airway cough syndrome.
why_wrong: A. An acute cough lasts only a few weeks. B. Acute bronchitis is a self-limiting illness of weeks, not months. D. A post-viral subacute cough settles within about two months, which this has outlasted. E. Recurrent cough describes repeated separate episodes rather than one continuous cough.
pearl: Adult cough: acute under 3 weeks, subacute 3 to 8 weeks (often post-viral), chronic beyond 8 weeks. A chronic cough deserves a chest X-ray and a look for asthma, reflux and rhinosinusitis.
thinking: Cough began with a cold ↓ It has continued for four months ↓ This is well beyond the subacute window ↓ Chronic cough
exam_trap: D, Subacute post-viral cough — the viral onset makes this tempting, but post-viral cough settles within weeks, and once a cough passes eight weeks it is chronic whatever started it.
takeaway: A cough lasting longer than eight weeks in an adult is chronic and needs assessment.

stem: A 38-year-old woman with asthma and nasal polyps took naproxen for period pain. Within an hour she became wheezy, with a streaming, blocked nose, and needed her reliever inhaler several times. She asks the community pharmacist what painkillers she should avoid in future. What is the most appropriate advice?

options.D: Avoid naproxen only, as ibuprofen is safe

correct_answer: B. Avoid all NSAIDs, including aspirin
why_correct: Asthma with nasal polyps and a respiratory reaction after an NSAID is NSAID-exacerbated respiratory disease. The reaction is due to COX-1 inhibition rather than allergy to one drug, so all non-selective NSAIDs, including aspirin and ibuprofen, can provoke it and should be avoided. The intolerance should be recorded clearly in her notes.
why_wrong: A. Paracetamol is generally tolerated and is a suitable alternative. C. Opioids do not provoke this reaction. D. Cross-reactivity between NSAIDs is the rule, so ibuprofen is not safe. E. Her reliever inhaler is needed to treat the bronchospasm, not avoided.
pearl: Asthma, nasal polyps and NSAID sensitivity form Samter's triad. The reaction is a class effect via COX-1 inhibition, so avoid all non-selective NSAIDs, including aspirin.
thinking: Asthma and nasal polyps ↓ Wheeze and rhinitis soon after naproxen ↓ COX-1 class effect, not a single-drug allergy ↓ Avoid all NSAIDs including aspirin
exam_trap: D, Avoid naproxen only — it seems sensible to avoid just the culprit, but the reaction is a class effect and other NSAIDs will provoke it too.
takeaway: Asthma flare after one NSAID means avoiding all NSAIDs, including aspirin.

stem: A 52-year-old woman with asthma tells her GP that food has lost its taste and that both sides of her nose have felt blocked for most of the past year, with a constant postnasal drip. Anterior rhinoscopy shows grey, glistening, mobile swellings in both nostrils that are not tender when touched with a probe. Which diagnosis best explains her symptoms?
why_correct: Bilateral nasal obstruction with loss of smell and taste and grey, glistening, mobile, insensate swellings is typical of nasal polyps, which are associated with chronic rhinosinusitis and asthma. First-line treatment is an intranasal corticosteroid. Polyps that are unilateral, bleeding or crusting need urgent ENT referral to exclude a tumour.
why_wrong: A. Inverted papilloma is usually unilateral and needs ENT assessment. B. A deviated septum is a fixed bony and cartilaginous deformity, not mobile swellings. C. Enlarged turbinates are pink and sensitive to touch, unlike polyps. D. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is typically unilateral, with bleeding, ear symptoms or neck nodes.
pearl: Polyps are grey, mobile and insensate; turbinates are pink and sensitive. Bilateral polyps with asthma are benign; a unilateral polyp needs ENT referral to exclude malignancy.
thinking: Long-standing bilateral blockage with loss of smell and taste ↓ Background of asthma ↓ Grey, glistening, mobile, insensate swellings on both sides ↓ Nasal polyps
exam_trap: C, Allergic rhinitis with turbinate hypertrophy — swollen turbinates can look like polyps, but they are pink and tender to the probe, whereas polyps are pale and insensate.
takeaway: Bilateral grey insensate nasal swellings with anosmia are polyps; unilateral needs ENT.

stem: A 52-year-old woman tells her GP that her eyes feel gritty and she is using lubricating drops many times a day. She cannot eat crackers without sipping water, her dentist has found several new cavities, and both cheeks in front of her ears have become swollen. She takes no regular medicines. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Dry, gritty eyes, a dry mouth causing difficulty with dry foods, dental caries and parotid swelling in a middle-aged woman are typical of Sjögren syndrome, an autoimmune condition targeting the lacrimal and salivary glands. Anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies support the diagnosis. Patients have an increased lifetime risk of lymphoma, so persistent gland swelling should be monitored.
why_wrong: A. Lupus causes rash, joint pain and multisystem features rather than predominant dryness. B. Sarcoidosis can enlarge the parotids but usually involves the lungs and lymph nodes. D. She takes no medicines, so a drug cause is unlikely. E. Rheumatoid arthritis presents with inflammatory joint disease, although secondary Sjögren syndrome can occur with it.
pearl: Dry eyes plus dry mouth plus parotid swelling suggest Sjögren syndrome. Check anti-Ro and anti-La, and remember the increased risk of lymphoma and of congenital heart block in pregnancy.
thinking: Gritty dry eyes needing frequent drops ↓ Dry mouth with dental caries ↓ Bilateral parotid swelling, no drug cause ↓ Sjögren syndrome
exam_trap: D, Medication-induced dry mouth — anticholinergic drugs are a common cause of dryness, but she takes no medicines and the parotid swelling suggests an autoimmune cause.
takeaway: Dry eyes, dry mouth and parotid swelling in a middle-aged woman: Sjögren syndrome.

stem: For several years, a 44-year-old teacher has noticed her fingers turning white then blue in the cold. Over the past year her finger skin has become thick and shiny and she can no longer make a full fist. There are small pitted scars on her fingertips, red spots on her face that blanch on pressure, and she has troublesome heartburn with food sticking on swallowing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Raynaud phenomenon with progressive thickening and tightening of the finger skin (sclerodactyly), digital pitting scars, telangiectasia and oesophageal dysmotility indicate systemic sclerosis. She needs rheumatology referral and screening for internal organ involvement, including the lungs, heart and kidneys.
why_wrong: A. Primary Raynaud phenomenon causes colour changes alone, without skin thickening or digital scars. C. Lupus causes rash, arthralgia and multisystem involvement but not sclerodactyly. D. Dermatomyositis causes proximal weakness with a heliotrope rash and Gottron papules. E. Rheumatoid arthritis causes inflammatory synovitis, not skin thickening.
pearl: Raynaud phenomenon plus skin tightening of the fingers, digital pits, telangiectasia and dysphagia suggest systemic sclerosis. Secondary Raynaud has digital ulcers or pits; primary does not.
thinking: Long-standing Raynaud phenomenon ↓ Thick, tight finger skin and digital pitting scars ↓ Telangiectasia and oesophageal symptoms ↓ Systemic sclerosis
exam_trap: A, Primary Raynaud phenomenon — the colour changes are the most obvious feature, but skin thickening and digital scars mean a secondary cause.
takeaway: Raynaud plus tight finger skin, digital pits and reflux suggests systemic sclerosis.

stem: A 71-year-old man with polymyalgia rheumatica has been taking oral prednisolone for four months and is expected to need it for at least a year. At a review, he asks why his GP has also prescribed weekly alendronic acid with daily calcium and vitamin D. Which complication of his steroid treatment are these medicines intended to prevent?
why_correct: Prolonged systemic glucocorticoid therapy reduces bone formation and increases bone loss, raising fracture risk early in treatment. Older people and those expected to take steroids for several months are offered bone protection, typically a bisphosphonate such as alendronic acid with adequate calcium and vitamin D. This reduces the risk of vertebral and other fragility fractures.
why_wrong: A. Peptic ulcer prevention uses a proton pump inhibitor, not a bisphosphonate. B. Adrenal suppression is managed by gradual tapering and sick-day guidance. C. Hyperglycaemia is managed by glucose monitoring and treatment. E. Steroid myopathy is not prevented by bisphosphonates.
pearl: Long-term oral steroids are a major cause of secondary osteoporosis. Consider bone protection early, particularly in older people or those with a previous fragility fracture.
thinking: Prolonged oral prednisolone ↓ Steroids reduce bone formation and increase bone loss ↓ Bisphosphonate plus calcium and vitamin D prescribed ↓ Prevention of osteoporosis and fragility fracture
exam_trap: A, Peptic ulceration — steroids are often co-prescribed with gastroprotection, but that is a proton pump inhibitor, whereas alendronic acid protects bone.
takeaway: Long-term steroids need bone protection to prevent osteoporotic fractures.

stem: A 44-year-old woman who moved to the UK from a country with a high incidence of tuberculosis 18 months ago sees her GP. She has had a cough for six weeks, feels feverish each evening, wakes soaked in sweat and has lost weight. Which is the most appropriate first investigation?
why_correct: When active pulmonary tuberculosis is suspected, a chest X-ray is the key first imaging test, looking for upper lobe consolidation, cavitation or lymphadenopathy. It should be accompanied by sputum samples for acid-fast bacilli microscopy, culture and molecular testing to confirm the diagnosis and check drug sensitivity.
why_wrong: B. A CT pulmonary angiogram looks for pulmonary embolism, which does not fit weeks of sweats and weight loss. C. Interferon-gamma release assays detect TB infection but cannot distinguish latent from active disease. D. Spirometry assesses airflow obstruction and does not diagnose infection. E. Bronchoscopy is reserved for when sputum cannot be obtained or is unhelpful.
pearl: Suspected active pulmonary TB: chest X-ray plus sputum samples for microscopy, culture and molecular testing. IGRA and Mantoux tests are for latent infection, not active disease.
thinking: Recent arrival from a high-incidence country ↓ Six weeks of cough, evening fevers, sweats and weight loss ↓ Suspected active pulmonary TB ↓ Chest X-ray first, with sputum samples
exam_trap: C, Interferon-gamma release assay alone — it is a TB blood test, but it detects infection rather than active disease and cannot replace imaging and sputum testing.
takeaway: Suspected active pulmonary TB: start with a chest X-ray and sputum samples.

stem: A 36-year-old woman was diagnosed with HIV last month and has a very low CD4 count; she has not yet started antiretroviral therapy. She now has three weeks of gradually worsening breathlessness on exertion and a dry cough. Her chest sounds almost clear, but her oxygen saturation falls markedly when she walks around the ward. Chest X-ray shows bilateral faint shadowing spreading out from the hila. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Subacute exertional breathlessness, a dry cough, marked desaturation on exercise despite few chest signs and bilateral perihilar interstitial shadowing in someone with advanced untreated HIV are typical of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia. It is an AIDS-defining opportunistic infection. First-line treatment is high-dose co-trimoxazole, with corticosteroids added when hypoxia is significant.
why_wrong: A. Pneumococcal pneumonia presents acutely with fever, productive cough and lobar consolidation. B. Pulmonary embolism causes sudden breathlessness and usually a clear chest X-ray. D. Kaposi sarcoma of the lung is less common and usually accompanies skin or mouth lesions. E. Mycoplasma pneumonia is not linked to severe immunosuppression and causes a milder, self-limiting illness.
pearl: In advanced HIV, gradual exertional breathlessness, dry cough and desaturation on walking with near-normal chest signs suggest PCP. Co-trimoxazole treats it and is also used as prophylaxis.
thinking: Advanced untreated HIV with low CD4 ↓ Subacute exertional breathlessness and dry cough ↓ Exercise desaturation with perihilar interstitial shadowing ↓ Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia
exam_trap: A, Pneumococcal pneumonia — bacterial pneumonia is common in HIV, but its acute onset, fever and lobar consolidation contrast with this subacute interstitial picture.
takeaway: Advanced HIV with exertional desaturation and perihilar shadowing: Pneumocystis pneumonia.

stem: A 27-year-old man attends an eye casualty clinic with a painful, red, blurred right eye. He has had crops of painful mouth ulcers several times a year since his teens and has scars on his scrotum from previous painful ulcers. A small pustule developed at the site of a blood test taken last week. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Recurrent painful oral ulcers, recurrent genital ulcers that scar, uveitis and pathergy (a pustule at a needle-puncture site) together form the classic picture of Behçet disease, a variable vessel vasculitis. Eye involvement can threaten sight, so he needs urgent ophthalmology management and rheumatology involvement.
why_wrong: A. Herpes simplex can cause recurrent oral or genital lesions but not uveitis with pathergy. B. Reactive arthritis causes arthritis, urethritis and conjunctivitis after infection, not recurrent oral and scarring genital ulcers. C. Crohn's disease can cause mouth ulcers and eye inflammation but genital ulcers and pathergy are not typical. E. Lupus can cause painless oral ulcers but not scarring genital ulcers or pathergy.
pearl: Recurrent oral ulcers plus genital ulcers, uveitis, skin lesions or pathergy suggest Behçet disease. It is more common in people from the Middle East and along the historic Silk Road.
thinking: Recurrent painful mouth ulcers ↓ Scarring genital ulcers ↓ Uveitis and pathergy reaction ↓ Behçet disease
exam_trap: C, Crohn's disease — oral ulcers and eye inflammation occur in Crohn's, but recurrent scarring genital ulcers and pathergy are characteristic of Behçet disease.
takeaway: Recurrent oral and genital ulcers with uveitis and pathergy suggest Behçet disease.

stem: A 29-year-old woman who works night shifts in a warehouse and rarely goes outside in daylight has had months of aching in her ribs and hips. She now struggles to climb stairs and to rise from a low chair without using her arms. Blood tests show a low-normal calcium, low phosphate, raised alkaline phosphatase and very low vitamin D. Which diagnosis fits best?
why_correct: Very low vitamin D impairs mineralisation of bone, causing diffuse bone pain and tenderness, proximal muscle weakness and a waddling gait. Biochemistry typically shows low or low-normal calcium, low phosphate, a raised alkaline phosphatase and secondary hyperparathyroidism. Limited sunlight exposure is a common UK cause, and treatment is vitamin D replacement with adequate calcium.
why_wrong: A. Osteoporosis is painless until a fracture occurs, and bone biochemistry is normal. B. Polymyositis causes proximal weakness with a raised creatine kinase, not bone pain and vitamin D deficiency. D. Paget disease typically affects older adults, with an isolated raised alkaline phosphatase and normal vitamin D. E. Primary hyperparathyroidism causes a raised calcium.
pearl: Osteomalacia: bone pain, proximal myopathy, low vitamin D, low or normal calcium, low phosphate and raised ALP. Osteoporosis: normal biochemistry and no pain until fracture.
thinking: Little sunlight exposure ↓ Diffuse bone pain and proximal muscle weakness ↓ Low vitamin D, low phosphate, raised ALP ↓ Osteomalacia
exam_trap: A, Osteoporosis — both weaken bone, but osteoporosis has normal biochemistry and no pain until fracture, whereas osteomalacia causes pain and abnormal bone chemistry.
takeaway: Bone pain, proximal weakness, low vitamin D and raised ALP point to osteomalacia.

stem: A 49-year-old woman with obesity and hypertension sees her GP about tiredness. She wakes with headaches, never feels refreshed and nods off while watching television in the evening. Her husband has moved to the spare room because she snores very loudly and he has heard her choke and gasp during the night. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Loud snoring with witnessed choking or gasping, unrefreshing sleep, morning headaches and excessive daytime sleepiness in a person with obesity and hypertension are typical of obstructive sleep apnoea, caused by repeated upper airway collapse during sleep. She should be assessed with a sleepiness score and referred for a sleep study. Weight loss helps, and CPAP is the main treatment for moderate to severe disease.
why_wrong: A. Narcolepsy causes sleep attacks and cataplexy, not loud snoring with choking. B. Hypothyroidism can cause tiredness and weight gain but does not explain witnessed choking episodes. D. Insomnia involves difficulty sleeping rather than excessive daytime sleepiness. E. Depression causes low mood and fatigue rather than snoring and nocturnal gasping.
pearl: Snoring, witnessed apnoeas or choking, and daytime sleepiness suggest OSA. Risk factors include obesity, a large neck and hypertension; ask about driving if sleepiness is excessive.
thinking: Obesity and hypertension ↓ Loud snoring with witnessed choking and gasping ↓ Unrefreshing sleep, morning headaches, daytime sleepiness ↓ Obstructive sleep apnoea
exam_trap: B, Hypothyroidism — it causes tiredness and weight gain and is worth checking, but it does not explain the witnessed choking and gasping during sleep.
takeaway: Snoring with witnessed choking and daytime sleepiness suggests obstructive sleep apnoea.

stem: A 22-year-old man telephones his GP surgery with three days of stinging when passing urine and a clear discharge from the tip of his penis. He started a new sexual relationship a fortnight ago and did not use condoms. He has no fever or loin pain. How should he be managed?

options.A: Prescribe trimethoprim for a urinary tract infection
options.D: Arrange testing for sexually transmitted infections, ideally via a sexual health clinic
options.E: Advise more fluids and review if not better in two weeks

correct_answer: D. Arrange testing for sexually transmitted infections, ideally via a sexual health clinic
why_correct: Dysuria with urethral discharge after unprotected sex suggests urethritis from a sexually transmitted infection, most commonly chlamydia or gonorrhoea. He should be assessed for STIs, ideally at a sexual health service, with nucleic acid amplification testing, treatment guided by the findings and partner notification. Urinary tract infection is uncommon in young men and should not be assumed.
why_wrong: A. Treating presumed UTI without STI testing may miss gonorrhoea or chlamydia and drives resistance. B. Urgent urology referral is not indicated for urethritis in a young man. C. Imaging does not diagnose urethritis. E. Delay risks complications such as epididymitis and onward transmission.
pearl: Urethral discharge in a man is an STI until proven otherwise; gonorrhoea treatment should be guided by culture and sensitivity because of rising resistance.
thinking: Dysuria and urethral discharge ↓ recent unprotected sex ↓ young man, so UTI unlikely ↓ STI assessment
exam_trap: A, trimethoprim for a urinary tract infection — dysuria triggers a UTI reflex, but discharge after unprotected sex makes an STI far more likely, and UTI antibiotics will not treat it reliably.
takeaway: Dysuria with discharge after unprotected sex needs STI testing, not presumed UTI treatment.

stem: A 9-year-old boy with asthma is reviewed by the practice nurse. His mother says his cough and wheeze flare every year from late spring into summer, at the same time as he has sneezing and itchy, watery eyes. His symptoms are worse on dry, windy days and settle by the autumn. Which category of trigger best explains his flares?
why_correct: Seasonal flares in late spring and summer, alongside hay fever symptoms, point to an inhaled allergen such as grass pollen acting on sensitised airways. Recognising this allows avoidance advice, treatment of the allergic rhinitis and stepping up preventer therapy ahead of the pollen season.
why_wrong: B. Viral infections cause flares mainly in autumn and winter and are not tied to hay fever symptoms. C. Exercise-induced symptoms occur during or after activity rather than seasonally. D. Cold air triggers symptoms mainly in winter. E. Irritants cause symptoms on exposure throughout the year rather than a seasonal pattern.
pearl: Treating co-existing allergic rhinitis, for example with an intranasal corticosteroid, can improve asthma control in children with pollen-triggered symptoms.
thinking: Asthma flares in late spring and summer ↓ with sneezing and itchy eyes ↓ worse on dry windy days (high pollen) ↓ inhaled allergen
exam_trap: B, viral respiratory infection — the commonest trigger of childhood asthma attacks overall, but its peak is in winter and it does not come with itchy eyes.
takeaway: Seasonal asthma flares with hay fever symptoms point to an inhaled allergen such as pollen.

stem: A 72-year-old man is reviewed on a stroke rehabilitation ward three weeks after a left middle cerebral artery infarct. Nursing staff report that he coughs and splutters during meals and his voice sounds wet and gurgly after drinks. He has had two chest infections since admission. Which underlying problem best explains these findings?

options.E: Hospital-acquired infection from poor hand hygiene

correct_answer: A. Aspiration due to unsafe swallowing
why_correct: Coughing while eating and drinking, a wet voice after swallowing and recurrent chest infections indicate dysphagia with aspiration, a common complication after stroke. Oral intake should be reviewed and his swallow formally reassessed by a speech and language therapist, who can advise on safe food and fluid textures and positioning.
why_wrong: B. Reflux causes heartburn and regurgitation, not coughing during swallowing with a wet voice. C. Heart failure causes breathlessness and orthopnoea, not symptoms linked to eating. D. Bronchiectasis causes chronic daily productive cough and would not begin with a stroke. E. Hospital infection does not explain coughing specifically during meals.
pearl: Patients with acute stroke should have their swallow screened before receiving any food, fluid or oral medication, with specialist assessment if the screen is failed.
thinking: Recent stroke ↓ coughing during meals and wet voice after drinks ↓ recurrent chest infections ↓ aspiration from unsafe swallowing
exam_trap: E, hospital-acquired infection from poor hand hygiene — recurrent inpatient chest infections tempt this, but the link to eating and a wet voice points to aspiration.
takeaway: Coughing on eating, a wet voice and recurrent chest infections after stroke mean aspiration: get a swallow assessment.

stem: A 34-year-old woman tells her GP that when she takes food from the freezer or walks to work on a chilly morning, several fingers suddenly turn pale and numb. They then become dusky purple and, on rewarming, flush and throb. Between episodes her hands look normal, and there are no ulcers, rashes or joint symptoms. What is this called?
why_correct: Episodic, cold-triggered colour change of the fingers from white (vasospasm) to blue (deoxygenation) to red (reactive hyperaemia) is Raynaud phenomenon. Normal hands between attacks with no ulcers, rash or joint symptoms suggest the primary form. Management is keeping the whole body and hands warm and stopping smoking, with nifedipine if symptoms are troublesome.
why_wrong: A. Chilblains are itchy or painful red-purple swellings that persist for days after cold exposure. B. Acrocyanosis is persistent, painless blue discolouration rather than episodic colour change. D. Carpal tunnel syndrome causes tingling in the median nerve distribution without colour change. E. Frostbite follows prolonged freezing exposure and causes tissue injury, not brief reversible episodes.
pearl: Features suggesting secondary Raynaud include onset later in life, digital ulcers, asymmetry, abnormal nailfold capillaries and symptoms of connective tissue disease.
thinking: Episodic cold-triggered finger changes ↓ white then blue then red ↓ normal between attacks ↓ Raynaud phenomenon
exam_trap: A, chilblains — also cold-related and affecting the fingers, but they are persistent inflammatory swellings rather than brief colour changes.
takeaway: Cold-triggered white-blue-red colour change of the fingers is Raynaud phenomenon.

stem: A 52-year-old man has noticed over four months that he struggles to lift his arms to shave and to get up from a low sofa. His thigh and upper arm muscles ache slightly. There is no rash, double vision or drooping of the eyelids, and sensation and reflexes are normal. He takes no regular medicines. His creatine kinase is markedly raised. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Gradually progressive, symmetrical weakness of the shoulder and hip girdle muscles with a markedly raised creatine kinase and normal sensation suggests an inflammatory myopathy such as polymyositis. The absence of rash argues against dermatomyositis. Further assessment includes myositis antibodies, EMG, muscle MRI or biopsy, and screening for an underlying malignancy.
why_wrong: A. Polymyalgia rheumatica causes pain and stiffness rather than true weakness, with a normal creatine kinase. C. Myasthenia gravis causes fatigable weakness, often with ptosis and double vision, and a normal creatine kinase. D. Guillain–Barré syndrome causes rapidly ascending weakness with lost reflexes over days. E. Motor neurone disease causes mixed upper and lower motor neurone signs such as fasciculations and brisk reflexes, without a markedly raised creatine kinase.
pearl: True proximal weakness with a high creatine kinase points to myopathy; stiffness with normal strength and a normal creatine kinase points to polymyalgia rheumatica.
thinking: Progressive difficulty lifting arms and rising from a seat ↓ symmetrical proximal weakness ↓ markedly raised creatine kinase, normal sensation, no rash ↓ polymyositis
exam_trap: A, polymyalgia rheumatica — also affects the shoulders and hips in older adults, but it causes stiffness rather than true weakness and does not raise creatine kinase.
takeaway: Symmetrical proximal weakness with a raised creatine kinase suggests an inflammatory myopathy such as polymyositis.

stem: An 81-year-old man has had three episodes over the past year of a hot, swollen knee or wrist, each settling over about a week.
