He is now seen on the medical admissions unit with a swollen left knee. A knee radiograph shows a thin line of calcification running through the cartilage and menisci, parallel to the joint surface. Synovial fluid Gram stain shows no organisms. Which diagnosis fits best?
why_correct: Calcification within articular cartilage and menisci (chondrocalcinosis) is the radiographic hallmark of calcium pyrophosphate deposition, which causes recurrent acute attacks of large-joint inflammation known as pseudogout, typically in the knee or wrist of older adults. Polarised microscopy of the aspirate would show weakly positively birefringent rhomboid crystals.
why_wrong: B. Gout classically affects the first toe joint and causes punched-out erosions rather than cartilage calcification. C. Reactive arthritis affects younger adults after a gut or genital infection. D. Septic arthritis is a single acute infection, not recurrent self-limiting episodes, and a negative Gram stain with chondrocalcinosis favours crystals, although culture is still needed. E. Osteoarthritis causes chronic mechanical pain with joint-space narrowing and osteophytes, not acute hot joints with chondrocalcinosis.
pearl: Chondrocalcinosis on an X-ray of an older person with recurrent hot knees or wrists points to calcium pyrophosphate disease. Always send the aspirate for culture, as infection and crystals can coexist.
thinking: Recurrent self-limiting hot large joints in an older man ↓ knee and wrist involvement ↓ linear calcification within cartilage on X-ray ↓ Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease
exam_trap: B, Gout — recurrent acute monoarthritis suggests gout, but gout favours the first toe joint and does not cause linear cartilage calcification.
takeaway: Recurrent hot knees or wrists with chondrocalcinosis indicate calcium pyrophosphate deposition.

stem: A 32-year-old woman at 26 weeks of her second pregnancy attends the antenatal clinic. She was offered a glucose tolerance test because her body mass index is raised and her first baby was large. Her booking HbA1c was normal, she has no previous history of diabetes, and both the fasting and 2-hour glucose values on the test are now raised. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Hyperglycaemia first detected in the second or third trimester in a woman with a normal booking HbA1c and no prior diabetes is gestational diabetes. It results from pregnancy-related insulin resistance, is first managed with diet and exercise, and needs postnatal glucose testing because of a raised lifetime risk of type 2 diabetes.
why_wrong: A. A normal booking HbA1c makes pre-existing type 2 diabetes unlikely. C. Maturity-onset diabetes of the young is a monogenic diabetes with a strong family history, and is not suggested here. D. Although insulin resistance rises in pregnancy, an abnormal glucose tolerance test is not normal. E. Type 1 diabetes presents with weight loss, polyuria and ketosis rather than an abnormal screening test.
pearl: Risk factors for gestational diabetes include a raised BMI, a previous large baby, previous gestational diabetes, a family history of diabetes and certain ethnic backgrounds. Recheck glucose after delivery.
thinking: Glucose tolerance test offered for risk factors ↓ raised values at 26 weeks ↓ normal booking HbA1c and no previous diabetes ↓ Gestational diabetes mellitus
exam_trap: A, Pre-existing type 2 diabetes — her risk factors overlap with type 2 diabetes, but the normal booking HbA1c shows the hyperglycaemia arose during pregnancy.
takeaway: Hyperglycaemia first found in later pregnancy after a normal booking HbA1c is gestational diabetes.

stem: A 47-year-old woman has a telephone consultation with her GP. Over the past eight months her cycles have lengthened to every six to nine weeks, and she wakes drenched in sweat most nights. She feels irritable and tired. Her last bleed was five weeks ago. She is otherwise well. Which term best describes her situation?
why_correct: Changing cycle length with vasomotor symptoms such as night sweats, while periods are still occurring, describes the perimenopause. NICE advises that in women over 45 with typical symptoms this can be diagnosed clinically without measuring FSH.
why_wrong: A. Premature ovarian insufficiency refers to loss of ovarian function before the age of 40. B. Postmenopause is diagnosed only after 12 months without a period, and she bled five weeks ago. D. Hypothyroidism causes tiredness but not night sweats with lengthening cycles in this pattern. E. Polycystic ovary syndrome causes long-standing irregular cycles from early adulthood, often with hirsutism, not new vasomotor symptoms in the late forties.
pearl: Over 45 with irregular periods and vasomotor symptoms: perimenopause is a clinical diagnosis. Remind her that contraception is still needed until menopause is confirmed.
thinking: Woman in her late forties ↓ lengthening cycles but still bleeding ↓ night sweats and mood change ↓ Perimenopause
exam_trap: B, Postmenopause — vasomotor symptoms suggest menopause, but postmenopause requires a full year without periods.
takeaway: Irregular but continuing periods with vasomotor symptoms over 45 indicate perimenopause.

stem: A 17-year-old is referred to the adolescent gynaecology clinic because she has never had a period. She is tall, with well-developed breasts, but has very scanty hair in the axillae and pubic area. There is a small, firm swelling in each groin. Pelvic ultrasound shows no uterus. Which diagnosis is most probable?
why_correct: In complete androgen insensitivity a 46,XY individual has testes, often in the groin or abdomen, that produce testosterone which the tissues cannot respond to. Testosterone is converted to oestrogen, giving breast development, while lack of androgen effect causes scanty body hair, and anti-Müllerian hormone from the testes prevents a uterus forming.
why_wrong: A. Müllerian agenesis also causes an absent uterus with normal breasts, but pubic and axillary hair are normal because androgen action is intact. B. Turner syndrome causes short stature and absent breast development from ovarian failure. C. Congenital adrenal hyperplasia causes androgen excess with virilisation, not scanty hair. E. Kallmann syndrome causes absent puberty with poor breast development and loss of smell.
pearl: Primary amenorrhoea with breasts but no uterus: check body hair. Scanty hair means androgen insensitivity; normal hair means Müllerian agenesis. Confirm with karyotype.
thinking: Primary amenorrhoea with good breast development ↓ absent uterus ↓ scanty pubic and axillary hair plus groin swellings that are likely testes ↓ Androgen insensitivity syndrome
exam_trap: A, Mayer–Rokitansky–Küster–Hauser syndrome — it shares primary amenorrhoea, normal breasts and an absent uterus, but body hair is normal because the patient is 46,XX with normal androgen response.
takeaway: Breasts, no uterus and scanty body hair point to androgen insensitivity syndrome.

stem: A 17-year-old attends her GP because she has not started her periods. She has no cyclical pelvic pain. She has normal height, normal breast development and normal pubic and axillary hair. Pelvic ultrasound shows two normal-looking ovaries, but no uterus can be seen. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Mayer–Rokitansky–Küster–Hauser syndrome (Müllerian agenesis) is failure of the uterus and upper vagina to develop in a 46,XX individual. Because the ovaries function normally, breast development and pubic and axillary hair are normal, but there is primary amenorrhoea with an absent uterus.
why_wrong: A. Androgen insensitivity also causes an absent uterus with breasts, but pubic and axillary hair are scanty and gonads are testes, not ovaries. B. Turner syndrome causes short stature and poor breast development from ovarian failure. C. An imperforate hymen causes cyclical pain with a normal uterus filled with blood. E. Constitutional delay produces delayed breast and hair development, not complete puberty with an absent uterus.
pearl: Normal secondary sexual characteristics with primary amenorrhoea suggest an anatomical cause. Absent uterus with normal hair and ovaries is Müllerian agenesis.
thinking: Primary amenorrhoea with normal breasts and normal body hair ↓ ovaries present, so ovarian and androgen function intact ↓ uterus absent ↓ Mayer–Rokitansky–Küster–Hauser syndrome
exam_trap: A, Androgen insensitivity syndrome — breasts with an absent uterus suggest it, but normal pubic and axillary hair and visible ovaries rule it out.
takeaway: Primary amenorrhoea with normal hair and ovaries but no uterus indicates Müllerian agenesis.

stem: A 71-year-old woman with long-standing hypertension and type 2 diabetes wakes with weakness of the left side of her face, her left arm and her left leg, all affected to a similar degree. Her speech content and understanding are normal, her visual fields are full and she has no neglect of the left side. Sensation is intact. Which type of stroke is most likely?
why_correct: A pure motor deficit affecting the face, arm and leg equally, without cortical signs such as dysphasia, visual field loss or neglect, is typical of a lacunar infarct. These small deep infarcts in the internal capsule or pons result from small-vessel disease, for which hypertension and diabetes are major risk factors.
why_wrong: A. A total anterior circulation infarct needs weakness plus both a higher cortical deficit and a visual field defect. B. A partial anterior circulation infarct includes a cortical feature such as dysphasia or neglect. D. Posterior circulation strokes cause cerebellar, brainstem or isolated visual field signs. E. A spinal cord lesion cannot cause facial weakness.
pearl: Lacunar strokes are pure motor, pure sensory, sensorimotor or ataxic hemiparesis syndromes without cortical signs. Cortical signs such as dysphasia, neglect or field loss point to an anterior circulation stroke.
thinking: Sudden one-sided weakness of face, arm and leg equally ↓ no dysphasia, field loss or neglect ↓ small-vessel risk factors ↓ Lacunar infarct
exam_trap: B, Partial anterior circulation infarct — dense one-sided weakness suggests a larger stroke, but without any cortical sign it does not meet the definition.
takeaway: Equal face, arm and leg weakness without cortical signs indicates a lacunar infarct.

stem: A 59-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes for 15 years attends her annual diabetes foot check. She says both feet tingle and feel numb, as though she is walking on cotton wool, and are worse at night. Ankle reflexes are absent on both sides and she cannot feel the monofilament on either sole. Muscle power in her legs is normal. Which pattern of nerve damage best fits?
why_correct: Long-standing diabetes typically damages the longest nerves first, giving symmetrical sensory loss, paraesthesia and burning in a stocking distribution with reduced ankle reflexes. Loss of protective sensation on monofilament testing places her at increased risk of foot ulceration, so she needs foot protection education and podiatry follow-up.
why_wrong: B. Mononeuritis multiplex affects several separate named nerves asymmetrically. C. Diabetic amyotrophy causes painful proximal thigh weakness and wasting, not distal sensory loss. D. Radiculopathy follows a dermatome, usually with back pain, and is rarely symmetrical. E. Tarsal tunnel syndrome is a focal entrapment affecting one sole, not a symmetrical stocking pattern.
pearl: Diabetic neuropathy is length-dependent: toes first, then a stocking distribution. Loss of monofilament sensation means loss of protective sensation and a high risk of foot ulcers.
thinking: Long-standing diabetes ↓ symmetrical distal tingling and numbness ↓ absent ankle reflexes and lost monofilament sensation on both feet ↓ Distal symmetrical polyneuropathy
exam_trap: C, Diabetic amyotrophy — it is a diabetes-specific neuropathy, so it tempts, but it causes proximal painful weakness rather than distal symmetrical sensory loss.
takeaway: Symmetrical stocking sensory loss in diabetes is distal symmetrical polyneuropathy.

stem: A 61-year-old man with prostate cancer that has spread to bone phones the acute oncology service. For two days he has had a band-like pain around his chest, his legs feel heavy and unsteady, and he is struggling to pass urine. On arrival at hospital he has brisk knee reflexes and reduced sensation below the level of his umbilicus. Which diagnosis must be urgently considered?
why_correct: Band-like radicular pain, bilateral leg weakness with upper motor neurone signs, a sensory level on the trunk and urinary retention in a man with bone metastases indicate metastatic spinal cord compression. He needs urgent whole-spine MRI, high-dose dexamethasone and urgent oncology and spinal surgical input to preserve function.
why_wrong: A. Cauda equina syndrome affects nerve roots below the cord, so it causes lower motor neurone signs and saddle anaesthesia rather than a thoracic sensory level and brisk reflexes. C. Guillain–Barré syndrome causes ascending weakness with absent reflexes and no sensory level. D. Peripheral neuropathy causes distal glove-and-stocking loss without a sensory level or retention. E. Mechanical back pain does not cause neurological deficit.
pearl: In a patient with cancer, new back pain with leg weakness, sensory change or sphincter problems is cord compression until MRI proves otherwise. Act on symptoms before deficits become permanent.
thinking: Known bone metastases ↓ band-like thoracic pain with heavy legs and urinary retention ↓ brisk reflexes and a sensory level on the trunk ↓ Spinal cord compression
exam_trap: A, Cauda equina syndrome — leg weakness with retention suggests it, but a thoracic sensory level and brisk reflexes place the lesion in the cord itself.
takeaway: Sensory level, leg weakness and retention in cancer means spinal cord compression: urgent MRI.

stem: A 38-year-old woman sees her GP with aching all over her body for over a year. She wakes unrefreshed, struggles to concentrate at work and feels exhausted. She is tender to light pressure at many sites across her trunk and limbs, but her joints look normal and muscle power is full. Full blood count, CRP, ESR, creatine kinase, thyroid function and calcium are all normal. What is the likeliest diagnosis?
why_correct: Chronic widespread pain with unrefreshing sleep, fatigue, cognitive difficulty and widespread tenderness, with normal examination of the joints and normal inflammatory and muscle markers, is typical of fibromyalgia. Management focuses on explanation, graded exercise, sleep hygiene and psychological approaches such as CBT.
why_wrong: A. Polymyalgia rheumatica affects people over 50 with shoulder and hip girdle stiffness and raised inflammatory markers. B. Hypothyroidism is excluded by normal thyroid function. D. Lupus usually causes inflammatory joint signs, rashes or abnormal blood tests. E. Polymyositis causes proximal weakness with a raised creatine kinase.
pearl: Fibromyalgia is a clinical diagnosis, but a short set of tests including inflammatory markers, thyroid function and creatine kinase is reasonable to exclude mimics.
thinking: Widespread pain over a year ↓ unrefreshing sleep, fatigue, poor concentration ↓ normal joints and muscle power ↓ normal inflammatory, thyroid and muscle tests ↓ fibromyalgia
exam_trap: A, polymyalgia rheumatica — widespread aching suggests it, but she is too young, has no girdle stiffness and her inflammatory markers are normal.
takeaway: Chronic widespread pain, fatigue and poor sleep with normal tests points to fibromyalgia.

stem: A 58-year-old woman with seropositive rheumatoid arthritis for 15 years attends the rheumatology clinic. She has noticed several painless rubbery lumps along the back of her forearm just below the elbow. They are firm, not fluctuant, mobile under normal overlying skin, and range from pea- to grape-sized. She smokes and takes methotrexate. What is the likeliest diagnosis?
why_correct: Firm, painless subcutaneous nodules over extensor surfaces and pressure points, particularly the proximal ulnar border of the forearm, are the commonest extra-articular feature of rheumatoid arthritis. They are associated with seropositive, long-standing disease and smoking, and methotrexate can increase nodule formation.
why_wrong: B. Olecranon bursitis is a single fluctuant fluid-filled swelling directly over the olecranon. C. Lipomas are soft and doughy rather than firm and are not linked to rheumatoid arthritis. D. Epidermoid cysts arise in the skin, often with a punctum. E. Ganglion cysts typically occur at the wrist or hand, arising from a joint or tendon sheath.
pearl: Rheumatoid nodules usually need no treatment, but they can ulcerate or become infected and occasionally occur in the lungs, where they may mimic other lesions on imaging.
thinking: Long-standing seropositive rheumatoid arthritis ↓ smoker on methotrexate ↓ firm painless non-fluctuant lumps ↓ extensor forearm below elbow ↓ rheumatoid nodules
exam_trap: B, olecranon bursitis — it occurs at the same site and is common in rheumatoid arthritis, but it is a single fluctuant swelling, not several firm nodules.
takeaway: Firm, painless lumps on the extensor forearm in seropositive RA are rheumatoid nodules.

stem: A 26-year-old woman in her first pregnancy, at 40 weeks and 3 days, attends the midwife-led unit. Yesterday she had irregular tightenings that came and went. Now the contractions are strong, regular and last about a minute each, and she has to stop and breathe through them. Her membranes are intact and there is no vaginal bleeding. On vaginal examination the cervix is fully effaced and has dilated further since an examination two hours earlier, but it is not yet fully dilated. What best describes her current situation?
correct_answer: D. Established first stage of labour
why_correct: The established first stage of labour is defined by regular painful contractions together with progressive cervical dilatation. Her earlier irregular tightenings were the latent phase, and the change in her cervix between examinations confirms she has progressed into established labour. Progress, maternal observations and fetal heart rate are now monitored regularly.
why_wrong: A. Braxton Hicks contractions are irregular, usually painless and produce no cervical change. B. Her membranes are intact. C. Abruption causes constant pain, a tense tender uterus and often bleeding. E. The second stage starts only once the cervix is fully dilated.
pearl: Women in the latent phase are usually supported at home if well, with advice to return when contractions become regular and strong or if waters break, bleeding occurs or fetal movements reduce.
thinking: Term pregnancy ↓ irregular tightenings yesterday = latent phase ↓ now strong regular contractions ↓ progressive cervical dilatation, not yet full ↓ established first stage of labour
exam_trap: A, Braxton Hicks contractions — tightenings at term can be dismissed as practice contractions, but these are regular, painful and changing the cervix.
takeaway: Regular painful contractions with progressive cervical dilatation mean established first-stage labour.

stem: A 37-year-old woman having her fourth baby delivers vaginally after a long labour augmented with an oxytocin infusion. The placenta and membranes are delivered and checked as complete, and the perineum is intact. Twenty minutes later there is brisk vaginal bleeding. On abdominal palpation the fundus is above the umbilicus and feels soft, but it firms up when rubbed. Which is the likeliest cause of the bleeding?
why_correct: Uterine atony is the commonest cause of primary postpartum haemorrhage. A soft, high fundus that contracts with rubbing confirms the uterus is failing to contract to compress the placental bed vessels. Risk factors here include multiparity and a prolonged oxytocin-augmented labour. Management includes calling for help, uterine massage, uterotonics and resuscitation.
why_wrong: B. Retained tissue is less likely as the placenta and membranes were checked and complete. C. Trauma causes bleeding despite a well-contracted uterus, and her perineum is intact. D. Coagulopathy is uncommon without risk factors such as abruption, pre-eclampsia or massive transfusion. E. Uterine inversion causes sudden shock with the fundus absent or dimpled on palpation.
pearl: Remember the 4 Ts of postpartum haemorrhage: tone, trauma, tissue and thrombin. Tone is by far the commonest.
thinking: Brisk bleeding soon after delivery ↓ placenta complete, perineum intact ↓ soft, high fundus that firms when rubbed ↓ uterus not contracting ↓ uterine atony
exam_trap: B, retained placental tissue — it is a common cause of PPH, but the placenta and membranes were checked as complete and the uterus responds to massage.
takeaway: A soft, high uterus with heavy bleeding after birth means atony, the commonest cause of PPH.

stem: A 31-year-old woman attends her GP because she plans to stop her combined contraceptive pill next month to try for a baby. She is healthy, takes no medicines, has a normal BMI and no family history of birth defects. She asks which supplement will reduce her baby's risk of spina bifida. Which supplement should she be advised to take?
why_correct: Folic acid taken from before conception until the end of the first trimester reduces the risk of neural tube defects such as spina bifida and anencephaly. The neural tube closes very early, often before a woman knows she is pregnant, so starting before conception is important. A standard low dose is advised for women without additional risk factors.
why_wrong: A. Vitamin D is recommended in pregnancy for bone health, not to prevent neural tube defects. B. Iron is given for anaemia, not neural tube defect prevention. D. High-dose vitamin A should be avoided in pregnancy because it is teratogenic. E. Iodine is important for fetal brain development but does not prevent neural tube defects.
pearl: A higher dose of folic acid is advised for women at increased risk, for example with a previous neural tube defect, diabetes, obesity, sickle cell disease or taking antiepileptic drugs.
thinking: Planning pregnancy ↓ wants to prevent spina bifida ↓ neural tube closes in early first trimester ↓ supplement must start before conception ↓ folic acid
exam_trap: A, vitamin D — it is also routinely recommended in pregnancy in the UK, but its role is bone health, not neural tube protection.
takeaway: Start folic acid before conception and continue through the first trimester to prevent neural tube defects.

stem: A 72-year-old man with lung cancer receiving palliative care is visited at home by his GP. Over three days he has become unsteady and both legs feel numb from his navel downwards. He has a mid-back pain that is worse when he coughs. He has not passed urine since the morning and a tender, distended bladder is palpable. He is fully orientated. Which diagnosis must be considered urgently?
why_correct: Back pain worse on coughing with progressive leg symptoms, a sensory level on the trunk and urinary retention in a patient with cancer are features of spinal cord compression. Lung cancer frequently spreads to the spine. Even in palliative care, prompt recognition matters because urgent treatment can preserve mobility and continence and improve quality of life.
why_wrong: A. Hypercalcaemia causes confusion, thirst, constipation and fatigue, not a sensory level. C. Brain metastases cause headache, seizures or focal weakness, not a sensory level with retention in an orientated patient. D. Peripheral neuropathy causes glove-and-stocking sensory loss, not a truncal level or retention. E. Opioids can cause retention but do not explain leg numbness with a sensory level.
pearl: A sensory level on the trunk localises the problem to the spinal cord. A level at the umbilicus corresponds to the T10 dermatome, and because cord segments lie higher than their matching vertebrae, the compressing lesion is at or above that level and often at a higher vertebral level than expected.
thinking: Known lung cancer ↓ mid-back pain worse on coughing ↓ leg numbness with a truncal sensory level ↓ urinary retention ↓ metastatic spinal cord compression
exam_trap: E, opioid-induced urinary retention — palliative patients on opioids often retain urine, but this does not explain the sensory level and unsteadiness.
takeaway: A sensory level with leg weakness and retention in cancer means spinal cord compression.

stem: A 41-year-old woman attends the gynaecology clinic with six months of bleeding between periods and periods that are heavier than before. Pelvic examination is normal and a cervical screening test is up to date and negative. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a normal-sized uterus with uniform myometrium and a small, well-circumscribed echogenic lesion within the endometrial cavity. Both ovaries are normal. What is the likeliest diagnosis?
why_correct: Endometrial polyps are localised overgrowths of endometrium projecting into the uterine cavity. They typically cause intermenstrual and heavy menstrual bleeding and appear as a focal, well-defined echogenic lesion within the cavity on ultrasound. Hysteroscopic removal confirms the diagnosis histologically and usually treats the bleeding.
why_wrong: B. Adenomyosis causes a diffusely bulky, tender uterus with heterogeneous myometrium, often with painful periods. C. Hyperplasia causes diffuse thickening of the endometrium rather than a focal lesion. D. Cervical ectropion can cause postcoital or intermenstrual bleeding but is seen on the cervix, not within the uterine cavity. E. PCOS causes irregular periods with multiple ovarian follicles, and her ovaries are normal.
pearl: Polyps are usually benign but can harbour hyperplasia or cancer, particularly in postmenopausal women or those with abnormal bleeding, so removed polyps are sent for histology.
thinking: Intermenstrual and heavy bleeding ↓ normal uterine size and myometrium ↓ focal well-defined echogenic lesion within the cavity ↓ normal ovaries ↓ endometrial polyp
exam_trap: C, endometrial hyperplasia — abnormal bleeding with an endometrial abnormality suggests it, but hyperplasia is diffuse thickening, not a discrete lesion.
takeaway: A focal, well-defined lesion in the uterine cavity causing intermenstrual bleeding suggests an endometrial polyp.

stem: A 66-year-old right-handed woman is brought to the emergency department 40 minutes after her husband noticed her face drooping on the left and that she could not lift her left arm. She also reports reduced feeling in the left hand. She speaks fluently and follows commands correctly. Where is the lesion most likely to be?
why_correct: Motor and sensory pathways from the cerebral hemispheres cross the midline, so weakness and sensory loss affecting the left face, arm and hand localise to the right cerebral hemisphere. Preserved fluent speech and comprehension fit sparing of the dominant (left) hemisphere in a right-handed person. She needs immediate stroke assessment and brain imaging.
why_wrong: A. A left hemisphere lesion would cause right-sided weakness and, in a right-handed person, often dysphasia. C. A cerebellar lesion causes ataxia and incoordination rather than facial and arm weakness. D. A cervical cord lesion would not cause facial droop. E. A brachial plexus lesion would not affect the face and would not come on suddenly without trauma.
pearl: Facial involvement places the lesion above the spinal cord. Contralateral face and arm weakness with dysphasia suggests the dominant hemisphere; with neglect or inattention, think of the non-dominant hemisphere.
thinking: Sudden left face and arm weakness ↓ Left-sided sensory loss ↓ Pathways cross, so lesion is contralateral ↓ Speech preserved, dominant hemisphere spared ↓ Right cerebral hemisphere
exam_trap: A, left cerebral hemisphere — candidates sometimes localise to the same side as the symptoms, forgetting that the corticospinal and sensory pathways decussate.
takeaway: One-sided face and arm weakness localises to the opposite cerebral hemisphere.

stem: An 11-year-old boy is seen by the practice nurse because he has a night-time cough and wheezes when he runs in the cold. He had eczema in the creases of his elbows as an infant, and every summer he sneezes and has itchy, watery eyes. His father has hay fever. Which underlying predisposition best links these problems?
why_correct: Atopy is an inherited tendency to produce IgE antibodies against common environmental allergens. It underlies the clustering of eczema, allergic rhinitis and asthma in the same person and family. Nocturnal cough and wheeze with seasonal rhinoconjunctivitis and a history of infantile eczema fit this allergic background well.
why_wrong: A. Cystic fibrosis causes chronic productive cough, recurrent chest infections and poor growth rather than seasonal allergic symptoms. B. Primary ciliary dyskinesia causes chronic wet cough, sinusitis and ear disease from early life, not seasonal itch and sneezing. D. IgA deficiency predisposes to recurrent infections and does not explain eczema and hay fever. E. Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency causes early emphysema and liver disease in adults, not childhood atopic disease.
pearl: Ask about eczema, hay fever and family history in any child with wheeze; a personal or family history of atopy makes asthma more likely.
thinking: Night cough and exercise wheeze ↓ Infantile eczema ↓ Seasonal sneezing and itchy eyes ↓ Family history of hay fever ↓ Atopy
exam_trap: A, cystic fibrosis — it is a classic cause of respiratory symptoms in children, but it gives a chronic wet cough and infections, not seasonal allergic features with eczema.
takeaway: Eczema, hay fever and asthma clustering in one child reflect an atopic predisposition.

stem: A 47-year-old woman with asthma attends the emergency department with acute wheeze and chest tightness that began about an hour after she took ibuprofen for back pain. She has no rash, her lips and tongue are not swollen and her blood pressure is normal. For several years she has had a constantly blocked nose and has lost her sense of smell. Anterior rhinoscopy shows grey, glistening, insensate masses in both nostrils. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: The combination of asthma, chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps and bronchospasm triggered by aspirin or other NSAIDs is aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (Samter's triad). Inhibition of cyclo-oxygenase shifts arachidonic acid metabolism towards leukotriene production, causing bronchoconstriction. She should be advised to avoid aspirin and other NSAIDs.
why_wrong: A. Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis causes poorly controlled asthma with fleeting infiltrates and bronchiectasis, not NSAID-triggered wheeze with polyps. C. Anaphylaxis would usually involve skin, mucosal or circulatory features, which are absent. D. EGPA causes asthma and polyps but with marked eosinophilia and vasculitic features such as neuropathy or rash. E. Cystic fibrosis can cause nasal polyps but presents with chronic infection from childhood, not a drug-triggered asthma attack.
pearl: Ask every adult with asthma about reactions to aspirin or NSAIDs, especially if they have nasal polyps or anosmia. Paracetamol is the usual safer alternative for pain.
thinking: Asthma with wheeze after ibuprofen ↓ No skin or circulatory features ↓ Chronic blocked nose and anosmia ↓ Bilateral nasal polyps ↓ Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease
exam_trap: C, anaphylaxis to ibuprofen — a drug followed by wheeze suggests anaphylaxis, but the absence of skin, mucosal or circulatory involvement and the polyps point to a non-allergic COX-inhibitor reaction.
takeaway: Asthma, nasal polyps and NSAID-triggered bronchospasm make up aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease.

stem: A 38-year-old man sees his GP because both sides of his nose have felt blocked for most of the past six months. He has thick yellow-green mucus running down the back of his throat, a dull pressure across his cheeks and forehead that worsens when he bends forward, and food tastes bland. He has no nosebleeds, and examination of the nose shows swollen, inflamed mucosa on both sides. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Long-standing bilateral nasal obstruction with discoloured discharge, facial pressure and reduced smell or taste is the typical picture of chronic rhinosinusitis. The persistence over many months distinguishes it from an acute sinusitis. First-line management is usually saline nasal irrigation and an intranasal corticosteroid, with ENT referral if symptoms persist.
why_wrong: A. Allergic rhinitis causes clear watery discharge, sneezing and itch rather than purulent discharge with facial pressure. B. Acute sinusitis follows a cold and settles over a few weeks rather than persisting for months. C. Malignancy typically causes unilateral obstruction, bleeding or cranial nerve signs rather than symmetrical bilateral symptoms. E. A dental abscess causes localised tooth pain and swelling, not months of bilateral nasal obstruction.
pearl: Bilateral, persistent symptoms suggest inflammatory sinus disease; unilateral obstruction, bleeding or facial numbness are red flags that need urgent ENT assessment.
thinking: Bilateral blockage for months ↓ Purulent postnasal discharge ↓ Facial pressure worse on bending ↓ Reduced taste and smell ↓ Chronic rhinosinusitis
exam_trap: B, acute bacterial sinusitis — the purulent discharge and facial pain fit sinus infection, but symptoms lasting most of six months make it chronic rather than acute.
takeaway: Months of bilateral blockage, purulent discharge and facial pressure indicate chronic rhinosinusitis.

stem: A 34-year-old woman in her third pregnancy is on the antenatal ward at 39 weeks with an unstable lie. Shortly after her waters break spontaneously, the CTG shows a prolonged fetal bradycardia. On vaginal examination the midwife feels a soft, pulsating loop in the vagina below the presenting part. There is no vaginal bleeding. Which emergency has occurred?
why_correct: A pulsating loop felt below the presenting part after rupture of the membranes, with sudden fetal bradycardia, is umbilical cord prolapse. An unstable lie and multiparity are recognised risk factors because the presenting part does not fill the pelvis. It is an obstetric emergency: call for help, relieve pressure on the cord by elevating the presenting part or positioning the mother knees-to-chest, and arrange urgent delivery.
why_wrong: A. Abruption causes abdominal pain, a tense uterus and often bleeding rather than a palpable loop of cord. B. Vasa praevia causes fresh bleeding at membrane rupture with fetal compromise, and there is no bleeding. D. Uterine rupture causes severe pain, maternal collapse and loss of the presenting part, usually with a previous caesarean scar. E. Shoulder dystocia occurs after delivery of the head.
pearl: Avoid handling the cord to reduce vasospasm; keep it in the vagina, elevate the presenting part and consider filling the bladder while arranging the quickest safe delivery.
thinking: Unstable lie, multiparous ↓ Spontaneous rupture of membranes ↓ Sudden fetal bradycardia ↓ Pulsating loop below presenting part ↓ Umbilical cord prolapse
exam_trap: B, vasa praevia — fetal compromise immediately after membrane rupture suggests it, but vasa praevia presents with bleeding, and here a loop of cord is felt.
takeaway: Fetal bradycardia after membrane rupture with a palpable cord is cord prolapse: relieve compression.

stem: A 29-year-old woman sees her GP 10 days after a vaginal delivery because her bleeding has become heavier, with clots, instead of settling. The delivery notes record that the placenta appeared incomplete. On examination the uterus is larger than expected for this stage and mildly tender, and the cervical os is open. Which underlying problem best explains her bleeding?

options.B: Uterine atony from a full bladder

why_correct: Heavy bleeding that increases rather than settling after delivery, with a bulky uterus, an open os and an incomplete placenta at delivery, indicates retained products of conception. Retained tissue prevents normal involution and is a common cause of secondary postpartum haemorrhage, often with associated endometritis. She needs same-day obstetric review, ultrasound and antibiotics, with surgical evacuation if indicated.
why_wrong: B. Atony is a cause of primary postpartum haemorrhage in the first 24 hours rather than at 10 days. C. Trauma typically causes bleeding immediately after delivery with a well-contracted uterus. D. A coagulopathy would usually cause bleeding from the start, often with other bleeding sites. E. Normal lochia gradually lessens and becomes paler, rather than becoming heavier with clots.
pearl: Check the placenta and membranes for completeness after every delivery. Secondary postpartum haemorrhage is usually due to retained products or infection.
thinking: Bleeding increasing 10 days postpartum ↓ Placenta incomplete at delivery ↓ Bulky tender uterus ↓ Open cervical os ↓ Retained placental tissue
exam_trap: B, uterine atony — it is the commonest cause of postpartum haemorrhage overall, but it causes bleeding in the first day; late bleeding with an incomplete placenta points to retained tissue.
takeaway: Postpartum bleeding with an incomplete placenta and open os suggests retained products.

stem: A 19-year-old woman who gave birth to her first baby three days ago is brought to the emergency department by ambulance after a witnessed fit with jerking of all four limbs. Earlier that day she complained of a severe frontal headache and flashing lights. She has no history of seizures. Her blood pressure is markedly raised and urinalysis shows protein. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: A generalised seizure in a woman in the postnatal period with severe hypertension, proteinuria, headache and visual disturbance is eclampsia. Eclampsia can occur for several days after delivery, not only during pregnancy. Treatment is intravenous magnesium sulfate to control and prevent seizures, with blood pressure control.
why_wrong: A. A first seizure with severe hypertension and proteinuria after delivery should not be attributed to epilepsy. C. Venous sinus thrombosis is a postpartum cause of headache and seizure, but it does not explain proteinuria with marked hypertension. D. Hypoglycaemia should be checked but does not explain the hypertension and proteinuria. E. Vasovagal episodes are brief and do not cause a prolonged tonic-clonic seizure with hypertension.
pearl: Eclampsia can occur before, during or after delivery. Magnesium sulfate is first-line for eclamptic seizures, and calcium gluconate reverses magnesium toxicity.
thinking: Three days postpartum ↓ Headache and visual disturbance ↓ Generalised seizure ↓ Severe hypertension with proteinuria ↓ Eclampsia
exam_trap: C, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis — a postpartum woman with headache and seizure fits, but marked hypertension with proteinuria is the hallmark of eclampsia.
takeaway: Seizure with hypertension and proteinuria after delivery is eclampsia: give magnesium sulfate.

stem: A 36-year-old woman who smokes and uses a combined hormonal pill for contraception is brought to the emergency department an hour after she suddenly dropped her cup and could not stand. She has weakness of the left arm and leg, a left facial droop and slurred speech. She has no history of migraine, and her capillary blood glucose is normal. What diagnosis must be urgently considered?
why_correct: Sudden onset of focal neurological deficit, with face, arm and leg weakness and dysarthria, is a stroke until proven otherwise, whatever the patient's age. Smoking and combined hormonal contraception both raise the risk of ischaemic stroke. She needs immediate brain imaging so that thrombolysis or thrombectomy can be considered if appropriate.
why_wrong: A. Hemiplegic migraine is a diagnosis of exclusion, usually with a history of similar attacks and headache, and should not delay stroke assessment. B. Bell's palsy affects only the face and does not cause limb weakness. C. A functional disorder cannot be assumed before structural causes are excluded. E. Hypoglycaemia can mimic stroke, but her glucose is normal.
pearl: Young age does not exclude stroke. Always check glucose first, then image urgently. Combined hormonal contraception, smoking and migraine with aura add to stroke risk.
thinking: Sudden onset symptoms ↓ Face, arm and leg weakness on one side ↓ Dysarthria ↓ Glucose normal, no migraine history ↓ Acute stroke
exam_trap: A, hemiplegic migraine — a young woman with focal weakness tempts a migraine diagnosis, but with no migraine history and sudden deficit, stroke must be excluded first.
takeaway: Sudden focal neurological deficit is stroke until proven otherwise, even in the young.

stem: At her booking appointment, a 31-year-old woman in her first pregnancy is found to be blood group O RhD-negative with no red cell antibodies. Her partner is RhD-positive. The midwife explains that she will be offered routine anti-D immunoglobulin in the third trimester. What is the main purpose of this treatment?

options.B: To prevent maternal sensitisation to fetal RhD antigen
options.C: To prevent ABO incompatibility in the newborn
options.D: To reduce the risk of pre-eclampsia
options.E: To neutralise anti-D antibodies she already has

correct_answer: B. To prevent maternal sensitisation to fetal RhD antigen
why_correct: If an RhD-negative woman is exposed to RhD-positive fetal red cells, she may produce anti-D antibodies that cross the placenta and cause haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn, mainly in later pregnancies. Anti-D immunoglobulin clears fetal red cells from her circulation before her immune system responds. Routine antenatal prophylaxis, together with doses after sensitising events and after birth if the baby is RhD-positive, greatly reduces this risk.
why_wrong: A. Anti-D is preventive and does not treat fetal anaemia, which needs specialist fetal medicine care. C. Anti-D has no effect on ABO incompatibility. D. Anti-D does not affect the risk of pre-eclampsia. E. Anti-D cannot reverse sensitisation once a woman has formed her own antibodies.
pearl: Give anti-D after potentially sensitising events such as abdominal trauma, bleeding after 12 weeks, external cephalic version and amniocentesis, in addition to routine prophylaxis.
thinking: RhD-negative mother, RhD-positive partner ↓ Fetus may be RhD-positive ↓ Fetal cells entering maternal circulation ↓ Anti-D clears them before an immune response ↓ Prevents maternal sensitisation
exam_trap: A, treat existing fetal anaemia — anti-D is associated with haemolytic disease, but it is prophylactic and only works before the mother has been sensitised.
takeaway: Anti-D prevents RhD-negative mothers from becoming sensitised to fetal RhD-positive cells.

stem: A 5-year-old girl is brought to the GP because several children at her nursery have been unwell. She has had a mild fever for two days and very itchy spots that started on her scalp and chest. On examination there are red papules, clear fluid-filled blisters and crusted lesions side by side, mostly on the trunk, with a few shallow ulcers inside her mouth. Her palms and soles are spared. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Chickenpox causes intensely itchy crops of lesions that progress from papules to vesicles to crusts, so lesions at different stages are seen together. The rash is concentrated on the trunk, scalp and face and may involve the mouth. Management is usually supportive, with advice on keeping her away from nursery until all lesions have crusted.
why_wrong: A. Hand, foot and mouth disease causes mouth ulcers with vesicles on the hands and feet, which are spared here. B. Measles causes a maculopapular rash that starts behind the ears, with cough, conjunctivitis and coryza. C. Impetigo causes honey-crusted lesions, usually around the nose and mouth, not widespread vesicles. E. Scarlet fever causes a fine sandpaper-like rash with a strawberry tongue and sore throat.
pearl: Lesions at different stages concentrated on the trunk point to chickenpox. Avoid NSAIDs in chickenpox because of the association with severe skin infection.
thinking: Nursery outbreak, mild fever ↓ Very itchy rash starting on scalp and chest ↓ Papules, vesicles and crusts together ↓ Truncal distribution, palms spared ↓ Chickenpox
exam_trap: A, hand, foot and mouth disease — mouth ulcers with vesicles in a nursery child suggest it, but the truncal rash with crops at different stages and spared palms and soles fit chickenpox.
takeaway: Itchy truncal crops of papules, vesicles and crusts together indicate chickenpox.

stem: A 23-year-old woman attends a sexual health clinic asking to start 'the pill'. She gets headaches a few times a year that are preceded by about 20 minutes of zigzag lines spreading across her vision. She does not smoke and her blood pressure is normal. Which contraceptive method is contraindicated?
why_correct: Her headaches are preceded by a spreading visual disturbance, which is migraine with aura. Migraine with aura already increases the risk of ischaemic stroke, and oestrogen-containing contraception increases it further, so combined hormonal methods are contraindicated (UKMEC 4). Progestogen-only and non-hormonal methods are suitable alternatives.
why_wrong: A. The copper IUD contains no hormones and is safe in migraine with aura. B. The progestogen-only pill does not carry the stroke risk of oestrogen and can be used. C. The implant is progestogen-only and is suitable. D. The levonorgestrel IUS is progestogen-only and is suitable.
pearl: Ask about aura before prescribing combined contraception; if a woman on the combined pill develops new migraine with aura, stop it and switch to a progestogen-only or non-hormonal method.
thinking: Wants contraception ↓ Headache preceded by spreading visual disturbance ↓ Migraine with aura ↓ Oestrogen adds to stroke risk ↓ Combined pill contraindicated
exam_trap: B, progestogen-only pill — it is a hormonal pill and some assume all hormonal methods are unsafe in migraine, but the stroke risk relates to oestrogen.
takeaway: Migraine with aura contraindicates oestrogen-containing contraception; progestogen-only methods are fine.

stem: A 20-year-old woman phones her GP surgery for advice. She has norovirus and vomited about an hour after taking her combined contraceptive pill this morning. She has been taking the pill correctly for a year and had unprotected sex two days ago. What is the key issue with today's pill?

options.A: It may cause liver damage while she is unwell
options.B: Her risk of venous thromboembolism has greatly increased
options.C: She has received a hormone overdose
options.D: The pill may not have been absorbed, so contraceptive cover may be reduced
options.E: She will need to stop the pill permanently

correct_answer: D. The pill may not have been absorbed, so contraceptive cover may be reduced
why_correct: Vomiting soon after taking the combined pill, or severe persistent diarrhoea, can prevent the hormones being absorbed. The dose may therefore count as missed and contraceptive protection may be reduced. She should take another pill as soon as possible and follow missed-pill advice if the vomiting continues, including using extra precautions where advised.
why_wrong: A. A short gastrointestinal illness does not make the combined pill hepatotoxic. B. Dehydration may slightly increase thrombotic risk, but the main concern after early vomiting is loss of absorption. C. Vomiting reduces rather than increases the hormone absorbed. E. A brief illness does not mean she needs to stop the pill permanently.
pearl: If vomiting occurs within a few hours of taking an oral contraceptive, take another pill; if illness continues, treat each affected day as a missed pill.
thinking: Combined pill taken this morning ↓ Vomited shortly afterwards ↓ Hormone may not be absorbed ↓ Dose may count as missed ↓ Reduced contraceptive protection
exam_trap: B, venous thromboembolism — the combined pill is linked with VTE and dehydration may add to this, but the immediate issue after early vomiting is lost contraceptive cover.
takeaway: Vomiting soon after the combined pill can mean a missed dose and reduced protection.

stem: A 57-year-old woman with primary Sjögren's syndrome attends a rheumatology review. Her eyes feel gritty, and she needs a sip of water to swallow crackers or bread. She asks which problem in her mouth she is most at risk of as a result of her condition. Which complication is most likely?
why_correct: Saliva washes away food debris, buffers acids and has antibacterial properties that protect the teeth. When saliva is reduced, as in Sjögren's syndrome, dental decay develops rapidly, often at unusual sites such as the gum margins. Regular dental review, high-fluoride toothpaste and saliva substitutes or stimulants help reduce the risk.
why_wrong: A. Gingival hyperplasia is typically caused by drugs such as phenytoin, ciclosporin or calcium channel blockers. B. Oral lichen planus is a separate inflammatory condition and is not caused by dry mouth. C. Tonsillar enlargement is not a recognised consequence of reduced saliva. D. Macroglossia is associated with conditions such as amyloidosis or hypothyroidism, not dry mouth.
pearl: Dry mouth also predisposes to oral candidiasis. People with Sjögren's syndrome should have regular dental checks and be aware of their increased lymphoma risk.
thinking: Sjögren's syndrome ↓ Reduced saliva ↓ Loss of buffering and antibacterial protection ↓ Rapid tooth decay ↓ Dental caries
exam_trap: A, gingival hyperplasia — it is a familiar oral complication in exams, but it is drug-induced rather than caused by dry mouth.
takeaway: Chronic dry mouth removes saliva's protection and greatly increases the risk of dental caries.

stem: A 30-year-old woman developed aching in her right forearm after a heavy weight-training session two weeks ago. She now finds it hard to pick up coins. When asked to pinch a sheet of paper between her thumb and forefinger, the tips of these digits straighten so that the pads, rather than the tips, meet. Sensation in her hand is entirely normal. Which nerve lesion is most likely?

options.A: Median nerve at the carpal tunnel
options.E: Radial nerve at the spiral groove

why_correct: The anterior interosseous nerve is a purely motor branch of the median nerve in the forearm, supplying flexor pollicis longus, the lateral part of flexor digitorum profundus and pronator quadratus. Its injury weakens flexion of the thumb interphalangeal joint and the index finger distal interphalangeal joint, so she cannot form a tip-to-tip pinch. Because the nerve carries no skin sensation, sensation in the hand is normal.
why_wrong: A. Median nerve compression at the carpal tunnel causes sensory symptoms in the lateral fingers and thenar weakness rather than loss of long flexors. B. Ulnar nerve lesions weaken the intrinsic hand muscles and cause sensory loss in the little finger. D. The posterior interosseous nerve supplies finger and thumb extensors, causing finger drop without sensory loss. E. Radial nerve injury at the spiral groove causes wrist drop with sensory loss over the dorsum of the hand.
pearl: A pure motor deficit with loss of the tip-to-tip pinch (an inability to make an 'OK' sign) and normal sensation suggests an anterior interosseous nerve lesion.
thinking: Forearm pain after exertion ↓ Weak tip pinch, pads meet instead of tips ↓ Weak thumb IP and index DIP flexion ↓ No sensory loss ↓ Anterior interosseous nerve
exam_trap: A, median nerve at the carpal tunnel — the AIN is a median branch, but carpal tunnel syndrome causes sensory symptoms and thenar weakness, not loss of long flexors with normal sensation.
takeaway: Weak thumb and index tip flexion with normal sensation indicates anterior interosseous nerve palsy.

stem: A 44-year-old man attends the emergency department with two days of severe low back pain radiating down both legs. He has not passed urine since the morning but does not feel the urge to. Examination shows reduced pinprick sensation over the perineum, around the anus, over the buttocks and on the inner thighs. Which term best describes this sensory finding?
why_correct: Reduced sensation over the perineum, perianal region, buttocks and inner thighs, the areas that would contact a saddle, is saddle anaesthesia. It reflects compression of the sacral nerve roots and, with bilateral sciatica and painless urinary retention, strongly suggests cauda equina syndrome. He needs an emergency MRI of the lumbosacral spine and urgent spinal surgical referral.
why_wrong: A. L5 loss affects the lateral leg and dorsum of the foot, not the perineum. B. Stocking distribution loss is typical of peripheral neuropathy and affects the feet and lower legs. C. Dissociated sensory loss, as in syringomyelia, affects pain and temperature but spares other modalities in a cape distribution. D. Brown-Séquard syndrome causes ipsilateral weakness and loss of proprioception with contralateral loss of pain sensation.
pearl: Red flags for cauda equina syndrome include bilateral sciatica, saddle sensory change, new bladder or bowel dysfunction and sexual dysfunction; arrange emergency MRI.
thinking: Back pain with bilateral leg pain ↓ Painless urinary retention ↓ Reduced sensation over perineum, buttocks and inner thighs ↓ Sacral root compression ↓ Saddle anaesthesia
exam_trap: A, L5 dermatomal loss — sciatica brings single nerve root lesions to mind, but perineal and buttock sensory loss reflects sacral roots and the saddle pattern.
takeaway: Perineal and buttock numbness with back pain is saddle anaesthesia: suspect cauda equina syndrome.

stem: A 62-year-old woman with generalised myasthenia gravis is admitted with a chest infection. Over the next 24 hours her voice becomes nasal, she struggles to swallow her saliva, she cannot lift her head off the pillow and her breathing becomes shallow. Her pyridostigmine dose has not been changed, and she has no excess sweating, salivation, diarrhoea or small pupils. Which complication is most likely?
why_correct: Myasthenic crisis is a life-threatening exacerbation in which bulbar and respiratory muscle weakness threaten the airway and ventilation, and infection is the commonest trigger. Neck flexion weakness and bulbar failure are warning signs of impending respiratory failure. She needs urgent senior and critical care input, serial bedside measurement of respiratory function (forced vital capacity rather than oxygen saturations) and specialist neurology treatment such as intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange.
why_wrong: A. Cholinergic crisis follows excess anticholinesterase dosing and causes muscarinic features such as sweating, salivation, diarrhoea and miosis, which are absent. B. Guillain–Barré syndrome is an ascending neuropathy with areflexia, not an exacerbation in a patient with known myasthenia. C. Lambert–Eaton syndrome is a separate, usually paraneoplastic, condition in which weakness improves with repeated effort. E. A brainstem stroke would be abrupt in onset with long-tract or cranial nerve signs, not a gradual infection-related decline.
pearl: In myasthenia, oxygen saturations fall late. Monitor forced vital capacity, look for neck flexion weakness and bulbar failure, and avoid drugs that worsen neuromuscular transmission such as aminoglycosides.
thinking: Known myasthenia gravis ↓ Trigger present: intercurrent infection ↓ Bulbar weakness, neck flexion weakness and shallow breathing ↓ No muscarinic features and no dose increase, so not cholinergic ↓ Myasthenic crisis
exam_trap: A, Cholinergic crisis — it tempts because it also causes worsening weakness in treated myasthenia, but it needs a recent rise in anticholinesterase dose and produces muscarinic features such as salivation, sweating and miosis, none of which are present here.
takeaway: Myasthenia plus bulbar and respiratory weakness after an infection is myasthenic crisis until proven otherwise.

stem: The daughter of a 74-year-old man with Parkinson's disease telephones his GP. Ten days after ropinirole was added to his co-careldopa, he began seeing small children playing in the garden who are not there. He is otherwise alert and orientated, his memory has been stable, he has no fever or urinary symptoms, and his eyesight is unchanged. Which explanation best accounts for these symptoms?

options.C: Adverse effect of the dopamine agonist

correct_answer: C. Adverse effect of the dopamine agonist
why_correct: Dopamine agonists such as ropinirole commonly cause visual hallucinations and other psychotic features, particularly in older people, and the close link in time to starting the drug points to this. He is alert with stable cognition, making delirium or a primary dementia less likely. Management is to review the most recently added drug and reduce it gradually with specialist advice, rather than adding a typical antipsychotic.
why_wrong: A. Delirium causes fluctuating attention and confusion, and he is alert with no sign of infection. B. Charles Bonnet syndrome occurs with significant visual loss, and his vision is unchanged. D. Dementia with Lewy bodies involves cognitive decline and fluctuation, which are absent, and does not explain the timing after a new drug. E. Schizophrenia rarely begins at this age and would not be tied to a medication change.
pearl: Never stop Parkinson's medication abruptly because of the risk of a neuroleptic malignant-like syndrome, and avoid haloperidol and other typical antipsychotics, which can severely worsen parkinsonism.
thinking: Parkinson's disease on dopaminergic therapy ↓ New dopamine agonist started days before ↓ Well-formed visual hallucinations with clear consciousness and stable cognition ↓ No infection and no visual loss ↓ Adverse effect of the dopamine agonist
exam_trap: D, Dementia with Lewy bodies — it tempts because visual hallucinations and parkinsonism are both core features, but there is no cognitive decline or fluctuation, and onset straight after a new dopamine agonist points to a drug effect.
takeaway: New hallucinations soon after starting a dopamine agonist are drug-induced until proven otherwise.

stem: A 52-year-old man is on the orthopaedic ward 36 hours after fixation of an ankle fracture. Nurses note that he has become shaky, sweaty and agitated, and he then has a generalised tonic-clonic seizure. Before admission he drank spirits every day, and his gamma-GT is raised. His capillary glucose and serum sodium are normal. Which is the probable cause of his seizure?
why_correct: Abrupt cessation of regular heavy drinking on admission produces withdrawal, with tremor, sweating and agitation typically starting within hours and seizures most often in the first day or two. Normal glucose and sodium make metabolic causes unlikely. He should be managed with a benzodiazepine-based withdrawal regimen according to local protocol and given parenteral thiamine to prevent Wernicke's encephalopathy.
why_wrong: A. Hypoglycaemia is excluded by the normal capillary glucose. C. Fat embolism typically follows long-bone or pelvic fractures and presents with hypoxia, confusion and a petechial rash rather than tremor and sweating. D. Wernicke's encephalopathy causes confusion, ataxia and eye signs, not withdrawal features with seizures. E. Hepatic encephalopathy causes drowsiness and asterixis in advanced liver disease, and seizures are not typical.
pearl: Withdrawal seizures occur early; delirium tremens, with hallucinations, confusion and autonomic instability, usually appears a little later and is a medical emergency.
thinking: Daily heavy drinker admitted to hospital ↓ Alcohol stopped abruptly on admission ↓ Tremor, sweating and agitation within a day or two ↓ Glucose and sodium normal ↓ Alcohol withdrawal seizure
exam_trap: D, Wernicke's encephalopathy — the alcohol history makes thiamine deficiency tempting, but Wernicke's presents with confusion, ataxia and ophthalmoplegia, whereas tremor, sweating and an early seizure point to withdrawal.
takeaway: A seizure with tremor and sweating a day or two after admission in a heavy drinker is alcohol withdrawal.

stem: A 31-year-old woman attends a preconception clinic. Two years ago she had an unprovoked deep vein thrombosis, and blood tests since then have repeatedly shown lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin antibodies. She is planning her first pregnancy and asks what problems she might face. Her condition is most characteristically linked with which complication of pregnancy?
why_correct: Her history fits antiphospholipid syndrome, in which antibody-mediated thrombosis in the placental circulation causes placental insufficiency. The classic obstetric associations are recurrent miscarriage and later fetal loss, with pre-eclampsia, fetal growth restriction and preterm birth also more common. She needs specialist preconception and antenatal care; pregnancy is usually managed with low-dose aspirin and low molecular weight heparin, and any warfarin must be switched early because it is teratogenic.
why_wrong: A. Gestational diabetes relates to insulin resistance and is not a feature of antiphospholipid syndrome. B. Obstetric cholestasis is a liver condition of pregnancy unrelated to antiphospholipid antibodies. D. Hyperemesis gravidarum is linked to high hCG states such as multiple or molar pregnancy, not thrombophilia. E. Placenta praevia relates to where the placenta implants and to previous uterine surgery, not antibody-mediated thrombosis.
pearl: Antiphospholipid syndrome is one of the few treatable causes of recurrent miscarriage, so women with recurrent losses should be tested for lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin antibodies.
thinking: Unprovoked thrombosis ↓ Persistently positive antiphospholipid antibodies ↓ Antiphospholipid syndrome ↓ Placental thrombosis and insufficiency ↓ Miscarriage and fetal loss
exam_trap: E, Placenta praevia — it is a placental complication, so it can seem linked, but it reflects where the placenta implants, not thrombosis within the placental circulation.
takeaway: Antiphospholipid syndrome characteristically causes recurrent miscarriage and fetal loss through placental thrombosis.

stem: A 22-year-old woman sees her GP for the third time in four months with burning on passing urine and frequency. Urine samples sent at her last two visits showed white cells but grew no organisms, and her symptoms did not settle with antibiotics for cystitis. She now also mentions a change in vaginal discharge and some bleeding after sex. She has had a new partner in the last six months and they do not use condoms. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Dysuria with sterile pyuria, abnormal discharge and post-coital bleeding in a young woman with a new partner suggests chlamydial urethritis and cervicitis. Chlamydia is the commonest bacterial sexually transmitted infection in the UK and is often missed when symptoms are labelled as a urinary infection. A vulvovaginal NAAT swab should be taken, and treatment is usually doxycycline, with partner notification and testing for other STIs.
why_wrong: A. Interstitial cystitis is a diagnosis of exclusion and does not explain discharge or post-coital bleeding. C. Bacterial vaginosis causes a thin, fishy-smelling discharge but not dysuria with pyuria or post-coital bleeding. D. Candidiasis causes itch and a thick white discharge rather than pyuria and cervical bleeding. E. True bacterial cystitis would grow organisms on culture and respond to antibiotics.
pearl: Sterile pyuria in a sexually active young adult should prompt testing for chlamydia and gonorrhoea; other causes include renal tuberculosis, stones and partially treated infection.
thinking: Recurrent dysuria not responding to cystitis treatment ↓ Pus cells but no growth: sterile pyuria ↓ Discharge and post-coital bleeding suggest cervicitis ↓ New partner without condoms ↓ Chlamydia trachomatis infection
exam_trap: E, Recurrent E. coli cystitis — urinary symptoms make it the default label, but repeated cultures with no growth, poor response to antibiotics and cervical symptoms point to a sexually transmitted cause.
takeaway: Dysuria with sterile pyuria and discharge in a sexually active young woman: test for chlamydia.

stem: An 81-year-old woman is admitted from her care home with three days of cough productive of green sputum, and a chest X-ray shows right lower lobe consolidation. Staff say that until yesterday she was fully orientated, but she now does not know where she is or what day it is. She has bronchial breathing at the right base and a raised white cell count. Which feature most clearly indicates more severe pneumonia?
why_correct: New confusion is one of the components of the CURB-65 score used in the UK to assess the severity of community-acquired pneumonia, alongside urea, respiratory rate, blood pressure and age. It reflects systemic illness and predicts higher mortality, so it should prompt senior review, consideration of more intensive treatment and close monitoring. Sputum colour, fever, white cell count and focal chest signs support the diagnosis but are not part of the severity score.
why_wrong: A. Purulent sputum supports a bacterial infection but does not predict severity. B. Fever is common in pneumonia and is not a CURB-65 criterion. C. A raised white cell count supports infection but is not used to grade severity. E. Bronchial breathing indicates consolidation, not how ill the patient is.
pearl: In primary care, CRB-65 (without urea) helps decide whether a patient with pneumonia needs hospital assessment. Always compare current mental state with the patient's usual baseline.
thinking: Community-acquired pneumonia confirmed ↓ Severity is graded with CURB-65 ↓ Confusion is a core component ↓ The other findings are diagnostic, not prognostic ↓ New confusion
exam_trap: C, Raised white cell count — it looks like an objective marker of how unwell she is, but it is not part of the CURB-65 score and correlates poorly with mortality.
takeaway: New confusion in pneumonia is a CURB-65 feature indicating more severe disease.

stem: A 24-year-old woman in her first pregnancy is on the labour ward at term. Her membranes ruptured more than a day ago and labour is being induced. She now has a high temperature and a fast pulse. Her uterus is tender between contractions and the draining liquor has become offensive-smelling. The CTG shows a rising fetal baseline heart rate. There is no vaginal bleeding. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Maternal fever and tachycardia, uterine tenderness, offensive liquor and fetal tachycardia after prolonged rupture of membranes indicate intrauterine infection (chorioamnionitis). It can lead to maternal sepsis and neonatal infection. Management follows the sepsis pathway with blood cultures and broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics, expediting delivery and informing the neonatal team.
why_wrong: A. Abruption causes pain, a tense uterus and often bleeding, but not fever or offensive liquor. B. Pyelonephritis causes fever with loin pain and urinary symptoms rather than uterine tenderness and offensive liquor. D. Epidural-related fever is usually low grade, does not cause uterine tenderness or offensive liquor, and no epidural is mentioned. E. Endometritis occurs after delivery, and she has not yet delivered.
pearl: Prolonged rupture of membranes, repeated vaginal examinations and group B streptococcus colonisation increase the risk of chorioamnionitis; the baby may need assessment and antibiotics after birth.
thinking: Prolonged rupture of membranes ↓ Maternal fever and tachycardia ↓ Uterine tenderness and offensive liquor ↓ Fetal tachycardia ↓ Chorioamnionitis
exam_trap: A, Placental abruption — uterine tenderness and fetal compromise are shared features, but abruption does not cause fever or offensive liquor.
takeaway: Fever, uterine tenderness and fetal tachycardia after prolonged membrane rupture mean chorioamnionitis.

stem: A 19-year-old woman who runs for her university athletics team has had no periods for eight months; her cycles were previously regular. She trains twice a day and has lost weight this season. Urine hCG is negative. Blood tests show low LH, FSH and oestradiol, with normal prolactin and thyroid function. She has no acne or excess hair growth. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Intense exercise, weight loss and low energy availability suppress hypothalamic GnRH release, causing low LH, FSH and oestrogen and secondary amenorrhoea. Normal prolactin and thyroid function exclude other common endocrine causes. The low-oestrogen state risks bone loss, so management focuses on restoring energy balance, often with dietetic and psychological support, and screening for disordered eating.
why_wrong: A. Polycystic ovary syndrome causes oligomenorrhoea with hyperandrogenism and normal or raised LH, not low gonadotrophins. B. Premature ovarian insufficiency causes high FSH with low oestrogen. D. A prolactinoma would cause raised prolactin. E. Asherman's syndrome follows uterine instrumentation and causes amenorrhoea with normal hormone levels.
pearl: Amenorrhoea in athletes may be part of relative energy deficiency in sport, which also affects bone health and performance; consider bone density assessment if amenorrhoea is prolonged.
thinking: Secondary amenorrhoea with a negative pregnancy test ↓ Heavy training and weight loss ↓ Low LH, FSH and oestradiol ↓ Prolactin and thyroid normal ↓ Functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea
exam_trap: B, Premature ovarian insufficiency — it also causes low oestrogen and amenorrhoea in a young woman, but FSH is high because the ovaries have failed, whereas here gonadotrophins are low.
takeaway: Amenorrhoea with low gonadotrophins after weight loss and heavy exercise is hypothalamic.

stem: A 31-year-old woman attends the emergency department with three days of increasing pain and swelling on the right side of her vulva, and she now finds it hard to sit or walk. She is afebrile. On examination there is a hot, very tender, fluctuant swelling in the lower part of the right labium majus, posterolateral to the vaginal entrance. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: The Bartholin's glands lie posterolaterally on either side of the vaginal entrance, and blockage of a duct causes a cyst that can become infected to form a painful, fluctuant abscess. Treatment is drainage, commonly with Word catheter insertion or marsupialisation, with antibiotics if there is surrounding cellulitis or systemic upset. A new Bartholin's swelling in an older woman should be biopsied to exclude malignancy.
why_wrong: A. Sebaceous cysts arise in hair-bearing skin, are usually small and are not specifically sited beside the introitus. B. Skene's glands lie beside the urethral opening anteriorly, not at the back of the vaginal entrance. C. Gartner's duct cysts lie within the anterolateral vaginal wall and are usually painless. E. An inguinal hernia extending into the labium arises from the groin and has a cough impulse.
pearl: Bartholin's abscesses often recur after simple incision, which is why Word catheter insertion or marsupialisation is preferred to keep the duct open.
thinking: Painful, enlarging vulval swelling ↓ Fluctuant and tender ↓ Lower labium, posterolateral to the introitus ↓ Site of the Bartholin's gland ↓ Bartholin's gland abscess
exam_trap: B, Skene's duct abscess — another paravaginal gland abscess, but Skene's glands sit beside the urethra at the front, not at the back of the vaginal entrance.
takeaway: A tender, fluctuant swelling posterolateral to the vaginal entrance is a Bartholin's abscess.

stem: A 66-year-old woman who has had four vaginal deliveries tells her GP she can feel something 'coming down' that is worse at the end of the day. She sometimes has to push the lump back to finish emptying her bladder, and has had two urinary infections this year. On examination with a Sims speculum, the front wall of the vagina bulges downwards when she strains, while the cervix stays high. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Descent of the anterior vaginal wall on straining is a cystocele, the bladder bulging into the vagina through weakened pelvic support. Incomplete emptying, needing to push the bulge back to void and recurrent urinary infections are typical. Vaginal birth, age, menopause and obesity are risk factors, and management ranges from pelvic floor muscle training and vaginal pessaries to surgical repair depending on symptoms and wishes.
why_wrong: A. A rectocele is a posterior wall bulge causing difficulty with bowel emptying. C. In uterine prolapse the cervix descends, but here it stays high. D. An enterocele is small bowel herniating through the upper posterior vaginal wall or vault, usually after hysterectomy. E. A urethral diverticulum gives a tender anterior mass with post-void dribbling and discharge, not a bulge on straining.
pearl: Use a Sims speculum with the patient in the left lateral position to examine the anterior and posterior walls separately, and ask her to strain to reveal prolapse.
thinking: Sensation of a vaginal lump ↓ Older woman after several vaginal births ↓ Bladder emptying problems and recurrent infections ↓ Anterior wall descends on straining, cervix high ↓ Cystocele
exam_trap: C, Uterine prolapse — the commonest image of prolapse, but the cervix remains high and the bulge comes from the anterior wall, so the bladder is the organ prolapsing.
takeaway: Anterior vaginal wall descent with bladder symptoms is a cystocele.

stem: A 22-year-old woman is admitted from the emergency department with severe central abdominal pain, vomiting, dark urine and weakness of both arms. She also seems anxious and briefly hallucinated overnight. Acute intermittent porphyria is suspected and the ward team is writing her drug chart. Which of the following should be avoided?

options.D: A medicine listed as porphyrinogenic, such as certain anticonvulsants

correct_answer: D. A medicine listed as porphyrinogenic, such as certain anticonvulsants
why_correct: Porphyrinogenic medicines induce hepatic ALA synthase and can worsen or prolong an acute attack, so they must be avoided. Many anticonvulsants, some antibiotics and hormonal preparations fall into this group, and the UK porphyria drug database should be checked before prescribing. Opioids, paracetamol and intravenous glucose are generally regarded as safe.
why_wrong: A. Glucose suppresses ALA synthase and is part of supportive treatment. B. Morphine is considered safe and is commonly needed for the severe pain. C. Paracetamol is considered safe in acute porphyria. E. Sodium chloride is safe and may be needed because hyponatraemia is common in attacks.
pearl: Hyponatraemia from SIADH is common in acute porphyria attacks and can cause seizures; managing these is challenging because many anticonvulsants are themselves porphyrinogenic.
thinking: Abdominal pain, dark urine, motor neuropathy ↓ Psychiatric symptoms ↓ Suspected acute porphyria ↓ Drugs that induce ALA synthase worsen attacks ↓ Avoid porphyrinogenic medicines
exam_trap: B, Morphine for pain — opioids feel risky in someone with neuropsychiatric symptoms, but they are considered safe in porphyria and adequate analgesia is essential.
takeaway: In suspected acute porphyria, check every medicine against a porphyria-safe list and avoid porphyrinogenic drugs.
review_note: key option is near-tautological; needs rewriting as specific drugs and a check against the UK porphyria drug database (dropped from pack 04, 17 Oct 2026)

stem: A 61-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and protein in her urine calls the GP surgery because of a tickly, dry cough that has kept her awake for several weeks. It began shortly after a new tablet was added for her blood pressure and kidneys. She has no fever, breathlessness or sputum and her chest sounds clear. Which drug is most likely responsible?
why_correct: A persistent dry cough is a well-known adverse effect of ACE inhibitors such as lisinopril, caused by accumulation of bradykinin. An ACE inhibitor is the expected choice for hypertension in type 2 diabetes with albuminuria because it protects the kidneys. If the cough is troublesome, NICE suggests switching to an angiotensin II receptor blocker.
why_wrong: A. Amlodipine typically causes ankle swelling, flushing and headache. B. Indapamide causes electrolyte disturbance such as hyponatraemia and hypokalaemia. C. Bisoprolol may cause tiredness, cold peripheries or bronchospasm in asthma, not a dry cough. D. Doxazosin causes postural hypotension.
pearl: Angiotensin II receptor blockers do not inhibit bradykinin breakdown, so they rarely cause cough and are the usual alternative.
thinking: Dry cough without infection ↓ Started after a new antihypertensive ↓ Diabetes with albuminuria suggests ACE inhibitor was chosen ↓ Bradykinin accumulation ↓ Lisinopril
exam_trap: C, Bisoprolol — beta-blockers are linked with breathing problems, but they cause bronchospasm in asthma, not a persistent dry cough.
takeaway: A new dry cough after starting an antihypertensive suggests an ACE inhibitor.

stem: In the third week of treatment on the cardiology ward for enterococcal endocarditis, a 71-year-old man receiving amoxicillin and gentamicin says the room seems to jump about when he turns his head, and his wife notices he now has the television much louder. Which adverse effect of one of his antibiotics best explains this?
why_correct: Gentamicin, an aminoglycoside, damages the hair cells of the vestibular apparatus and cochlea, causing oscillopsia, imbalance and hearing loss that may be permanent. The risk rises with prolonged courses, older age and renal impairment, all relevant in endocarditis treatment. Levels should be monitored and the need for gentamicin reviewed urgently.
why_wrong: A. Gingival hyperplasia is linked with phenytoin, ciclosporin and calcium-channel blockers. B. Hyperprolactinaemia follows dopamine antagonists. C. Pulmonary fibrosis is associated with drugs such as amiodarone and nitrofurantoin. E. Photosensitivity is typical of tetracyclines and amiodarone, not aminoglycosides or amoxicillin.
pearl: People with the mitochondrial m.1555A>G variant are at very high risk of aminoglycoside deafness even after a single dose, so testing is advised where it will not delay urgent treatment.
thinking: Prolonged aminoglycoside course ↓ Oscillopsia and reduced hearing ↓ Cochlear and vestibular hair-cell damage ↓ Cumulative dose-related toxicity ↓ Ototoxicity
exam_trap: E, Photosensitive skin rash — antibiotics commonly cause rashes, which tempts, but his symptoms are vestibular and auditory, the hallmark of aminoglycoside toxicity.
takeaway: Aminoglycosides cause ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity, so monitor levels, hearing and renal function.

presentation: Antimicrobial stewardship in viral respiratory infection
stem: The mother of a 4-year-old boy brings him to the GP surgery after three days of runny nose, mild cough and a low-grade fever. She asks for antibiotics because his nursery wants him to get better quickly. He is alert, drinking well, and examination shows clear chest, normal breathing and no signs of ear or tonsil infection. What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Prescribe a five-day course of amoxicillin to prevent a chest infection
options.B: Explain that antibiotics are unlikely to help, and give advice on symptom care and when to seek help
options.C: Prescribe amoxicillin and clarithromycin together to cover all likely organisms
