options.D: Give a single dose of azithromycin to cover atypical bacteria
options.E: Prescribe phenoxymethylpenicillin because his sibling responded to it last month

correct_answer: B. Explain that antibiotics are unlikely to help, and give advice on symptom care and when to seek help
why_correct: This is a self-limiting viral upper respiratory tract infection in a well child with no features of bacterial infection. NICE advises against antibiotics here because they do not shorten the illness, cause side effects and drive resistance. The parent should be given advice on fluids, antipyretics, expected duration and clear safety-netting about red flags.
why_wrong: A. Antibiotics do not prevent complications of viral colds in well children. C. Combined broad cover is unnecessary and increases resistance and side effects. D. A single macrolide dose has no role in a viral illness. E. Another person's response to an antibiotic is not an indication.
pearl: Uncomplicated colds usually last about one to two weeks, and a cough can persist for up to three weeks; telling families this reduces repeat consultations.
thinking: Well child with coryza and cough ↓ No signs of bacterial infection ↓ Viral and self-limiting ↓ Antibiotics give no benefit but cause harm and resistance ↓ Explain, give symptom advice and safety-net
exam_trap: A, Prescribing amoxicillin to prevent a chest infection — it seems protective and pleases the parent, but it does not reduce complications and adds harm.
takeaway: In a viral upper respiratory tract infection, explain why antibiotics will not help and give clear symptom and safety-net advice.

presentation: Aspirin and Reye syndrome in children
stem: At a community pharmacy, a father asks whether he can give aspirin to his 9-year-old daughter, who has chickenpox with fever and itchy spots. He takes aspirin himself for headaches and has some at home. The pharmacist advises against it. Which serious risk is the main reason?
why_correct: Aspirin given to children during viral illnesses, particularly chickenpox and influenza, is associated with Reye syndrome, a rare but life-threatening disorder causing acute encephalopathy and liver failure. For this reason aspirin is not recommended for children under 16 unless specifically prescribed by a specialist, for example in Kawasaki disease.
why_wrong: A. Aspirin does not cause appendicitis. B. Nephrotic syndrome is not a recognised risk of aspirin in children. D. Aspirin can worsen existing aspirin-sensitive asthma but does not cause asthma in every child, and this is not the main reason it is avoided. E. Congenital heart disease is present from birth and cannot be caused by aspirin in childhood.
pearl: Ibuprofen should also be avoided in chickenpox because of an association with severe skin and soft tissue infection, so paracetamol is the preferred antipyretic.
thinking: Child under 16 ↓ Viral illness with fever ↓ Parent wants to give aspirin ↓ Associated with Reye syndrome ↓ Advise paracetamol instead
exam_trap: D, New-onset asthma — aspirin can provoke bronchospasm in sensitive people, which makes this tempting, but Reye syndrome is the reason aspirin is avoided in children.
takeaway: Aspirin is avoided in children under 16 with viral illnesses because of the risk of Reye syndrome.

stem: A 19-year-old man is in the emergency department resuscitation bay with acute severe asthma. Over the past two hours he has received back-to-back nebulised salbutamol with ipratropium and oral prednisolone. His wheeze is easing, but the nurse notices new flattened T waves and U waves on his cardiac monitor. Which blood abnormality is most likely?
why_correct: Beta-2 agonists such as salbutamol stimulate the sodium-potassium pump and drive potassium into cells, lowering serum potassium. Repeated high doses in acute asthma, often with corticosteroids, can cause significant hypokalaemia, and flattened T waves with U waves are typical ECG changes. Potassium should be monitored and replaced when needed.
why_wrong: A. Salbutamol does not raise calcium. B. Sodium is not typically affected by nebulised salbutamol. C. Magnesium is used as a treatment in severe asthma but salbutamol does not raise it. D. Salbutamol does not cause raised bilirubin.
pearl: Hyperglycaemia, tachycardia, tremor and lactic acidosis are other recognised effects of high-dose beta-2 agonist therapy.
thinking: Acute severe asthma ↓ Repeated nebulised salbutamol ↓ Beta-2 stimulation shifts potassium into cells ↓ Flat T waves and U waves ↓ Hypokalaemia
exam_trap: C, Hypermagnesaemia — magnesium is part of severe asthma management, so it comes to mind, but it is not caused by salbutamol and does not produce U waves.
takeaway: Repeated beta-2 agonist doses can cause hypokalaemia, so check potassium in severe asthma.

stem: A 79-year-old woman attends her GP with several weeks of dizziness on standing and tiredness. Three months ago an ophthalmologist started timolol eye drops for open-angle glaucoma. She takes no other regular medicines. Her pulse is regular at 46 beats per minute and her blood tests are normal. Which adverse drug effect best explains her symptoms?
why_correct: Timolol is a non-selective beta-blocker, and enough is absorbed from eye drops to reduce sympathetic drive to the heart. This can slow the heart rate and cause light-headedness and fatigue, particularly in older people. Her slow pulse after starting the drops points to beta-blocker-induced bradycardia.
why_wrong: B. Beta-blockers mask features of hyperthyroidism rather than cause it, and her bloods are normal. C. Hyperglycaemia does not slow the pulse, and her blood tests are normal. D. Urinary retention is an antimuscarinic effect. E. Diarrhoea is not a typical beta-blocker effect.
pearl: Topical beta-blocker eye drops can also trigger bronchospasm in asthma, so always ask about eye drops when taking a drug history.
thinking: Dizziness and fatigue ↓ Recently started timolol drops ↓ Timolol is a beta-blocker absorbed systemically ↓ Pulse slow ↓ Beta-blocker-induced bradycardia
exam_trap: D, Urinary retention — eye drops for glaucoma can bring to mind anticholinergic effects, but timolol is a beta-blocker and slows the heart.
takeaway: Beta-blockers, including eye drops, can cause symptomatic bradycardia.

stem: A 63-year-old woman is on the general surgical ward after an emergency laparotomy and has been nil by mouth for four days. Her regular atenolol for hypertension and ischaemic heart disease has not been prescribed in any other form since admission. She now reports a pounding heartbeat and tightness in her chest when walking to the bathroom. Her pulse is 118 and regular. What is the most likely explanation?

options.E: Permanent loss of cardiac beta receptors

correct_answer: A. Rebound increase in sympathetic activity
why_correct: Long-term beta-blockade upregulates beta receptors, so when the drug is suddenly stopped, normal levels of adrenaline and noradrenaline produce an exaggerated response. This rebound causes tachycardia, palpitations, raised blood pressure and worsening angina, and can precipitate myocardial infarction. Beta-blockers should be continued around surgery where possible, or given by another route, and tapered rather than stopped abruptly.
why_wrong: B. Stopping a beta-blocker does not cause insulin deficiency. C. Beta-blocker withdrawal does not reduce thyroid hormone production. D. Red cell production is not affected within days of stopping a beta-blocker. E. Beta receptors are increased, not destroyed, by long-term blockade.
pearl: Ischaemic heart disease, rather than hypertension alone, carries the greatest risk from rebound after stopping a beta-blocker.
thinking: Long-term atenolol ↓ Suddenly omitted for several days ↓ Upregulated beta receptors ↓ Tachycardia and exertional chest tightness ↓ Rebound sympathetic activity
exam_trap: C, Reduced thyroid hormone production — palpitations suggest thyroid disease, but the timing after stopping atenolol points to rebound, and withdrawal would not lower thyroid output.
takeaway: Abrupt withdrawal of a beta-blocker can cause rebound tachycardia and angina, so avoid sudden omission.

stem: A 41-year-old man is admitted to the surgical assessment unit with suspected appendicitis, and the surgical team want to start intravenous antibiotics. The allergy section of his drug chart is blank. He has had morphine, is drowsy and says he 'might have reacted to something once' but cannot say what. His partner is on her way in, and his GP record is accessible online. What is the safest approach before prescribing?

options.A: Write 'no known drug allergies' on the chart and prescribe as planned
options.B: Record a penicillin allergy to be safe and choose a different regimen
options.C: Prescribe as planned and ask nurses to observe him closely
options.D: Clarify his allergy history from the available sources before prescribing
options.E: Give a small test dose of the planned antibiotic first

correct_answer: D. Clarify his allergy history from the available sources before prescribing
why_correct: Allergy status must be established and documented before any prescription is written. Here there are quick ways to clarify it: the Summary Care Record or GP record and his partner, as well as asking him again once he is more alert. This takes minutes and allows a safe, appropriate antibiotic choice without guessing.
why_wrong: A. Recording no known allergies without checking is inaccurate and could lead to a harmful prescription. B. Inventing a penicillin allergy creates a false label that may restrict his care for years. C. Observing for a reaction is not a substitute for asking about one first. E. Test doses are not a safe way to screen for unknown allergies on a ward.
pearl: The allergy box on a drug chart should never be left blank: it should state the allergy and reaction, 'no known drug allergies', or that status could not be confirmed.
thinking: Antibiotics needed ↓ Allergy status blank and patient unsure ↓ Quick sources available ↓ Clarify and document first ↓ Then prescribe
exam_trap: B, Recording a penicillin allergy as a precaution — it feels protective, but a false label is hard to remove and can lead to less effective antibiotic choices.
takeaway: Clarify and record allergy status before prescribing; never guess it in either direction.

presentation: Purpose of blood monitoring for a medicine
stem: A 30-year-old woman with schizophrenia that has not responded to two other antipsychotics is about to start clozapine in a community mental health clinic. She is told that she will need frequent blood tests and asks the doctor why. Which is the best explanation?

options.A: So that her prescription can be repeated without any review
options.B: Because blood tests are a legal requirement for all medicines
options.C: To detect harmful adverse effects early and make sure it remains safe to continue
options.D: To prevent side effects from developing in the first place
options.E: To confirm that the diagnosis of schizophrenia is correct

correct_answer: C. To detect harmful adverse effects early and make sure it remains safe to continue
why_correct: Some medicines can cause serious adverse effects that are silent at first. Clozapine can cause neutropenia and agranulocytosis, so regular full blood counts allow these to be detected before infection develops, and treatment stopped if needed. Monitoring therefore keeps treatment safe rather than preventing side effects altogether.
why_wrong: A. Monitoring is part of review, not a way of avoiding it. B. Most medicines do not need blood monitoring; it is required for specific drugs with particular risks. D. Monitoring detects side effects early but cannot stop them from occurring. E. Blood tests do not confirm a psychiatric diagnosis.
pearl: Clozapine needs full blood count monitoring weekly for the first 18 weeks, then less often, through a registered monitoring service.
thinking: Medicine with serious silent risks ↓ Blood tests can show harm before symptoms ↓ Early detection allows action ↓ Treatment continues only if safe ↓ Monitoring supports safety
exam_trap: D, Preventing side effects — it is tempting to think monitoring stops harm happening, but it only detects it early so action can be taken.
takeaway: Blood monitoring for a medicine detects adverse effects early so that treatment remains safe.

stem: An 81-year-old man with stage 3 chronic kidney disease lives in a care home and takes several regular medicines. A GP prescribes trimethoprim for a urinary tract infection. Trimethoprim reduces potassium excretion in the distal nephron in a similar way to amiloride. Which complication should be monitored for?
why_correct: Trimethoprim blocks epithelial sodium channels in the distal nephron, reducing potassium excretion in the same way as amiloride. In older people with chronic kidney disease, or those taking other potassium-raising medicines such as ACE inhibitors or spironolactone, this can cause clinically significant hyperkalaemia. Potassium and renal function should be checked, especially if the course is prolonged.
why_wrong: A. Trimethoprim does not raise calcium. B. Reduced potassium excretion raises, not lowers, potassium. C. Hypoglycaemia is not a typical effect of trimethoprim. E. Trimethoprim does not cause iron deficiency.
pearl: Common potassium-raising drugs include ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, spironolactone, amiloride, trimethoprim, NSAIDs and heparin.
thinking: Older man with CKD ↓ New drug that reduces renal potassium excretion ↓ Potassium accumulates ↓ Risk greater with other potassium-raising medicines ↓ Monitor for hyperkalaemia
exam_trap: B, Hypokalaemia — many diuretics cause potassium loss, but drugs acting like amiloride retain potassium instead.
takeaway: Drugs that reduce renal potassium excretion can cause hyperkalaemia, especially in chronic kidney disease.

stem: An 80-year-old man who takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation is brought to the emergency department after tripping at home. A cut on his shin keeps oozing despite pressure, and his INR is far above his target range. He is alert, with stable observations. What should be done first?

options.A: Continue warfarin and recheck the INR next week
options.B: Dress the wound and leave the warfarin dose unchanged
options.C: Switch to a direct oral anticoagulant and discharge
options.D: Give tranexamic acid and continue warfarin as before
options.E: Assess the severity of bleeding and correct the over-anticoagulation

correct_answer: E. Assess the severity of bleeding and correct the over-anticoagulation
why_correct: Active bleeding with a markedly raised INR needs assessment of how severe the bleed is, followed by correction of anticoagulation. For minor bleeding this usually means withholding warfarin and giving intravenous vitamin K, while major bleeding requires prothrombin complex concentrate as well. The reason for the high INR, such as interacting drugs or illness, should also be sought.
why_wrong: A. Continuing warfarin with a very high INR and active bleeding risks further haemorrhage. B. Local treatment helps the wound but leaves the dangerous INR uncorrected. C. Switching drug does nothing about the current excess warfarin effect. D. Tranexamic acid does not reverse warfarin, and continuing the same dose is unsafe.
pearl: Vitamin K takes several hours to work; prothrombin complex concentrate gives immediate reversal and is used with vitamin K for major bleeding.
thinking: On warfarin with persistent bleeding ↓ INR well above target ↓ Judge whether the bleed is minor or major ↓ Withhold warfarin and reverse with vitamin K, adding PCC if major ↓ Find the cause of the high INR
exam_trap: B, Dress the wound and continue warfarin — local measures seem enough for a skin wound, but the underlying excessive anticoagulation is the real problem and must be corrected.
takeaway: Bleeding with a high INR means assess severity and reverse the anticoagulation accordingly.

stem: A 66-year-old man with stable angina returns to his GP two weeks after being given a glyceryl trinitrate spray. He says it relieves his chest tightness within minutes, but each time he uses it he gets a throbbing headache and feels flushed. He has no other neurological symptoms and is otherwise well. What is the most likely explanation for the headache?
correct_answer: C. Vasodilation caused by the nitrate
why_correct: Glyceryl trinitrate releases nitric oxide and causes vasodilation, including of the meningeal and cerebral vessels, which produces a throbbing headache and flushing. This is a common, predictable and usually benign adverse effect that often lessens with continued use. He can be advised to sit down when using the spray, as dizziness and postural hypotension can also occur.
why_wrong: A. Raised intracranial pressure causes persistent, worsening headache with vomiting or visual change, not brief headaches after each dose. B. Hypoglycaemia causes sweating, tremor and confusion, and has no link with nitrate use. D. Meningitis causes fever, neck stiffness and illness, not a headache timed with each spray. E. Iron deficiency causes tiredness and breathlessness, not headache immediately after a dose.
pearl: Nitrates must not be combined with phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors such as sildenafil because of the risk of profound hypotension.
thinking: Headache after each GTN dose ↓ Accompanied by flushing ↓ Nitrates release nitric oxide ↓ Vasodilation of cranial vessels ↓ Benign expected adverse effect
exam_trap: A, Raised intracranial pressure — a repeated throbbing headache can raise concern, but the clear timing with each dose and lack of other features point to simple vasodilation.
takeaway: Headache and flushing after GTN are expected effects of vasodilation, not a warning sign.

stem: At the pharmacy counter, a 70-year-old man collecting his repeat prescription notices that his atorvastatin tablets are now white and oval instead of the pink tablets he had before. He worries he has been given the wrong medicine or a weaker version. The pharmacist explains that this is a generic product. Which explanation is correct?

options.A: Generic tablets contain less of the active drug to keep costs down
options.B: Generic tablets are licensed only for milder disease
options.C: Generic tablets contain the same active ingredient and must meet the same quality standards
options.D: Generic tablets contain a related but chemically different drug
options.E: Generic tablets are new products still in clinical trials

correct_answer: C. Generic tablets contain the same active ingredient and must meet the same quality standards
why_correct: Generic medicines contain the same active ingredient at the same strength as the branded product and must show bioequivalence and meet MHRA quality standards. Their colour, shape and inactive ingredients may differ, which explains the change in appearance. He can be reassured that his treatment is unchanged.
why_wrong: A. Generics contain the same dose of active drug. B. Generics are not restricted to milder disease; they are licensed for the same conditions as the original product. D. The active ingredient is chemically identical, not a related analogue. E. Generics are established medicines, produced after the original patent expires.
pearl: For a few drugs, such as certain antiepileptics, ciclosporin and tacrolimus, prescribers keep patients on a consistent brand or manufacturer because small differences in bioavailability can matter.
thinking: Tablet looks different ↓ Patient worries it is weaker or wrong ↓ It is a generic product ↓ Same active ingredient and strength ↓ Must meet the same quality standards
exam_trap: A, Less active drug to keep costs down — the lower price makes this myth tempting, but generics are cheaper because development costs are not repeated, not because they contain less drug.
takeaway: Generic medicines look different but contain the same active ingredient and meet the same quality standards.

stem: A 48-year-old woman saw a private gastroenterologist, who recommended a branded version of omeprazole for her reflux. At her GP practice she is told the NHS prescription will be issued generically, and she asks whether the generic will work as well. What is the key principle to explain?

options.A: Branded medicines are safer than generic versions
options.B: The generic contains the same active ingredient as the branded product
options.C: Generic medicines usually work less well than brands
options.D: Generic prescribing needs specialist approval on the NHS
options.E: The generic is a similar but chemically different compound

correct_answer: B. The generic contains the same active ingredient as the branded product
why_correct: A generic medicine contains the same active ingredient as the branded version and is required to be bioequivalent, so it produces the same therapeutic effect. Prescribing by generic name is standard NHS practice and helps reduce cost without reducing effectiveness. She can expect the same benefit from generic omeprazole.
why_wrong: A. Branding does not make a medicine safer; both must meet the same standards. C. Generics are not inherently less effective, as bioequivalence must be shown. D. Generic prescribing is routine and needs no specialist approval. E. The active ingredient is identical, not a different compound.
pearl: Generic prescribing is encouraged across the NHS; brand prescribing is reserved for situations where formulations are not interchangeable.
thinking: Patient worried generic is inferior ↓ Generic contains the same active ingredient ↓ Must be bioequivalent ↓ Same expected therapeutic effect ↓ Generic prescribing is routine NHS practice
exam_trap: A, Branded medicines are safer — many patients assume a brand means higher quality, but generics must meet the same regulatory standards for quality and safety.
takeaway: A generic medicine has the same active ingredient as the brand and is expected to work the same way.

stem: A 37-year-old woman is admitted to the gynaecology ward with pelvic sepsis and started on intravenous gentamicin alongside other antibiotics. The ward pharmacist asks the team to ensure appropriate monitoring is in place while the aminoglycoside continues. Which adverse effect is particularly important to monitor for?
why_correct: Gentamicin is an aminoglycoside that accumulates in renal tubular cells and can cause acute kidney injury, as well as dose-related ototoxicity. Serum creatinine and gentamicin levels should be monitored, with dosing adjusted to levels and renal function according to local protocol. Courses are kept as short as possible to reduce toxicity.
why_wrong: B. Gingival overgrowth is linked to phenytoin, ciclosporin and calcium-channel blockers, not gentamicin. C. Constipation is not a characteristic gentamicin toxicity. D. Gentamicin does not affect thyroid function. E. Hypoglycaemia is not a recognised toxicity of gentamicin.
pearl: Gentamicin ototoxicity can be irreversible and affects both hearing and balance, so ask about tinnitus, hearing loss and unsteadiness during treatment.
thinking: Patient on intravenous gentamicin ↓ Aminoglycosides accumulate in the kidney and inner ear ↓ Main toxicities are nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity ↓ Monitor creatinine and drug levels ↓ Adjust dosing to levels and renal function
exam_trap: B, Gingival overgrowth — it is a well known drug side effect that appears in many lists, but it belongs to phenytoin and ciclosporin, not aminoglycosides.
takeaway: Gentamicin requires monitoring of renal function and drug levels because of nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity.

stem: An 8-year-old girl had amoxicillin for an ear infection last year without any problem. Today she is given the first dose of a new course of co-amoxiclav suspension at the GP surgery. Within twenty minutes she is scratching at raised itchy weals on her chest and her eyelids have become puffy. Her voice is normal, she has no wheeze or stridor, and her pulse and blood pressure are normal for her age. Which mechanism underlies this reaction?

options.A: Deposition of immune complexes in small blood vessels
options.B: Antibody-directed destruction of red blood cells
options.D: Direct dose-dependent toxicity of the drug
options.E: Cross-linking of IgE on mast cells causing release of histamine and other mediators

correct_answer: E. Cross-linking of IgE on mast cells causing release of histamine and other mediators
why_correct: Onset within minutes of a drug, with urticaria and swelling, is an immediate type I hypersensitivity reaction. The drug cross-links specific IgE bound to mast cells, which degranulate and release histamine and other mediators. There are no airway, breathing or circulation features, so this is not anaphylaxis, but penicillin allergy should be documented clearly.
why_wrong: A. Immune complex deposition is type III hypersensitivity, as in serum sickness, which develops days later. B. Antibody-directed red cell destruction is type II hypersensitivity and causes haemolysis. C. T-cell mediated reactions are type IV and appear hours to days later, such as many drug rashes. D. Dose-dependent toxicity would not cause rapid urticaria and swelling after a normal first dose.
pearl: IgE-mediated allergy needs prior sensitisation, so it typically appears on re-exposure to a drug; reactions within an hour suggest IgE, whereas rashes appearing after several days are usually T-cell mediated.
thinking: Previous penicillin exposure, new course ↓ Reaction within minutes ↓ Urticaria and eyelid swelling ↓ No airway, breathing or circulation compromise ↓ Type I reaction driven by mast-cell degranulation
exam_trap: C, Delayed T-cell mediated inflammation — drug rashes are often T-cell driven, but those appear days later, not within twenty minutes.
takeaway: Immediate drug allergy is type I: IgE on mast cells triggers histamine release.

stem: A 26-year-old woman who works as a hairdresser is seen in the dermatology clinic with painful cystic acne on her back and jawline that has left scarring despite two courses of oral antibiotics with topical treatment. She is in a relationship and is not currently using contraception. The consultant plans to start oral isotretinoin. Which risk is most important to address before the first prescription?

options.E: Severe harm to an unborn baby

correct_answer: E. Severe harm to an unborn baby
why_correct: Isotretinoin is highly teratogenic, causing serious birth defects even with short exposure. She could become pregnant and is not using contraception, so she must be enrolled in the Pregnancy Prevention Programme, with highly effective contraception and negative pregnancy tests before, during and after treatment. Mood changes should also be discussed and monitored.
why_wrong: A. Isotretinoin does not cause hypoglycaemia; it can raise lipids and liver enzymes. B. Hearing loss is associated with aminoglycosides, not isotretinoin. C. Iron deficiency is not a recognised adverse effect. D. Premature epiphyseal closure is a rare reported effect in adolescents and is irrelevant in a 26-year-old adult.
pearl: Pregnancy testing and highly effective contraception are required throughout isotretinoin treatment and for one month after it stops.
thinking: Severe scarring acne despite antibiotics ↓ Isotretinoin planned ↓ Woman of childbearing potential without contraception ↓ Isotretinoin is highly teratogenic ↓ Pregnancy Prevention Programme first
exam_trap: D, Premature closure of growth plates — retinoids can affect bone, but she is an adult and this is not the key safety issue.
takeaway: Before isotretinoin in anyone who could become pregnant, pregnancy prevention is the priority.

stem: A 41-year-old nurse who works permanent night shifts has primary hypothyroidism. Her TSH has stayed above the reference range at three checks despite two dose increases, and she says she never misses a tablet. On questioning, she takes her levothyroxine when she gets home in the morning, together with her main meal of the day, before going to sleep. What is the most likely reason for her results?

options.A: Increased clearance of thyroxine by the kidneys
options.B: Excess iodine in her diet blocking the drug
options.D: Faster breakdown of thyroxine by the liver
options.E: Reduced absorption because she takes it with a meal

correct_answer: E. Reduced absorption because she takes it with a meal
why_correct: Levothyroxine is absorbed less well when it is taken with food, so taking it with a large meal can leave her under-replaced even though she is adherent. It should be taken on an empty stomach, usually at least 30 minutes before food or caffeine, at a consistent time. Adjusting the timing to suit her shifts and rechecking TSH after a few weeks is more sensible than further dose increases.
why_wrong: A. Renal excretion of thyroxine is not a recognised cause of under-replacement. B. Dietary iodine does not block levothyroxine. C. Thyroid hormone resistance is a rare genetic condition and is unlikely when there is a clear reversible cause. D. Enzyme induction by drugs can increase thyroxine metabolism, but she takes no such drug and the timing with food is the obvious problem.
pearl: Calcium, iron, antacids and proton pump inhibitors also reduce levothyroxine absorption, so they should be separated by several hours.
thinking: Persistently high TSH despite dose increases ↓ Adherence appears good ↓ Tablet taken with her main meal ↓ Food reduces levothyroxine absorption ↓ Take on an empty stomach at a consistent time
exam_trap: C, Tissue resistance to thyroid hormone — it seems to explain a poor response to rising doses, but it is rare and a simple absorption problem is far more likely.
takeaway: Check how levothyroxine is taken before increasing the dose; food reduces absorption.

stem: During a heatwave, the wife of a 52-year-old landscape gardener with bipolar disorder phones his community mental health nurse. He has been working outdoors all week and drinking little. For two days he has had loose stools and vomiting, his hands have developed a coarse tremor, and today he seems muddled and slow to answer. He takes lithium. What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.A: Increase his lithium dose to cover a possible relapse
options.B: Continue lithium and check the level at his next routine blood test
options.C: Halve the lithium dose and review him in a week
options.D: Add propranolol for the tremor and continue lithium
options.E: Withhold lithium and arrange urgent same-day medical assessment with lithium level and renal function

correct_answer: E. Withhold lithium and arrange urgent same-day medical assessment with lithium level and renal function
why_correct: Dehydration from heat and gastrointestinal losses reduces lithium excretion, and coarse tremor, vomiting, diarrhoea and confusion are features of lithium toxicity. Lithium should be stopped and he needs urgent assessment with a serum lithium level, urea and electrolytes and fluid replacement. Severe toxicity may need specialist treatment such as haemodialysis.
why_wrong: A. Increasing the dose would worsen toxicity. B. Waiting for routine monitoring delays care for a potentially fatal problem. C. A reduced dose still adds lithium and delaying review is unsafe. D. Propranolol treats the fine tremor seen at normal levels, but a coarse tremor with confusion signals toxicity.
pearl: A fine tremor is common at therapeutic lithium levels, whereas a coarse tremor, ataxia, vomiting and confusion suggest toxicity.
thinking: Lithium user in hot weather ↓ Poor fluid intake with vomiting and diarrhoea ↓ Dehydration reduces lithium clearance ↓ Coarse tremor and confusion ↓ Stop lithium and assess urgently
exam_trap: D, Adding propranolol for the tremor — propranolol is used for lithium tremor, but that applies to fine tremor at normal levels, not toxicity with confusion.
takeaway: Suspected lithium toxicity needs lithium withheld and same-day assessment with levels and renal function.

stem: At her annual medication review with the practice pharmacist, a 74-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation and heart failure says she has felt very well for months and would like to stop her bisoprolol, as she thinks she no longer needs it. She takes five regular medicines in total. How should the pharmacist respond?

options.A: Agree that she can stop it today because she is well
options.B: Suggest she halves the dose and judges how she feels
options.C: Tell her all her medicines must be continued for life
options.D: Review why bisoprolol was started and the benefits, risks and withdrawal effects of stopping before advising
options.E: Advise her to stop it and restart only if symptoms return

correct_answer: D. Review why bisoprolol was started and the benefits, risks and withdrawal effects of stopping before advising
why_correct: Any decision to stop a medicine should start with its indication and the balance of benefit and harm for this patient. Bisoprolol here controls her heart rate and improves outcomes in heart failure, so feeling well may reflect that it is working; abrupt withdrawal of a beta-blocker can also cause rebound tachycardia and worsening heart failure. A shared decision based on this review respects her wishes while keeping her safe.
why_wrong: A. Feeling well may be a result of the medicine, and stopping without review risks deterioration. B. Self-directed dose reduction without assessing the indication is unsafe. C. Medicines should be reviewed regularly and some can appropriately be stopped. E. Stopping and waiting for symptoms ignores the indication and risks rebound effects and harm.
pearl: Structured medication review supports deprescribing where appropriate, but each drug should be judged on its indication, ongoing benefit and any withdrawal risk.
thinking: Patient wants to stop a medicine because she feels well ↓ Feeling well may mean the drug is working ↓ Check why it was started ↓ Weigh benefit, harm and withdrawal effects ↓ Make a shared decision
exam_trap: E, Stopping and restarting if symptoms return — it sounds patient-centred, but for drugs that prevent future harm or cause rebound effects, symptoms may appear too late.
takeaway: Before stopping any medicine, review its indication, benefits, risks and withdrawal effects with the patient.

stem: A 71-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes is booked for CT coronary angiography. On the pre-scan checklist, the radiographer sees that she takes metformin and that her latest kidney function shows moderate impairment. The radiology protocol says the decision to pause metformin around the scan depends on her renal function and the risk of contrast-related kidney injury. What is the underlying reason her kidney function matters here?

options.A: Metformin itself makes iodinated contrast more toxic to the kidney
options.B: Metformin is largely broken down by the liver, so the kidneys are irrelevant
options.C: Metformin is cleared by the kidneys, so if they are impaired it can accumulate and cause lactic acidosis
options.D: Metformin is directly toxic to renal tubules, like aminoglycosides
options.E: Metformin frequently causes acute kidney injury after contrast

correct_answer: C. Metformin is cleared by the kidneys, so if they are impaired it can accumulate and cause lactic acidosis
why_correct: Metformin is not metabolised but excreted unchanged in the urine. If iodinated contrast causes acute kidney injury in someone whose renal function is already reduced, metformin may accumulate and increase the risk of lactic acidosis. That is why her renal function and contrast risk determine whether metformin is withheld temporarily, typically restarting once renal function is confirmed stable.
why_wrong: A. Metformin does not increase the nephrotoxicity of contrast; the concern is its accumulation if kidney injury occurs. B. Metformin is renally excreted with negligible hepatic metabolism. D. Metformin is not directly nephrotoxic. E. Metformin does not itself cause acute kidney injury after contrast.
pearl: People with normal renal function having a standard dose of intravenous contrast usually do not need to stop metformin; the precaution targets those with significant renal impairment or other risk factors.
thinking: Metformin user needs iodinated contrast ↓ Existing renal impairment ↓ Contrast may worsen kidney function ↓ Metformin is renally excreted and can accumulate ↓ Risk of lactic acidosis guides withholding
exam_trap: A, Metformin making contrast more nephrotoxic — the two are linked in protocols, but the risk runs the other way: contrast harms the kidney and metformin then accumulates.
takeaway: Renal function matters with contrast because metformin is renally cleared and can accumulate, causing lactic acidosis.

presentation: Missed monitoring for a high-risk medicine
stem: A 66-year-old man with bipolar disorder has taken lithium for many years. A repeat prescription request reaches his GP, who notices that he has not attended for blood tests to check his lithium level, kidney function and thyroid function for nine months despite reminders. He says he has been busy caring for his wife. What is the safest course of action?

options.A: Stop lithium permanently and inform him by letter
options.B: Arrange the overdue blood tests and a review before issuing more supplies
options.C: Increase the lithium dose because the level is probably low
options.D: Ask him to judge from his symptoms whether his kidneys are affected
options.E: Issue a further six months of supplies and check again at the annual review

correct_answer: B. Arrange the overdue blood tests and a review before issuing more supplies
why_correct: Lithium has a narrow therapeutic range and can cause kidney damage and hypothyroidism, so it should only be continued with regular monitoring. The safe step is to arrange the overdue tests and a review promptly, issuing only a short supply if needed to avoid an abrupt stop, and to explore what has made attending difficult. Prescribing further supplies without results risks undetected toxicity.
why_wrong: A. Stopping lithium abruptly without review risks relapse of bipolar disorder, and he has not been assessed. C. Changing the dose without a level could cause toxicity. D. Kidney damage and toxicity can be silent until advanced, so symptoms are not a safe guide. E. Continuing long-term supplies without monitoring defeats the purpose of the safety checks.
pearl: Lithium toxicity is precipitated by dehydration, intercurrent illness and interacting drugs such as NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and diuretics.
thinking: High-risk medicine needing blood monitoring ↓ Monitoring overdue for months ↓ Toxicity may be silent ↓ Avoid abrupt withdrawal ↓ Arrange tests and review before issuing more supplies
exam_trap: A, Stopping lithium permanently — it seems to remove the risk, but abrupt withdrawal without review exposes him to relapse and is not a shared decision.
takeaway: Medicines that need monitoring should not be supplied long term without the monitoring being done; arrange review before further supplies.

stem: A 47-year-old man attends the emergency department with aching thighs and difficulty climbing stairs. He has taken simvastatin for years, and five days ago an out-of-hours GP gave him clarithromycin for a chest infection. Since yesterday his urine has looked like cola. Dipstick testing is strongly positive for blood, but microscopy shows no red cells. Which adverse drug effect is most likely?

options.A: Immune haemolysis triggered by the antibiotic
options.B: Cholestatic liver injury from the macrolide

why_correct: Clarithromycin inhibits CYP3A4, so simvastatin levels rise sharply and can cause muscle breakdown. Proximal muscle pain and weakness with dark urine that is dipstick positive for blood but has no red cells on microscopy indicates myoglobinuria. Creatine kinase should be checked urgently, the statin stopped and intravenous fluids given to protect the kidneys.
why_wrong: A. Haemolysis gives dark urine but not muscle pain and weakness. B. Cholestasis darkens urine through bilirubin and causes jaundice and itch, not proximal myalgia. C. Interstitial nephritis causes rising creatinine, often with rash and fever, without primary muscle symptoms. D. Demyelinating neuropathy causes ascending weakness and areflexia, without myalgia or pigmented urine.
pearl: Simvastatin and atorvastatin are metabolised by CYP3A4, so the BNF advises stopping simvastatin temporarily while clarithromycin or erythromycin is given.
thinking: Long-term simvastatin ↓ New CYP3A4 inhibitor (clarithromycin) ↓ Proximal myalgia and weakness ↓ Cola urine, dipstick blood but no red cells = myoglobin ↓ Statin-induced rhabdomyolysis
exam_trap: A, Immune haemolysis — dark urine after a new antibiotic suggests haemolysis, but haemolysis does not explain proximal muscle pain and weakness.
takeaway: Muscle pain with dipstick-positive urine but no red cells in a patient on a statin plus an interacting drug suggests rhabdomyolysis.

stem: At a community pharmacy, a 63-year-old woman asks to buy naproxen for a flare of lower back pain. On questioning she says she was treated for a bleeding duodenal ulcer two years ago. The pharmacist advises against it and suggests she speaks to her GP. What is the main reason for this advice?
correct_answer: C. Recurrent ulceration with gastrointestinal bleeding
why_correct: NSAIDs block cyclo-oxygenase and reduce the prostaglandins that protect the stomach and duodenal lining. A previous ulcer, especially one that bled, is one of the strongest risk factors for NSAID-related ulceration and bleeding. NICE CKS advises avoiding NSAIDs in people with a history of peptic ulcer, or using gastroprotection and specialist advice if one cannot be avoided.
why_wrong: A. Gum overgrowth is linked to phenytoin, ciclosporin and calcium channel blockers, not NSAIDs. B. NSAIDs do not usually cause hypoglycaemia. D. Hearing loss is a feature of aminoglycosides and loop diuretics, not standard NSAID doses. E. NSAIDs do not affect thyroid function.
pearl: The highest risk of NSAID-related gastrointestinal bleeding is in people over 65, people with previous ulcer or bleeding, and people also taking anticoagulants, antiplatelets, SSRIs or corticosteroids.
thinking: Request for an over-the-counter NSAID ↓ Past bleeding duodenal ulcer ↓ NSAIDs reduce protective mucosal prostaglandins ↓ High risk of recurrent ulcer and bleeding ↓ Advise avoidance and a GP review
exam_trap: D, Sensorineural hearing loss — ototoxicity is a known drug adverse effect so it sounds credible, but it belongs to aminoglycosides and high-dose loop diuretics, not naproxen.
takeaway: A previous peptic ulcer, especially one that bled, is a strong reason to avoid NSAIDs because of the risk of further ulceration and bleeding.

presentation: NSAID avoidance in gout with prior ulcer
stem: A 52-year-old painter and decorator attends his GP surgery with a hot, swollen first toe joint typical of acute gout. Three years ago endoscopy showed a gastric ulcer, which healed after Helicobacter pylori eradication. The GP prescribes colchicine rather than an anti-inflammatory such as naproxen. Which adverse effect of naproxen is the GP mainly trying to avoid?
correct_answer: E. Recurrent peptic ulceration and bleeding
why_correct: NSAIDs inhibit COX-1 in the gastric mucosa, reducing prostaglandin-mediated mucus, bicarbonate and blood flow. In a man with a previous gastric ulcer this greatly increases the risk of further ulceration and gastrointestinal bleeding. NICE recommends colchicine as an alternative first-line option for acute gout when an NSAID is unsuitable.
why_wrong: A. Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus is a classic adverse effect of lithium. B. Posterior subcapsular cataract is linked to long-term corticosteroids. C. Parkinsonism is caused by dopamine antagonists such as antipsychotics and metoclopramide. D. Hypothyroidism is linked to lithium and amiodarone, not NSAIDs.
pearl: If an NSAID must be used in someone at raised gastrointestinal risk, NICE advises co-prescribing a proton pump inhibitor at the lowest effective NSAID dose for the shortest time.
thinking: Acute gout needing anti-inflammatory treatment ↓ History of gastric ulcer ↓ NSAIDs reduce COX-1 mucosal protection ↓ Risk of recurrent ulceration and bleeding ↓ Choose colchicine instead
exam_trap: B, Posterior subcapsular cataract — it is linked to the other common gout treatment, corticosteroids, which makes it tempting, but it is not an NSAID effect.
takeaway: NSAIDs are best avoided in anyone with a previous peptic ulcer because they increase the risk of recurrent ulceration and bleeding.

presentation: Digoxin accumulation in acute kidney injury
stem: An 86-year-old woman living in a care home has taken digoxin for atrial fibrillation for many years. After a week of diarrhoea, her blood tests show that her creatinine has roughly doubled from baseline. Her GP reviews her medicines during a visit. What is the main concern about continuing her usual digoxin dose?

options.A: Faster clearance leading to loss of rate control
options.B: Reduced absorption from the gut making the drug ineffective
options.C: A higher chance of an allergic reaction
options.D: Accumulation of the drug with a risk of toxicity
options.E: No concern, because digoxin is cleared mainly by the liver

correct_answer: D. Accumulation of the drug with a risk of toxicity
why_correct: Digoxin has a narrow therapeutic index and is excreted mainly unchanged by the kidneys. When renal function falls, as in this acute kidney injury caused by dehydration, digoxin accumulates and toxicity such as nausea, confusion, visual disturbance, bradycardia and arrhythmias can occur. The dose should be withheld or reduced and a level and potassium checked.
why_wrong: A. Reduced kidney function slows clearance rather than speeding it up. B. Renal impairment does not stop oral absorption. C. Kidney injury does not increase allergy risk. E. Digoxin is cleared mainly by the kidneys, so renal decline matters a great deal.
pearl: Hypokalaemia, often from diarrhoea or diuretics, increases the risk of digoxin toxicity even when the plasma level is within the usual range.
thinking: Digoxin = narrow therapeutic index ↓ Mainly renally excreted ↓ Acute kidney injury from fluid loss ↓ Reduced clearance and rising levels ↓ Risk of toxicity, so review the dose
exam_trap: A, Faster clearance — it sounds reasonable that a sick patient loses control of her heart rate, but a falling glomerular filtration rate slows digoxin elimination.
takeaway: When kidney function falls, renally cleared narrow therapeutic index drugs accumulate and can quickly become toxic.

stem: A 41-year-old woman with bipolar disorder is started on lithium by her community mental health team. She asks why she needs repeated blood tests when a friend taking sertraline has none. Which property of lithium best explains the need for monitoring?

options.A: Small changes in plasma concentration can cause toxicity or loss of effect
options.B: There is a wide margin between the effective and the toxic level
options.C: Its effect does not depend on the plasma concentration
options.E: Its dose never needs changing for kidney function

correct_answer: A. Small changes in plasma concentration can cause toxicity or loss of effect
why_correct: Lithium has a narrow therapeutic index, so the concentration that controls mood is close to the concentration that causes toxicity. Dehydration, intercurrent illness or interacting drugs such as NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and diuretics can push levels into the toxic range, while a small fall can lead to relapse. Regular serum levels with renal and thyroid tests are therefore needed.
why_wrong: B. A wide margin describes a wide therapeutic index, which would not need close monitoring. C. Lithium effect and toxicity are closely related to plasma concentration. D. Allergy is not the reason for level monitoring. E. Lithium is renally excreted, so kidney function strongly affects dosing.
pearl: Lithium levels are taken 12 hours after the last dose, and the person should carry a lithium record book and know the early signs of toxicity such as coarse tremor, diarrhoea and vomiting.
thinking: Patient asks why lithium needs blood tests ↓ Therapeutic and toxic levels lie close together ↓ Small concentration changes alter effect ↓ Toxicity or relapse possible ↓ Narrow therapeutic index explains monitoring
exam_trap: B, A wide margin between effective and toxic level — the wording sounds technical and familiar, but it describes the opposite of a narrow therapeutic index.
takeaway: Narrow therapeutic index drugs such as lithium need monitoring because small concentration changes can cause toxicity or loss of effect.

stem: On the orthopaedic ward, a 67-year-old man is three days into his recovery from a hip replacement. He has been taking regular oral morphine for pain and has not opened his bowels since surgery. His abdomen is soft and bowel sounds are present. Which mechanism best explains his constipation?

options.C: Reduced gut motility through mu-opioid receptors in the bowel wall
options.E: Increased fluid secretion into the bowel lumen

correct_answer: C. Reduced gut motility through mu-opioid receptors in the bowel wall
why_correct: Morphine acts on mu-opioid receptors in the enteric nervous system, reducing propulsive peristalsis and increasing segmental contractions. Slower transit allows more water to be absorbed from the stool and intestinal secretion falls, so stools become hard and infrequent. This is a predictable pharmacological effect, which is why a laxative should be prescribed alongside regular opioids.
why_wrong: A. Opioids reduce effective propulsive peristalsis rather than increasing it. B. Opioids delay gastric emptying. D. Bile secretion is not the mechanism of opioid constipation. E. Opioids reduce intestinal secretion, which further dries the stool.
pearl: Tolerance develops to opioid nausea and sedation but hardly at all to constipation, so laxatives are needed for as long as the opioid continues.
thinking: Regular morphine after surgery ↓ No bowel opening, soft abdomen, bowel sounds present ↓ Mu receptors in the bowel wall ↓ Less propulsive motility and less secretion ↓ Hard, infrequent stool
exam_trap: E, Increased fluid secretion into the bowel lumen — it sounds physiological, but more secretion would cause loose stool; opioids actually reduce secretion.
takeaway: Opioids cause constipation by slowing gut motility and reducing intestinal secretion through enteric mu receptors.

stem: A 26-year-old woman who carries a diagnosis of acute intermittent porphyria books a GP appointment to discuss starting some new treatments. She has had two attacks in the past, one of which needed admission. When choosing any medicine for her, which group must generally be avoided because it can trigger an attack?

options.C: Medicines that induce hepatic haem synthesis

correct_answer: C. Medicines that induce hepatic haem synthesis
why_correct: Acute porphyrias are disorders of haem synthesis. Drugs that induce hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes increase demand for haem, which up-regulates the first enzyme in the pathway and leads to build-up of toxic precursors. Examples include some anticonvulsants, barbiturates, sulfonamides and some hormonal treatments, so each new medicine should be checked against a porphyria drug safety database.
why_wrong: A. Emollients are not porphyrinogenic. B. Oral rehydration salts are safe. D. Calcium carbonate does not precipitate attacks. E. Glucose actually suppresses haem synthesis and is used in the treatment of mild attacks.
pearl: Severe acute porphyria attacks are treated with intravenous haem arginate, along with removal of triggers and safe analgesia such as opioids.
thinking: Known acute intermittent porphyria ↓ Attacks triggered by increased haem demand ↓ Enzyme-inducing drugs raise demand ↓ These are porphyrinogenic ↓ Check every new drug for porphyria safety
exam_trap: E, Intravenous glucose — a drip in a sick patient sounds risky, but carbohydrate loading suppresses the haem pathway and is part of treatment.
takeaway: In acute porphyria, avoid porphyrinogenic drugs, which are mainly those that induce hepatic haem synthesis.

presentation: Correcting a prescribing error before administration
stem: Late in a night shift on the children's ward, a junior doctor realises that the intravenous gentamicin he prescribed for a 4-year-old boy was calculated using the wrong weight. The nurse has not yet drawn up the dose. What should he do?

options.A: Wait for the consultant ward round in the morning
options.B: Leave the prescription as it is, since no harm has occurred
options.C: Correct the prescription at once and tell the nurse caring for the child
options.D: Cross out the prescription without leaving any note
options.E: Ask the parents which dose they would prefer

correct_answer: C. Correct the prescription at once and tell the nurse caring for the child
why_correct: A prescribing error found before administration should be corrected straight away so the wrong dose is never given. The doctor should amend the prescription clearly, tell the nurse responsible, document the change and consider reporting it as a near miss through the local incident system. This is in line with GMC guidance on openness and learning from errors.
why_wrong: A. Waiting allows the incorrect dose to be given in the meantime. B. The error remains on the chart and could still cause harm. D. Crossing out without explanation is unclear and unsafe. E. Parents should not be asked to choose a dose, which is the prescriber's responsibility.
pearl: Near misses should still be reported through the local incident system because they reveal system weaknesses before harm occurs.
thinking: Error found before administration ↓ Wrong weight used for a child's dose ↓ Correct it immediately ↓ Tell the nurse and document ↓ Report as a near miss
exam_trap: B, Leave it because no harm has occurred — no harm has happened yet, but the wrong dose is still on the chart waiting to be given.
takeaway: Correct a prescribing error immediately and clearly as soon as it is noticed, even if no harm has occurred yet.

stem: A 61-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and heart failure asks her community pharmacist for thrush treatment for the third time in four months, describing vulval itching and a thick white discharge. Earlier this year, the cardiology team added dapagliflozin to her medicines. Which adverse effect of this drug class is most likely responsible?
why_correct: SGLT2 inhibitors such as dapagliflozin block glucose reabsorption in the proximal tubule, producing glycosuria. The glucose-rich urine encourages Candida growth in the genital area, so recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis is one of the most common adverse effects. Good genital hygiene and prompt treatment usually allow the drug to be continued.
why_wrong: A. Pulmonary fibrosis is linked with drugs such as amiodarone and nitrofurantoin, not SGLT2 inhibitors. C. Parkinsonism is caused by dopamine antagonists, not SGLT2 inhibitors. D. Neutropenia is not a class effect of SGLT2 inhibitors. E. Hearing loss is associated with aminoglycosides and loop diuretics, not SGLT2 inhibitors.
pearl: SGLT2 inhibitors are also associated with Fournier's gangrene, a rare but serious necrotising infection of the perineum that needs urgent treatment.
thinking: Recurrent vulvovaginal thrush ↓ Recently started dapagliflozin ↓ SGLT2 inhibitors cause glycosuria ↓ Glucose-rich urine favours Candida ↓ Genital candidiasis
exam_trap: D, Neutropenia — recurrent infection makes an immune problem seem likely, but the cause here is local glycosuria, not a fall in white cells.
takeaway: SGLT2 inhibitors cause glycosuria and commonly lead to genital fungal infections.

stem: Six months after spironolactone was added for resistant hypertension, a 58-year-old man tells his GP that he is embarrassed by tender swelling beneath both nipples. Examination confirms soft, rubbery glandular tissue under each areola. Which adverse effect of the new medicine is the most likely explanation?
why_correct: Spironolactone has anti-androgenic effects: it blocks androgen receptors and alters the balance of oestrogen and testosterone. This commonly causes painful enlargement of male breast tissue, which is dose-related and usually reversible on stopping. Eplerenone, a more selective mineralocorticoid antagonist, is much less likely to cause it.
why_wrong: A. Spironolactone is potassium-sparing and causes hyperkalaemia, not hypokalaemia. C. Pulmonary fibrosis is linked with amiodarone, methotrexate and nitrofurantoin. D. Peptic ulceration is associated with NSAIDs and corticosteroids. E. Osteoporosis is associated with long-term corticosteroids, not spironolactone.
pearl: When spironolactone causes gynaecomastia in a patient who still needs a mineralocorticoid antagonist, eplerenone is a suitable alternative.
thinking: Man recently started on spironolactone ↓ Tender swelling beneath both nipples ↓ Glandular breast tissue on examination ↓ Spironolactone is anti-androgenic ↓ Gynaecomastia
exam_trap: A, Hypokalaemia — electrolyte disturbance is the best-known spironolactone problem, but it causes high potassium, and potassium changes do not cause breast enlargement.
takeaway: Spironolactone's anti-androgenic action commonly causes gynaecomastia; eplerenone is an alternative.

stem: Eight weeks after starting high-intensity atorvastatin following a heart attack, a 66-year-old man tells the cardiac rehabilitation nurse that his thighs and calves ache even at rest and that climbing stairs has become harder. He has started no other new medicines. What is the most likely cause?

options.E: Intermittent claudication from peripheral arterial disease

why_correct: Muscle aches and weakness that begin weeks after starting a statin, particularly at high intensity, are typical of statin-associated muscle symptoms. He should have a creatine kinase checked and be assessed for severity, and thyroid function should be checked because hypothyroidism increases the risk. Depending on the findings, the statin may be paused, reduced or changed, rather than stopped for good.
why_wrong: B. Polymyalgia rheumatica causes shoulder and hip girdle stiffness, worse in the morning, without true weakness. C. He is not taking corticosteroids. D. Thyrotoxic myopathy has no supporting features and is not a drug effect. E. Claudication occurs on walking and eases with rest, whereas his aches occur at rest.
pearl: Muscle pain with a creatine kinase more than ten times the upper limit of normal, or dark urine, suggests rhabdomyolysis and the statin should be stopped immediately.
thinking: Recently started high-intensity statin ↓ Aching thigh and calf muscles at rest ↓ Difficulty climbing stairs ↓ No other new drugs ↓ Statin-associated myopathy
exam_trap: B, Polymyalgia rheumatica — it is common at this age and causes girdle aches, but it causes morning stiffness rather than weakness and does not follow starting a new drug.
takeaway: New muscle pain or weakness after starting a statin should prompt assessment for statin-associated myopathy.

stem: A 59-year-old man who drives a heavy goods vehicle for a living has type 2 diabetes that remains above target on metformin alone. At his practice nurse appointment it is agreed to add gliclazide. He asks what he most needs to know about the new tablet, particularly in relation to his job. Which adverse effect is the most important to counsel him about?
why_correct: Gliclazide is a sulfonylurea that stimulates insulin release from pancreatic beta cells regardless of the blood glucose level, so it can cause hypoglycaemia. For a group 2 (lorry) driver this has important safety and licensing implications: he must monitor his glucose, know how to recognise and treat a hypo, and follow DVLA requirements. This makes hypoglycaemia the priority counselling point.
why_wrong: A. Genital thrush is characteristic of SGLT2 inhibitors. B. Lactic acidosis is a rare concern with metformin, not sulfonylureas. C. Pancreatitis is linked to GLP-1 receptor agonists and DPP-4 inhibitors. D. Weight gain does occur with sulfonylureas, but it is far less dangerous than hypoglycaemia, especially for a professional driver.
pearl: Drivers on sulfonylureas or insulin should check their glucose before driving and at intervals on long journeys, and must not drive if it is low.
thinking: Adding gliclazide ↓ Sulfonylurea increases insulin secretion independent of glucose ↓ Main risk is hypoglycaemia ↓ Professional driver raises the stakes ↓ Counsel on hypos, glucose checks and DVLA rules
exam_trap: D, Weight gain — it is a genuine sulfonylurea effect, which makes it tempting, but it is not the most important safety issue.
takeaway: Hypoglycaemia is the key adverse effect to discuss when starting a sulfonylurea.

stem: A 69-year-old woman is started on indapamide for hypertension by her GP. Six weeks later she telephones the surgery because she woke in the night with a hot, red, exquisitely tender big toe and cannot bear even the bedsheet touching it. She has never had anything like this before. Which effect of her new medicine is most likely to have contributed?
why_correct: Indapamide is a thiazide-like diuretic, and this class reduces renal excretion of urate by competing for tubular secretion and by causing volume contraction. The resulting rise in serum urate can precipitate a first attack of gout, classically in the first metatarsophalangeal joint, as here. Her antihypertensive choice should be reviewed once the acute attack is treated.
why_wrong: A. Thiazides cause low, not high, potassium. B. Vitamin B12 deficiency is linked to metformin and proton pump inhibitors, not thiazides. D. Thiazides reduce urinary calcium loss and tend to raise serum calcium. E. Hyperbilirubinaemia does not explain an acute monoarthritis.
pearl: Thiazide and loop diuretics both raise serum urate, whereas losartan has a mild uricosuric effect.
thinking: New thiazide-like diuretic ↓ Acute hot swollen first MTP joint ↓ Picture of acute gout ↓ Thiazides reduce urate excretion ↓ Hyperuricaemia is the link
exam_trap: D, Hypocalcaemia — electrolyte disturbance is a familiar diuretic side effect, but thiazides tend to cause hypercalcaemia and calcium has no role in gout.
takeaway: Thiazide and thiazide-like diuretics can precipitate gout by raising serum urate.

stem: A 66-year-old man with atrial fibrillation has taken warfarin for many years with a stable INR. At a hospital rheumatology clinic he is started on a new tablet for his inflammatory arthritis, and nobody informs his GP or the anticoagulation service. The anticoagulation nurse learns about it when he mentions it at his next visit. Why is it important that new medicines are flagged for patients on warfarin?

options.A: Many medicines can raise or lower the INR, increasing the risk of bleeding or thrombosis
options.B: Warfarin only interacts with antibiotics and antifungals
options.C: Once the INR is stable, warfarin's effect cannot be altered
options.D: Warfarin interactions are rarely of clinical significance
options.E: INR checks are only needed if he has a bleed

correct_answer: A. Many medicines can raise or lower the INR, increasing the risk of bleeding or thrombosis
why_correct: Warfarin has a narrow therapeutic index and is metabolised mainly by hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes, so many drugs can either potentiate or reduce its effect. A raised INR increases the risk of bleeding, while a lowered INR exposes him to stroke from his atrial fibrillation. Any new medicine should prompt an interaction check and, where needed, closer INR monitoring.
why_wrong: B. Interactions extend well beyond anti-infectives, including antiepileptics, amiodarone, NSAIDs and some herbal products. C. A stable INR can change quickly when an interacting drug is introduced. D. Many warfarin interactions are serious and well documented. E. Waiting for a bleed misses both over- and under-anticoagulation.
pearl: Herbal remedies such as St John's wort can lower the INR, and patients should be asked specifically about over-the-counter products.
thinking: Long-term warfarin, stable INR ↓ New drug started elsewhere ↓ Warfarin has many interactions ↓ INR may rise or fall ↓ Risk of bleeding or thrombosis
exam_trap: C, A stable INR cannot be altered — years of stability are reassuring, but any interacting drug can change it within days.
takeaway: New medicines in a patient on warfarin can shift the INR in either direction, so they must be flagged and checked.

stem: A 58-year-old woman who takes warfarin after two unprovoked pulmonary emboli is seen in a psychiatry outpatient clinic. The psychiatrist plans to start carbamazepine as a mood stabiliser for her bipolar disorder but is worried that it may affect her anticoagulation. What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.A: Start it without further action, as most interactions are minor
options.B: Check the interaction in the BNF and plan closer INR monitoring with dose adjustment if needed
options.C: Halve her warfarin dose in advance without checking the INR
options.D: Start it and check the INR at her next routine anticoagulation appointment
options.E: Stop warfarin for the whole time she takes carbamazepine

correct_answer: B. Check the interaction in the BNF and plan closer INR monitoring with dose adjustment if needed
why_correct: Carbamazepine induces hepatic enzymes and can substantially lower the INR, which would expose her to recurrent thromboembolism. The right approach is to check the specific interaction, inform her anticoagulation service and arrange more frequent INR checks with warfarin dose adjustment, or to consider an alternative drug. This balances the need for psychiatric treatment against the risk to her anticoagulation.
why_wrong: A. Many warfarin interactions are clinically important, and this one can significantly reduce anticoagulation. C. Halving the dose blindly would be the wrong direction for an enzyme inducer and is unsafe without monitoring. D. A routine appointment may be too late to detect a change in INR. E. Stopping warfarin would leave her at high risk of further pulmonary emboli.
pearl: Enzyme inducers such as carbamazepine, phenytoin and rifampicin lower the INR, whereas enzyme inhibitors such as clarithromycin and fluconazole raise it.
thinking: Warfarin for recurrent pulmonary emboli ↓ New drug proposed ↓ Possible interaction ↓ Check the specific interaction ↓ Plan INR checks and dose changes
exam_trap: C, Pre-emptively halving the dose — it seems cautious, but without checking the interaction it can be exactly wrong, as here where the INR is likely to fall.
takeaway: When a new drug may interact with warfarin, check the interaction and plan INR monitoring and dose adjustment.

stem: An 83-year-old man who lives in a care home takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation. He needs an antibiotic, and the visiting GP is weighing up several possible choices. Before prescribing, she checks which option is most likely to cause a marked rise in his INR. Which antibiotic carries the greatest risk?
why_correct: Clarithromycin is a macrolide that inhibits the cytochrome P450 enzymes which metabolise warfarin, so it can cause a substantial and rapid rise in the INR with a risk of bleeding. If it must be used, the INR should be checked within a few days and the warfarin dose adjusted. Other antibiotics such as metronidazole, ciprofloxacin and co-trimoxazole also potentiate warfarin.
why_wrong: A. Nitrofurantoin is not known to cause a clinically important rise in INR. C. Phenoxymethylpenicillin has little effect on warfarin metabolism. D. Topical fusidic acid has negligible systemic absorption. E. Flucloxacillin, if anything, may slightly reduce the anticoagulant effect rather than markedly raise the INR.
pearl: Any antibiotic can alter the INR indirectly through illness and changes in gut flora and diet, so INR monitoring is sensible whenever a course is started.
thinking: Warfarin plus a new antibiotic ↓ Which raises INR most ↓ Macrolides inhibit warfarin metabolism ↓ Clarithromycin is a strong enzyme inhibitor ↓ Greatest INR rise
exam_trap: E, Flucloxacillin — it is a commonly prescribed systemic antibiotic, so it seems a likely culprit, but it does not inhibit warfarin metabolism.
takeaway: Clarithromycin can markedly increase the INR in patients on warfarin.
